T. Lucretius Carus
On
The Nature of Things
Six Books

IAMBIC DIMETER
CATALECTIC

The red gulf's pearls,    Agenor's dark gems,
Silver shells,    Granddaughters, of no delay,
And a myrrh-worked vessel,    Likenesses more lovely,
Or a bronze piece from Corinth,    Known, in their small detail,
Or figures carved against the sky,    Have carried off their wealth,
Vivid in the colors    By which recently recast
Of a practiced art's forms,    The books of Lucretius, dear to you,
Are given as a gift to you,    Dear ones to become yours,
Thomas, upon whom with a serene    Of a finer polishing
Face Fortune has smiled,    Of a long-smoothed file.
Those who with flowing purple    These, graspable in the hand,
Sweep through homes and with gold    Bringing to you the leisure
Drink, from ivory chairs,    Of a more honorable care,
And trample in their beds    The nature of things that is their parent,
The Muses, seeing me poor    And the elements of the vast world
In resources, chaste,    That contain all things,
Woven through with little books,    Compressed into a small volume,
And singing to the lyre,    You will marvel at beholding.
On pure salt crystals    Perhaps not unskillfully
And garden herbs unbought    The deed of a most rare client
To sustain life day by day.    You will carry to the stars.
But lest, empty-handed,    He who thought he had given
You frequent the sacred hearths    Nothing to the Muses, not even a trifle,
Of the Muses and Apollo    With this his little gift
Without contribution,    Has left nothing behind for the rest.

Petrus Candidus to Thomas Sotherinus, greetings.

It is recorded in tradition that Empedocles of Agrigentum, by far the most famous of all the Pythagoreans, who had afterward visited most of the cities of Greece wearing Delphic crowns and golden garlands, cast himself into the craters of Etna — so that, with his body removed from sight without any witnesses, he might acquire a reputation for divinity — and that he left to his Greek posterity a most brilliant poem on the nature of things. Not many ages later in Latium, T. Lucretius Carus emulated him, having encompassed the doctrine of Epicurus with the rich light of verse. When I found, most distinguished Thoma Sotherinus, that this most elegant of poets had been, through the fault of those who — either wholly ignorant of philosophy or unacquainted with humane letters — had stumbled upon the reading of him, and had each distorted what they had poorly grasped according to their own understanding, so defiled with festering sores, so riddled with ulcers, so foully (if I may say so) disfigured with monstrous corruptions — since copies conceived from all manner of sources, wretchedly mangled in various ways, utterly inconsistent with one another, were being passed about — I judged it would be a service worth performing, urged on as I was by men of the highest and likewise most profound learning, and earnestly pressed by them to undertake this task, if, by collating the ancient manuscripts which we have acquired here in our city — that nurse of all the best arts and disciplines, ever since their foundations were laid — along with copies of the most eminent [scholars of the age...

of our own poets Pontanus and Marullus, who recklessly applied obeli to expunge passages — rather than, as has been done by most people, covering over with a superficial remedy those festering sores that flow so foully in an elegant poet — I determined to cut them out to the very quick, root and branch, and to utterly destroy those monstrous things of that sort which had for so long and so wretchedly mangled what was dear to us. Especially since it is the duty of those of good and noble character, through whom one has made some progress in attaining learning, to defend them by every means possible, insofar as it is lawful, from injury. Marullus was indeed a friend of ours of old, most delightful, whose critical judgment in this work we have chiefly followed; he was so devoted to the Lucretian charm throughout his whole life that he scarcely went anywhere without him as his companion, and never retired to bed (as is told of Archesilaus and Homer's rhapsodist) without having read through some portion of and carefully examined the poems of Lucretius. Indeed, from that pitiful loss of the Latin Muses in the very waves of the Cecina, with its signal disaster, Lucretius alone was recovered. But in order that we may honor the memory of so illustrious and so rare a friend with some lasting monument, there will be issued from us, printed in these same types, besides the books of epigrams and natural hymns which are commonly found in hand, first a volume from four (for so many was he bringing forth) in the same heroic verse on the subject of a prince, and also laments, and certain epigrams not yet published. Now regarding the poem of Lucretius, as far as the very practice of writing is concerned, we have always judged that noble maxim of Favorinus worthy of preservation above all: that as one must live according to the customs of the ancients, so one must speak according to the words of the present. For in what manner can anyone read in so...

so polished, so refined a poet in every respect, words like "frondes," "acherunta," "volgus," and "volnera" — though I would not in truth deny that this was the customary way of expressing things in that age. Yet most of these forms were afterward rejected by the younger generation as having been produced in the manner of rustics. For instance: "Nullast," "Haudquaquast," and likewise "Speculust," "Animaist," and countless others of that kind — who would not see that these forms, when put in the mouths of actors on stage, befit them more fittingly and without any dispute? For this reason, forms such as these, restored to exactness, are found throughout the twenty Varronian comedies of Accius and Plautus, which will soon come forth from our workshop into public circulation by means of handbooks of this kind, far more polished indeed than those now held in hand. This purer manner of writing in Caro, with ears washed in biting vinegar — and above all Marullus, whose judgment in literature is exceedingly keen, and whose quickness of mind (κὲυ τὸ τῆς γνώμης ἀγχίνουν) I have never regarded without the highest admiration — has long since been approved against the opposition of all litigious disputants. But if anyone shall nonetheless wish to preserve these old forms from antiquity, along with other things likewise that create a vast and particularly dark forest, they must be left aside; for it will result that the poet, regarded by all as most charming, will continuously lose his genuine luster. And so, accepting a very few forms from the usage of later and most eminent writers, we shall leave the rest without any ill will to those who, being themselves worn out and rancid, admire with excessive ambition the mere dregs of language. And we shall not reluctantly make repeated use of that saying of Caecilius: "I want neither flowers nor floces — I want my wine." Yet Lucretius tends to seem somewhat rough and harsh in his diction to some, for whom our...

his opinion is sufficient, and moreover, beyond that, the age that followed him struggled greatly with a somewhat softer style. The poet himself skillfully defends his own position when he says:
Nor does it escape my mind that the obscure discoveries of the Greeks
Are difficult to illuminate in Latin verse,
Especially when much must be treated in new words,
On account of the poverty of the language and the novelty of the subject matter.
And indeed Manilius sang most elegantly thus:
The subject itself, content to be taught, refuses to be adorned.
And if any terms are cited from a foreign tongue,
This will not be the work of a poet. Not all words can be inflected,
And proper terms are better noted under their own name.
Nevertheless, throughout all his poetry, in that genre of writing, such is Lucretius's elegance, such his brilliance, such his majesty, that nothing seems to have been worked out by lamplight that is not worthy of comparison with Aristophanes and even Cleanthes himself. In whose work it is to be thought that not bees upon his lips, as is said of Plato, nor a nightingale, as is reported of Stesichorus, but the very Graces and Muses themselves held their seat. Concerning which, and likewise that saying which, by the testimony of all the most learned men, can no less truly be pronounced of him than that which was said of Euripides by that Aetolian: "Whatever else one might write, his verses have achieved the sweetness of honey." Nor indeed should we pass over what is written in the books on the Latin language by M. Varro: that Lucretius used the opening of one and twenty of his books — "to seek the life-giving season of sky and earth." Yet nonetheless I would wish all young people warned by me of this matter no less earnestly: that Lucretius is not to be approached by them

those who are imbued with pure and true philosophical principles, who furthermore wish to penetrate more deeply into the very storehouse of nature — these men I, with great enthusiasm and without any hesitation, refer wholeheartedly to Aristotle of Stagira and to the divine Plato, those two lights of all wisdom, where they may harvest the fruits of the highest disciplines more purely, more abundantly, and more sacredly — these I dismiss from other guides. But to those who wish to learn in what manner, and by what poetic forms, figures, or meters, the doctrines of philosophy are contained in Carus (Lucretius), I urge them straightaway to turn directly to him. For, if truth be told, I do not find among the ancients anyone to place before Lucretius for this purpose. Our present work, which we have undertaken in emending this noble poet under your patronage, most splendid Thomas, and which is dedicated to your incomparable virtue, will henceforth become better known to all students of the liberal arts through you. And not only in poetry and oratory, in which you excel so greatly, but also in all other disciplines — you, whose house has always stood open most generously to the best and most learned of all, whose hereditary and eminent wisdom, and the gift of God himself, supreme and greatest, has raised your uncle's glory to the highest peak — so that, like two brightest stars shining over Italy in this age, all lovers of humane letters will forever confess themselves indebted to you. And for me, toward whom your remarkable merits, and those especially of your most Reverend uncle, are so outstanding, nothing could happen more welcome than to learn that, through the keen and great judgment of you both, our work of emendation on Lucretius has been found satisfactory. Farewell, and good fortune to you.

THE LIFE OF LUCRETIUS

Titus Lucretius Carus, from the family of the Lucretii, which was distinguished and considered ancient at Rome, is believed to have been born somewhat earlier than Terentius Varro and Marcus Tullius, a fact carefully noted by some. For in those annals which we have received from the Greeks, many things are set down falsely and contrary to the reckoning of dates. He is said to have been of the highest genius, particularly aroused in the writing of verse. He was accustomed, at intervals of time, not without a certain frenzy of mind — as the ancient writers report — to turn to poetry. From this arose that famous line of Papinius: "And the lofty frenzy of learned Lucretius." Quintilian, when he discusses the Latin poets, testifies that Aemilius Macer and Titinius yield to Lucretius in elegance. Yet he also says that Lucretius's verse retains no small degree of difficulty — which arose for him not only from the subject matter itself, which by its very nature tends to seem rather obscure, but also, as he himself says, from the poverty of the Latin language and the novelty of the topics. He wrote six books on the nature of things, in which he followed the doctrine of Epicurus and likewise Empedocles, whose verse and genius he especially admired. Nor were there lacking those who maintained that Lucretius's work had been corrected and edited by Cicero. And indeed this seems quite plausible, since on account of his untimely death it was left by him incomplete and in need of correction. His brother Quintus conceded a great deal to the verses of Carus, and reports that his poem contains much of either art or genius. Nor indeed ought one to be surprised,

If the Lucretian verses sometimes seem rather rough and similar to prose, this was a characteristic peculiarity of that age, as is attested by Furius Albinus in Macrobius, when he says: No one should think the ancient poets inferior on the grounds that their verses seem rough to us. For that style was particularly pleasing at the time, and the age that followed labored long to accommodate itself more to the smoother manner. And so it is no surprise that those who lived under the Vespasians did not lack for readers who preferred Lucretius to Virgil, and Lucilius to Horace. Lucretius dedicated his work to C. Memmius, son of L. Memmius, who after conquering Achaia took that surname, sacked the city of Corinth, and stripped it of its statues and paintings. Not that there are lacking those who have held a very different opinion. But these people, having given insufficient consideration to the historical circumstances, can easily be refuted by anyone. Indeed, Publius Virgil not only took a number of phrases from the poem of Lucretius, but also transferred from him whole passages nearly intact, as the ancient grammarians have recorded. Concerning his poetry, there is that judgment of Ovid, committed to literary monuments with great praise: "The verses of sublime Lucretius shall perish only on the day that shall bring destruction to the earth." Lucretius died in the prime of life, when he had completed only a few years beyond forty. Eusebius indeed reports that, having been driven mad by a love potion, he killed himself by his own hand on the very day that Virgil assumed the toga of manhood, when Gnaeus Pompeius and Marcus Licinius Crassus were consuls for the second time. Moreover, besides other ancient authorities, as is recorded by Fulgentius in his commentary on archaic words, Lucretius is counted among the comic poets.

QUINTILIAN:
For Macer and Lucretius are to be read,
but not so that they form the style, that is, so that they make the body of eloquence —
each elegant in his own subject matter.
But one is plain,
the other difficult.

THE SAME (QUINTILIAN):
Grammar cannot be ignorant of philosophy, since in almost all poems there are very many passages drawn from the deep subtlety of questions about nature,
and moreover because of Empedocles among the Greeks, and Varro and Lucretius among the Latins, who handed down the precepts of wisdom in verse.

VARRO:
From whose bipartite division Lucretius took the beginning of his single work of twenty books, namely this line:
To seek the generative time of heaven and earth.

WHAT IS CONTAINED IN EACH BOOK

BOOK ONE.

Praise of discoverers. An example of religion. The end of pain. On the soul. That nothing is born from nothing. That nothing passes into nothing. On bodies that cannot be seen. On wind, smell, heat, cold, and sound. That clothes become wet and dry out. That a ring, like other things, is worn away by use. On the void. How fish swim. That body and void are the nature of things. That a third nature besides body and void does not exist. On time. That the solid exists. That all things are consumed. On soft nature, like water. Against Heraclitus. Against Empedocles. Against Anaxagoras. On the limits of solid bodies. The extension of time.

BOOK TWO.

On the motion of first principles, and that they are infinite. What appears in the rays of the sun. That no particles travel upward, but bodies pressed from their roots rise up. On the swerve of motion. On the shapes of atoms. On oil, honey, and wormwood. On the screeching of a saw. On diamond, iron, flint, and bronze. On salty sweat and sea water. That there are many shapes. That seeds exist in the earth. On the Great Mother. Every...

That the nature of the gods exists of itself. That white things do not necessarily arise from white principles. That colors do not exist. On the color of doves. On the tail of the peacock. That from what is without sensation, sensation is born. That the infinite extends in all directions. The universe is infinite. That a world is born and many similar ones. That the world is already old, and all small things are born.

BOOK THREE.

That men fear death above all else. On greed. On the nature of the mind and soul, and their senses. That the mind and soul are joined together. On the nobility of the mind. That the third soul is the intellect. The fourth soul without a name. The union of the mind and souls. On the variety of the mind. On the sensation of body and mind. Against Democritus on the mind and soul. That the body does not feel on its own without the movement of the soul. That the soul is born and mortal. That the soul and body are born together and grow together and perish together. On drunkenness. On epilepsy. On the senses of the soul and mind. That the soul is not deprived at birth. That what is counted among the things of the underworld are the vices of this life. That all die. That men desire what they do not have.

BOOK FOUR.

What he finds pleasurable, in that he reveals clear light to mortals. On images. On visual representations. Animals small and large. On clouds. On the speed of images. Why an image is seen beyond a mirror. Why things in darkness are seen from the light, but not the reverse. Why multiple images are produced. On the shadow of a person, and of other moving things. On vision. On true sensation, and how it is recognized. On false sensation. On things heard. That the voice is corporeal. On the images of voices. How vision does not pass through where the voice passes through. On taste. Why some things are contrary to others. On smell. On the motion of the mind. Why whatever one wishes is immediately thought of. That eyes, tongue, and ears were formed before their use. On the movement of limbs, that is, on walking. How sleep comes about. On dreams. On sexual matters.

BOOK FIVE.

That the discoverer of wisdom has contributed more to humanity than Ceres, Bacchus, or Hercules. That the soul is native. That the world is both native and mortal. On the course of the sun and moon. That the sea, sky, and earth are destined to perish. That the mind and soul cannot exist without the body.

That the world was not established by the gods. The division of the earth, or its beginning. What part of it is natural, and that the whole is natural. On earth, water, air, or the spirit. On fire and the sun. On the lamp and the lantern. Why natural things enter buildings. Why he calls all things natural. Why eternity is possible. On Phaethon. On the origin of the world and all things. On iron. On the size, motion, and rising of the sun and moon. On the size and heat of the sun. Democritus on the sun. On the course of the moon. The vision of the sun from Ida. On the long day and short night. On the light of the moon. On the seasons of the year. On the effect of the sun and moon. On the novelty of the world and the arrangement that exists within it. On centaurs, Scylla, the chimera, gold-bearing rivers, wondrous peoples. On the life of those who once lived on the newly formed earth. On the invention of speech. Whence fire was given to mortals. To whom dominion was granted. Whence religion arose, and fear of the gods above. How gold, silver, lead, and iron were discovered. How weapons, wars, and music were invented. On the first primitive life.

BOOK SIX.

Those who attribute the governance of the world to the gods must attribute to them the same anxieties. On thunder and lightning. That seeds of fire are present in clouds. On lightning, its nature and its forces. That lightning is born high up from denser clouds. On thunderclaps and earthquakes. That lightning and thunder occur more in autumn and spring. How clouds grow dense. On rains. On the rainbow. On the cause of earthquakes. Why the sea does not grow larger. On Etna. On the Nile. On the Avernian lake. That crows do not approach the temple of Minerva in Athens. That in Syria there is a place that instantly kills four-footed animals. Why water in wells is colder in summer. On the spring of Ammon. That a torch burns in water. That there is a freshwater spring in the sea.

On the magnet. That emanations flow from all things. Whence plague arises. On the dreadful plague of the Athenians.

BOOK SIX.

Do not be reluctant, learned reader, to read through what we have noted at the end, and likewise there to rescue from the errors of the printers, and to select the more correct readings.

Ovid:
Then shall the poems of lofty Lucretius perish,
When one day shall give the earth to destruction.

Papin:
And the fierce, soaring frenzy of learned Lucretius.

T. LUCRETIUS CARUS: ON THE NATURE OF THINGS
BOOK ONE

Mother of the descendants of Aeneas, pleasure of men and gods,
nurturing Venus, who beneath the gliding signs of heaven
fills the ship-bearing sea and the fruit-bearing lands with your presence —
through you every kind of living creature is conceived
and rises up to behold the light of the sun.
Before you, goddess, the winds flee, before you the clouds of heaven scatter;
at your coming the skillful earth sends up sweet flowers,
the seas smile, and the sky, now calm, shines with flooding light.
For as soon as the vernal face of day is revealed
and the fertile breeze of the west wind blows free and strong,
the birds of the air first proclaim you, divine one,
their hearts struck through by your power, signaling your arrival.
Then wild beasts bound across the joyful pastures
and swim swift rivers — so captured are they by your charm —
and through your allurements all the natures of living things
eagerly follow wherever you lead them on.
At last, through seas and mountains and rushing rivers,
through the leafy homes of birds and the greening plains,
striking tender love into the hearts of all,
you bring it about that through desire they propagate their kind from generation to generation.
Since you alone govern the nature of things,
and without you nothing comes forth into the bright shores of light

There arises nothing joyful or lovely,
I seek you as my companion in writing these verses,
which I endeavor to compose concerning the nature of things
for our Memmius, whom you, goddess, at every moment
have willed to excel, adorned with every excellence.
Therefore, o divine one, grant all the more an eternal charm to my words,
and bring it about that meanwhile the savage works of war
may rest and be stilled over seas and lands.
For you alone can aid mortals with tranquil peace,
since Mars, mighty in arms, who governs the savage works of war,
often casts himself into your lap, conquered by the eternal wound of love,
and thus gazing up with his smooth neck thrown back
he feeds his eager eyes, gaping with love upon you, goddess,
and his breath hangs upon your lips as he reclines.
As he lies resting upon your sacred body, bend over him
and pour from your lips sweet words,
seeking, glorious one, gentle peace for the Romans.
For neither can we, in this troubled time of our country,
attend with calm mind to our task, nor can the noble line of Memmius
be absent from the common welfare in such circumstances.
As for the rest, lend me your ears, Memmius, with mind freed from cares, and yourself
withdrawn from anxieties, apply yourself to true reason,
lest my gifts, laid out for you with faithful devotion,
you leave aside before they are understood and grasped.
For I shall begin to discourse to you on the highest order of heaven and of the gods,
and shall unfold the first beginnings of things,
from which nature creates all things, increases and nourishes them,
and into which that same nature dissolves them when they perish,
which we call matter and the generative bodies of things.

These we are accustomed to call the seeds of things,
And to apply to them these same names likewise,
The first bodies, from which all things in the beginning are made.
When human life lay foul before our eyes,
Crushed upon the earth beneath heavy religion,
Which thrust its head from the regions of heaven,
Looming over mortals with horrible aspect,
A man of Greece was first who dared to raise
His mortal eyes against it, and first to stand against it—
Whom neither the fame of the gods, nor lightning bolts, nor the sky
With its threatening roar could subdue—but all the more
It stirred the keen courage of his mind, so that he longed
To be the first to break the tight-barred gates of nature.
Therefore the living force of his mind prevailed,
And he passed on far beyond the flaming walls of the world,
And traversed in mind and spirit the immeasurable whole,
From which he brings back to us as victor what can arise,
What cannot, and by what law each thing has
Its power limited, and its boundary set deep.
Therefore religion is trodden under foot,
His victory lifts us level with the heavens.
In this matter I fear you may perhaps suppose
That you are entering upon the principles of impiety,
And treading the path of wickedness. But in fact
Religion more often has given birth to deeds wicked and impious.
As once at Aulis the altar of the virgin goddess of the crossroads
Was foully stained with Iphianassa's blood
By the chosen leaders of the Danaans, the foremost of men.
When the ribbon, placed equally about her maiden tresses on both sides,
Streamed down from each cheek in equal lengths,

BOOK.

He saw his grieving father standing before the altars,
And nearby the attendants hiding their swords from him,
And the citizens pouring tears at the sight of her,
While she, mute with fear, fell to her knees upon the ground,
Nor could it avail the poor girl in such a moment
That she had first bestowed upon the king the name of father.
For she, lifted up by the hands of men, trembling,
Was led to the altars — not so that, with solemn rites
Of marriage duly performed, she might be escorted by the bright wedding-hymn,
But so that, chaste herself, at the very season of marriage,
She might fall as a victim, slaughtered mournfully by a father's hand,
In order that a lucky and favorable departure might be granted to the fleet.
So great are the evils that religion could urge men to commit.
You yourself, at any time now, overcome by the terrifying
Words of the prophets, will seek to fall away from us.
For indeed they can conjure up for you many
Dreams which might overturn the plans of your life
And trouble all your fortunes with fear.
And rightly so — for if men could see a certain end
To their troubles, by some reasoning they would be able
To resist the power of religion and the threats of prophets.
But as it is, there is no means, no faculty of resistance,
Since eternal punishments in death are to be feared.
For it is unknown what the nature of the soul is,
Whether it is born with us, or instead enters into those being born,
And whether it perishes with us when dissolved by death,
Or whether it visits the darkness and vast chasms of the underworld,
Or whether by divine will it enters into other animals,
As our Ennius sang, who first brought down from lovely
Helicon a garland of undying leaves.

Book I, Book III

Through the Italian peoples, renowned for the clarity of its fame —
And if moreover Ennius sets forth that the halls of Acheron exist,
Expounding it in his immortal verses,
Where neither souls nor our bodies endure permanently,
But only certain phantoms pale in wondrous ways,
From which he says the vision of ever-flourishing Homer
Rose before him and began to shed salt tears
And to unfold the nature of things in words —
Therefore we must rightly reason about the things above:
The courses of the sun and moon,
By what principle they move, and by what force each thing is driven
On earth; and above all, with keen reasoning,
We must see what the nature of the soul and mind consists of,
And what it is that confronts our minds when we are wakeful
And terrorizes us when afflicted by disease or buried in sleep,
So that we seem to see and hear face to face
Those whose bones the earth embraces in death.
Nor does it escape my mind that it is difficult
To illuminate the obscure discoveries of the Greeks in Latin verses,
Especially when much must be handled with new words,
On account of the poverty of our language and the novelty of the subjects.
Yet your virtue, and the hoped-for pleasure
Of sweet friendship, persuades me to endure any labor,
And leads me to keep watch through the calm nights,
Seeking by what words and by what verse at last
I may spread clear light before your mind,
So that you may see to the depths of things hidden from sight.
This terror and darkness of the mind, therefore,
Not the rays of the sun, nor the bright shafts of day,
Can scatter, but only the aspect and reason of nature.

From this point our argument will take its beginning:
Nothing is ever created by divine power out of nothing.
For fear holds all mortals in its grip,
Because they see so many things happening on earth and in the sky
Whose causes they are utterly unable to understand,
And so they suppose that a divine power is at work.
But once we have seen that nothing can be created from nothing,
We will then discern more clearly what we are seeking:
Both the source from which each thing can be created,
And how all things come about without the agency of the gods.
For if things came from nothing, every kind of thing
Could be born from any source and would need no seed.
Men could arise first from the sea, fish from the earth,
The scaly race of creatures could burst forth from the sky,
Cattle and other beasts and every kind of wild animal
Would inhabit cultivated land and wilderness alike with random birth,
Nor would the same fruits remain constant on the same trees,
But everything would change, and all things could bear anything.
For if there were no generative particles proper to each thing,
How could there be a fixed mother for each thing?
But as it is, because each thing is created from specific seeds,
It is born and comes forth into the shores of light
Only where the proper matter and primary particles exist,
And for this reason not everything can be produced from everything,
Because each kind of thing contains a distinct and hidden power.
Moreover, why do we see roses in spring, grain in summer's heat,
And grapes brought forth by autumn's urging,
If it is not because, when the fixed seeds of things
Have flowed together at their proper time, whatever is created comes forth,
While the seasons favor it and the living earth

Book I, Book IIII

Safely brings forth tender things into the shores of light.
For if they came from nothing, they would suddenly spring up
At uncertain times and in seasons foreign to them,
Since there would be no first-beginnings that, by generative
Union, could be kept apart at an unfavorable time,
Nor would there be any need of time for the growth of things,
If from nothing seeds could grow to fullness.
For young men would spring suddenly from tiny infants,
And trees would leap up all at once from the earth,
None of which ever happens, since all things grow
Little by little, as is fitting, from a fixed seed,
And as they grow they preserve their kind, so you may know
That each thing grows and is nourished from its own matter.
Add to this that without the fixed rains of the year
The joyful earth cannot put forth its fruits,
Nor can the nature of living things, deprived of food,
Propagate its kind and preserve life.
So you should rather think that many bodies are common to many things,
As we see words share their letters,
Than that anything can exist without first-principles.
Moreover, why could nature not produce men
Of such size that they could wade across the sea on foot
And tear apart great mountains with their hands,
And outlive many generations of living creatures,
If it is not because a fixed matter has been assigned
To the begetting of things, from which it is determined what can arise?
Therefore it must be admitted that nothing can come from nothing,
Since things require seed, by which each created thing
May be brought forth into the gentle breezes of the air.
Finally, since we observe that cultivated lands surpass uncultivated ones

LIB.

That cultivated lands, and hands that bring forth better fruits,
Show that there are indeed first-beginnings of things in the earth,
Which, as we turn the fertile clods with the plowshare,
And work the soil of the land, we summon into birth.
But if there were none such, without any labor of ours
You would see all things spontaneously spring up far better.
To this is added, that nature dissolves each thing back
Into its own elements, and does not destroy things into nothing.
For if anything were mortal in all its parts,
Each thing would perish, snatched suddenly from our eyes.
There would be no need of any force to bring about
A separation of its parts and dissolve their bonds.
But now, since all things consist of eternal seed,
Until some force strikes and shatters them with a blow,
Or penetrates within through the void and dissolves them,
Nature permits no destruction of anything to be seen.
Moreover, whatever age removes through the passage of time,
If it utterly destroys it, consuming all its matter,
From where does Venus restore the generations of animals
Into the light of life? And from where does the inventive earth
Feed and nourish them, supplying sustenance to each kind?
From where do the springs of native waters flow? And from afar,
From where do rivers replenish the sea? From where does the aether feed the stars?
For infinite time and all the days gone by
Should have consumed all things that are of mortal body.
But if in that vast span of time now past,
The things existed from which this sum of the world is rebuilt,
They are surely endowed with an immortal nature.
Therefore, no things can return to nothing.
And finally, all things are driven by the same force and cause throughout.

It would destroy all things, unless eternal matter held them
Bound to each other, now less, now more tightly entwined.
For touch alone would surely be cause enough for death,
Since there would be no eternal bodies whose
Interwoven fabric any force would need to dissolve.
But as things are, because the bonds of the first-beginnings
Are unlike one another, and matter is eternal,
Things remain intact in body, until some force
Strong enough to overcome the texture of each is met.
Nothing, therefore, returns to nothing, but all things
At their dissolution return to the bodies of matter.
Finally, the rains perish, when father sky
Has hurled them into the lap of mother earth.
But bright crops spring up, and branches grow green
On the trees, the trees themselves grow and are weighed down with fruit.
From this our human race and the race of beasts is nourished,
From this we see glad cities flowering with children,
And leafy forests ringing everywhere with young birds singing,
From this weary flocks lay down their fat and satisfied bodies
Through the rich pastures, and the gleaming white liquid of milk
Flows from swollen udders; from this a new generation
Frolics on weak limbs through the tender grass,
Their young minds drunk with pure milk.
Nothing, therefore, that appears to perish truly perishes utterly,
Since nature repairs one thing from another, and allows
Nothing to be born except aided by the death of something else.
Now, since I have taught you that nothing can be created
From nothing, and likewise that what is born cannot be recalled to nothing,
Lest perhaps you begin to distrust my words
Because the first-beginnings of things cannot be seen by the eyes —

Learn furthermore what bodies must necessarily
exist in things, though they cannot be seen.
First, the force of wind, aroused, lashes the sea,
overwhelms great ships, and scatters the clouds,
sometimes sweeping across the plains with rapid whirlwind,
strewing great trees, and battering the highest mountain tops
with forest-breaking blasts; so fiercely does the sea rage
with fierce roaring and threatening murmur.
Therefore the winds are surely invisible bodies,
which sweep the sea, the lands, and finally the clouds of heaven,
and, rushing upon them, snatch them up in sudden whirlwind,
and flow in no different way, spreading devastation,
than when a flood of soft water is borne along suddenly
in an overflowing river, swelled by heavy rains,
with a great rush of water down from the high mountains,
hurling together fragments of forests and whole groves,
and the strong bridges cannot withstand the force
of the oncoming water — so mightily does the river,
turbid with great rain, rush against the piers with powerful force.
With great roar it spreads ruin, and rolls great boulders
beneath its waves; wherever anything stands in its path, the flood overwhelms it.
So likewise must blasts of wind be carried along,
and when, like a mighty river, they have swept forward,
they drive everything before them in whatever direction, and rush on
with repeated blows, and sometimes with a twisting eddy
they seize things and carry them spinning in rapid whirlwind.
Therefore again and again: winds are invisible bodies,
since they are found to rival great rivers in deeds and nature,
rivers whose body is open to the sight.
Then again we perceive the various scents of things,

Yet we never see the scents that drift toward our nostrils,
Nor can we observe heat or cold with our eyes,
Nor are we accustomed to see sounds with our sight,
Yet all these things must consist of a bodily nature,
Since they are able to strike upon our senses;
For nothing can touch or be touched except body.
Moreover, clothes hung up on a surf-beaten shore
Grow damp, and then dry out in the blazing sun.
Yet we have not seen how the moisture of water
Soaks in, nor again how it flees before heat.
The moisture therefore is dispersed into tiny parts
Which eyes are wholly unable to perceive.
Indeed, as many years circle back with the sun,
A ring on the finger grows thin from wearing,
The dripping of water hollows a stone, the curved blade
Of the iron plow secretly diminishes in the fields,
And we see the stone-paved roads worn down
By the feet of the multitude; and near the gates, bronze
Statues show their right hands worn thin
By the frequent touch of those who greet them in passing.
We see, then, that all these things are diminished by wear,
But what particles depart at any given time,
Envious nature has blocked from our power of seeing.
Finally, whatever nature and time grant to things,
Adding little by little, compelling gradual growth,
No keenness of eyesight, however intent, can observe;
Nor again can you perceive what things lose over time
Through age and decay, or what the sea's salt spray
Gnaws away from overhanging cliffs, bit by bit.
Nature therefore conducts her work through invisible bodies.

BOOK I.

Yet all things are not packed and held together by body on every side,
for there is void in things —
a fact that will prove useful for you to know in many matters,
and will not allow you, wandering in doubt, to keep questioning forever
about the sum of things, and to distrust our words.
Therefore there exists a space, untouched and empty, void;
for if it did not exist, things could in no way be moved;
since matter, whose function it is to obstruct and block,
would at all times be present to everything —
nothing, therefore, could advance,
since nothing could give way and yield.
But now, across the seas and lands and the heights of heaven,
we see many things moved in many ways by varied causes
before our eyes; which, if there were no void,
would not merely lack that restless motion,
but could never have been born at all,
since matter would lie packed and motionless on every side.
Furthermore, however solid objects are thought to be,
yet from this you may see that they are of rare texture:
in caves and rocks the liquid moisture of water seeps through,
and all things weep with abundant drops;
food disperses itself through the whole body of every living creature;
trees grow, and in due season put forth their fruit;
because food travels all the way from the lowest roots
through the trunks and along all the branches.
Voices pass through walls and fly through the closed spaces of houses;
rigid cold penetrates to the very bones.
If there were no voids through which each body could pass,
you would see none of this happen by any means.
Finally, why do we see some things surpass others

Do things have weight according to their size and no more?
For if there is just as much matter in a ball of wool as
In a lump of lead, they ought to weigh the same,
Since the function of matter is to press everything downward.
But void by its nature has no weight.
Therefore, what is equally large but appears lighter
Declares that it contains more void within itself.
On the other hand, what is heavier contains more matter within itself
And much less empty space inside.
Therefore that which we seek with keen reasoning,
Which we call void, is mixed in among things.
I am compelled to run through a point here, lest
Something that certain people invent lead you away from the truth.
They say that water yields to the pressing of scaly fish,
And opens up liquid pathways, because the fish
Leave space behind them, into which the yielding waves can flow together.
In the same way, they say, other things too can move among themselves
And change their place, even though everything is full.
But this whole argument has been accepted on false reasoning.
For where can the scaly fish advance at all,
Unless the water gives them space? And where in turn
Can the waves yield, when the fish cannot go there?
Either all bodies must be deprived of motion,
Or it must be said that void is mixed in among things,
From which each thing can take its first beginning of movement.
Finally, if two broad bodies meeting in collision
Spring quickly apart, air must necessarily
Fill the void that forms between them.
However swiftly the air rushes in from all sides,
It will not be able to fill the whole space in one moment.

To fill a space: for first it is necessary that each thing
Occupies that place, and then all things may be possessed.
But if anyone supposes, when bodies have leapt apart,
That this happens because the air condenses,
He is wrong. For then a void exists where none existed before,
And likewise what had stood firm is filled again with void.
Nor can air be made denser by such reasoning.
Nor if it could, could it, I think, without void
Draw itself inward and gather its parts into one.
Therefore, however much you delay with argument,
You must confess that void exists within things.
And many further proofs can be brought to your attention
To give credibility to what I say.
But these small traces are enough for a keen mind,
By which you yourself can discern the rest.
For just as hounds that roam the mountains often
Find with their noses a quarry hidden in the leafy stillness,
Once they have picked up the certain tracks of the way,
So you, one thing from another, will be able to see for yourself
In such matters, and to penetrate the hidden recesses
And draw forth the truth from them.
But if you grow lazy and fall back a little from the task,
This much I can promise you plainly, Memmius:
So great shall be the abundant draughts that flow from great springs,
Poured sweet from my rich breast by my tongue,
That I fear old age with its slow step may creep
Through our limbs and loosen the bonds of life within us,
Before the full store of arguments on any single topic
Has been sent through your ears in verse.
But now let me resume and continue to weave what I have begun.

All of nature, then, as it exists in itself, consists
of two things: for there are bodies, and there is void,
in which they are situated and through which they move in different directions.
That body exists in itself is declared by the common witness
of the senses; unless this primary trust stands firm,
there will be no basis by which, in matters of the hidden,
we can confirm anything in our minds by reason.
Then again, place and space, which we call void,
if it did not exist, bodies could nowhere be situated,
nor could they move in any direction whatsoever —
as I have already shown you somewhat above.
Besides, there is nothing that you can say is apart from
all body, separated and removed from void,
that would stand as a third distinct nature of things.
For whatever exists must itself be something,
whether it be of great or small extent.
If it has any touch, however light and slight,
it will add to the sum of body and join its number.
But if it is intangible, so that from no part can it
prevent anything from passing through it freely,
then it will be that void which we call the empty.
Furthermore, whatever exists of itself will either do something,
or it will have to be acted upon by other agents,
or it will be such that things can exist and happen within it.
But nothing can act or be acted upon without body,
nor can anything provide room, except void and empty space.
Therefore, besides void and bodies, no third
nature can by itself be reckoned among things,
neither one that can ever fall within our senses,
nor one that anyone can grasp by the reason of the mind.

BOOK 4.

For whatever things are known, either you will find them among these two categories of things, or you will see them as outcomes of these.
A property is that which cannot be separated without fatal dissolution from that to which it belongs, just as weight is to stone, heat to fire, moisture to water,
Touch to all bodies, untouchability to the void,
Slavery and poverty and riches on the other hand,
Freedom, war, harmony, and all the rest, whose
Coming and going leaves nature's essence unharmed —
These we are accustomed, as is right, to call accidents.
Time, likewise, has no existence of itself, but from things themselves
The sense follows of what has passed in ages gone,
What situation presses now, what further follows after.
Nor must we admit that anyone feels time by itself
Separated from the motion of things and their calm repose.
Again, when men say that the rape of Tyndareus's daughter and the conquest of the Trojan-born peoples took place, we must take care
Lest these events by themselves compel us to admit their existence,
Since those generations of men, of whom these events were part,
Irreversible time has now carried away into the past.
For whatever has been done can be called an event
Of the lands, or of the regions themselves.
Furthermore, if there had been no matter of things,
And no place and space in which all things are carried on,
Never would the fire of love for the form of Tyndareus's daughter, blazing in the Phrygian breast of Alexander,
Have kindled the fierce contests of cruel war,
Nor would the wooden horse, unknown to the Trojans, at its nighttime birth of armed men, have set Pergamum aflame —
So that you may see clearly that all past deeds
Have no existence of themselves.

Not so —

Not so that body exists and has being in itself in that way,
Nor is known by the same reasoning by which void exists,
But rather you might rightly call them events
Of body and of place, in which each thing is carried on.
Bodies moreover are in part the first-beginnings of things,
In part those things which are formed from a union of first-beginnings.
But those which are the first-beginnings of things, no force
Can quench, for they overcome all by their solid body in the end.
And though it seems difficult to believe that anything
Can be found in things possessed of solid body,
Yet the thunderbolt of heaven passes through the walls of houses,
As the sound of a voice travels. Iron glows red in fire,
And rocks burst asunder with scorching steam.
Indeed the hardness of gold is loosened and dissolved by heat.
Then ice, conquered by fierce flame, melts away.
Heat penetrates silver, and likewise cold,
When holding cups in both hands in the proper way
We have felt it, with the dew of liquid poured in from above.
So far does it seem that there is nothing solid in things.
But because the true reasoning and nature of things
Compels it, come, let us set forth in a few verses
That there exist things which consist of solid and eternal body,
Which we teach are the seeds of things and their first-beginnings,
From which the whole sum of all things now created is composed.
First, since the twofold nature of two unlike
Things has been found to stand far apart,
That of body and of place, in which all things occur,
Each must exist pure and alone in itself.
For wherever space lies empty, which we call the void,
Body is not there; and wherever body in turn extends itself

BOOK I.

Body and void together make up all that exists, and nothing else.
Therefore the primary bodies are solid and free of void.
Moreover, since void exists within created things,
solid matter must surround it,
and nothing can be shown by true reasoning
to hide void within itself and contain it inside,
unless you grant that what holds it together is solid.
And that can be nothing other than an assemblage of matter
which is able to contain the void enclosed within it.
Matter therefore, which consists of solid body,
can be eternal, while everything else dissolves.
Furthermore, if there were nothing that could be empty,
everything would be solid; but on the other hand, unless
there were bodies to fill the spaces they occupy wherever they go,
everything that is space would exist as empty void.
Therefore body and void alternate and are distinct from each other,
since the world is neither entirely full nor entirely empty.
There are therefore solid bodies,
which can mark off space from the surrounding void.
These cannot be broken apart by blows struck from outside,
nor can they be unlocked by penetration from within,
nor can they give way when attacked by any other means —
as we have already shown you a little earlier above.
For nothing can seem to collide without void,
nor be broken, nor split into two by cutting,
nor take in moisture, nor penetrating cold,
nor fire, by which all things are consumed;
and the more void a thing contains within itself,
the more it yields and gives way when attacked by these forces.
Therefore, if the primary bodies are solid and free of void,

These things, as I have taught, must of necessity be eternal.
Besides, if matter had not been eternal,
All things would long since have utterly dissolved into nothing,
And whatever we see would have arisen from nothing.
But since I have shown above that nothing can be created
From nothing, and that what has been born cannot be recalled to nothing,
The first-beginnings must be of immortal body,
So that all things can be dissolved at their final hour,
That matter may be available for the renewal of things.
Therefore the first-beginnings are solid in their simplicity,
And in no other way, preserved through the ages,
Could they renew things from infinite time past.
Add to this that, although the primal bodies of matter
Are perfectly solid, all soft things can still be produced:
Air, water, earth, vapors, as they come to be,
How they come about and by what force each is governed,
Since void is mixed together with things.
But on the other hand, if the first-beginnings of things were soft,
From where could hard flints and iron be created?
No account could be given, for the entire
Foundation of nature would lack its grounding.
Therefore the first-beginnings are solid and powerful in their simplicity,
By whose denser combination all things
Can be compressed and display their mighty forces.
Moreover, since now a fixed limit is established for each kind
Of growing things, and for the sustaining of life,
And since each thing can only do what the laws of nature allow,
And nothing further, since the sacred compact holds,
And nothing changes when all things remain constant —
So various birds, in their order, one and all...

They show that general blemishes exist throughout the body,
That matter must have an immutable substance —
And rightly so. For if the first elements of things
Could be changed by any force that binds them,
It would then be uncertain what could come to be,
What could not, and what limit belongs to each thing,
And by what principle that deep-set boundary holds.
Nor could successive generations so often reproduce
The nature, movements, way of life, and customs of their parents.
Moreover, since every outermost tip
Of that body which our senses
Can no longer perceive, exists without parts,
And consists of the smallest possible nature, and never was
A separate thing on its own, nor will it hereafter be able to be,
Since it is itself a part of another — first the lowest and highest,
Then other and yet other similar parts in order,
Fill out the body's nature in a dense mass.
Since these cannot exist on their own, it is necessary
That they cling together, unable to be torn away by any means.
The first elements are therefore solid in their simplicity,
Packed tight together in their smallest parts,
Not composed by the gathering of many smaller things,
But rather powerful in their eternal simplicity,
From which nature, preserving the seeds of things,
Allows nothing to be torn away or diminished.
Furthermore, unless there is a minimum, the very smallest
Bodies will consist of infinite parts.
For wherever a half of a part always has
Its own half, with nothing setting a limit —
Therefore, between the sum of all things and the smallest, what would there be?

Nothing will differ. For however infinite the whole sum of things may be in its entirety, yet the smallest things that exist will equally be composed of infinite parts. But since true reason protests against this and denies that the mind can believe it, you must admit, overcome, that there exist things which are possessed of no parts and are of the smallest nature; and since they are such, you must also acknowledge that they are solid and eternal. Furthermore, if nature, the creator of things, had been accustomed to compel all things to be resolved into their smallest parts, by now she would be unable to restore anything from them, because things which are increased by no parts cannot possess what generative matter must have: the varied connections, weights, blows, collisions, and motions through which all things are carried on. Moreover, if no limit has been set upon the breaking of bodies, then each body that exists must have survived from eternal time until now, not yet having been tried by any danger. But since things exist endowed with a fragile nature, it is inconsistent that they could have remained through eternal time, battered by countless blows throughout the ages. Finally, if nature had set no end to the breaking of things, by now all bodies of matter would have been reduced by the breaking action of ages past, so that nothing conceived from them could, from a fixed point in time, reach the full flower of its growth. For we see that anything can be dissolved more quickly than it is restored again. Therefore, all the long age of infinite past time

BOOK I.

What it had broken and destroyed and dissolved,
Could never thereafter be repaired in the remaining time.
But now there is clearly a fixed limit to breaking,
Since we see things restored, and likewise
Definite lifespans are set for things,
By which they may reach the flower of their age.
Therefore, those who believed that fire is the matter of things,
And that the sum of all rests on fire alone,
Are seen to have strayed far from true reasoning.
Heraclitus leads them into battle as their first champion,
Famous among the foolish more for his obscure language,
Than among the serious Greeks who seek the truth.
For fools admire and love all things more greatly
That they see lying hidden beneath twisted words,
And they take for truth whatever can pleasingly touch
The ears, and whatever is colored with charming sound.
For I ask how such varied things could exist,
If they are made from fire alone and pure fire.
It would do no good for hot fire to grow denser,
Nor to grow rarer, if the parts of fire kept the same
Nature that the whole fire itself possesses.
For a fiercer heat would result from compressed parts,
And a weaker one from dispersed and scattered parts.
There is nothing more that you could suppose possible
From such causes, still less could the great variety of things
Come from fire, whether dense or rare.
And if they grant that void is mixed into things,
The fires may be compressed or left rarefied.
But because many see many contradictions,
And avoid leaving pure void in the world,

While fearing the heights, they lose the true path,
And do not see that, once the void is removed from things,
All things are packed together and become one body,
Able to emit nothing from itself,
As the summer-bearing fire casts light and heat,
So that you may see it is not made of densely packed parts.
But if any believe by some reasoning it is possible
For fiery elements to compress and change their substance,
That is, if they grant this can be done from any part,
The fire's heat will utterly perish into nothing,
And all things that are created will come from nothing.
For whatever passes beyond its own boundaries in change,
That immediately is the death of what it was before.
Therefore something must survive unharmed from those things,
Lest all matter return utterly to nothing,
And the supply of things, reborn from nothing, flourish.
Now therefore, since there are certain most fundamental bodies
Which preserve always the same nature,
Through whose departure, arrival, and changed order, they alter
The nature of things and transform bodies into one another,
You may know these primary bodies of things are not made of fire.
For it would make no difference that some depart and arrive,
And that some are assigned elsewhere and changed in order,
If all things retained only the nature of fire.
For fire would be everything that it creates.
But the truth, as I think, is this: there are certain bodies
Whose meetings, motions, order, position, and shapes
Produce fires, and when their order is changed, they alter
Their nature, and are not similar to fire, nor to anything else
That is able to send forth bodies from itself.

BOOK [I]

To touch our senses and reach us by contact.
To say that fire follows all things, and that nothing real
Exists among the number of things, except fire,
Seems itself the product of raving madness.
For he fights against the senses using the senses themselves,
And undermines the very foundations on which all belief rests,
The same foundations from which he himself came to know fire.
For he trusts the senses to perceive fire truly,
But does not trust them for other things, equally clear—
Which seems to me as foolish as it is mad.
For what shall we cite as more certain than our own
Senses, by which we can distinguish true from false?
Besides, why should anyone rather do away with everything
And wish to leave only the nature of heat alone,
Than deny fire, yet keep some sum of things remaining?
Either claim seems equally insane.
Therefore those who supposed that matter consists of fire,
And that the whole of things is made of fire,
And those who made air the first principle for generating things,
Or those who thought that moisture was the source,
That it by itself could fashion things or create
All things from earth, and transform them into all natures—
These men seem to have wandered very far from truth.
Add to them those who double the first elements,
Joining air with fire, and earth with water,
And those who think all things can arise from four,
From fire, earth, spirit, and rain.
Among whom foremost is Empedocles of Akragas,
Whom the island bore within its three-cornered shores,
Around which the flowing sea with its great winding curves

And the Ionian and Libyan seas wash its shores with their waves,
And the narrow strait with its rushing current divides the sea with its waves,
From the lands of Italy at its boundaries.
Here is the vast Charybdis, and here the Etnaean thunders
Of flames threaten to gather their rage anew,
So that its force may once more vomit forth erupted fires from its jaws,
And hurl the lightning flashes of flame to the heavens again.
Though this region seems wondrous in many great ways
To the peoples of mankind, and is said to be worth seeing,
Rich in good things, fortified with the great strength of men,
Yet nothing is thought to have been more glorious in this man himself,
Nor is anything held more sacred, more wondrous, or more dear.
Indeed the poems of his divine spirit
Are proclaimed aloud and set forth his brilliant discoveries,
So that he seems hardly to have been born of human stock.
Yet he, and those we mentioned above as his inferiors,
Were in many respects far and greatly less than he,
Though finding many things well and with divine insight,
They gave forth responses from the inner sanctuary of their heart
More sacredly and with far surer reason
Than the Pythia who speaks from Phoebus's tripod and laurel-boughs;
Yet in their first principles they brought ruin upon their systems,
And heavily did those great men fall there in great collapse.
First, because they exclude void from things and set up motion,
They posit soft and rare substances,
Air, sun, fire, earth, living creatures, crops,
Yet do not admit void into the body of these things.
Then because they make no end at all for the secondary
Bodies, nor any pause in their breaking,
Nor any smallest thing to persist at all in the world.

Since we see that the outermost tip of anything
is what appears to our senses as the smallest thing,
you may infer from this what cannot be seen:
the extreme minimum that things possess.
Add to this that, since the first-beginnings of things
constitute what we perceive as soft and living bodies,
and these must be altogether mortal in nature,
the sum of all things should then return to nothing,
and from nothing a renewed abundance of things spring forth —
how far both conclusions stray from truth, you will understand.
Moreover, these elements are in many ways mutually hostile, and their very
properties are at war with each other; so either when they meet they will perish,
or they will scatter apart, as in a storm we see
lightning scatter, and rains, and winds.
Furthermore, if all things are created from four elements,
and all things dissolve back into them,
how can those four be called the first-beginnings of things
rather than, conversely, things being prior to them?
For they are alternately born and exchange their colors,
and throughout all time exchange their entire nature with each other.
But if you think that fire and earth combine
to form body, and the airy breezes and moisture of water,
and that nature changes nothing in their union,
then nothing could ever be created from them —
no living creature, nothing with a soul joined to a body, like a tree.
For each element in the mingling of the shifting mass
reveals its own nature, and air will appear
mixed together with earth and with moisture alike.
But the first-beginnings, in generating things, must
bring a hidden and unseen nature to bear.

Lest anything diminish what opposes and obstructs,
Preventing whatever is created from properly existing.
When they also return from the sky and its fires,
And claim that fire first turns itself into the breezes
Of air, then rain is born from this, and earth is created
From rain, and then all things return back from earth,
First moisture, then air, then finally heat,
And these things never cease from passing among themselves,
From sky to earth, from earth to the stars of the world —
This is something that the first-beginnings must in no way do.
For something unchangeable must necessarily survive,
Lest all things be utterly reduced to nothing.
For whatever passes out of its bounds through change,
This is immediately the death of what existed before.
Therefore, since what we have just spoken of above
Passes into transformed states, it must necessarily consist
Of other things that cannot be converted anywhere,
Lest all things be utterly reduced to nothing for you.
Rather, you should suppose that certain bodies exist,
Endowed with such a nature, that if they chanced to create fire,
The same bodies, with a few removed and a few added,
With order and motion changed, can make the breath of air.
Thus all other things are transformed into one another.
But, you say, manifest reality plainly shows that all things
Grow from the earth into the air, and so forth.
And unless the storm grants favorable time
With rains, the trees waver under the wasting of the clouds.
The sun in its part fosters them and bestows its warmth,
So that crops, trees, and living creatures may grow.
Surely, unless dry food and tender moisture

It aids, with the body now gone, that all the life
Be loosened from all nerves and bones.
For we are aided, beyond doubt, and nourished
By certain things, while other things in turn nourish other things —
Because clearly, in many ways, the common first-beginnings of many things
Are mixed together in the substance of many things,
And so various things are nourished by various things.
And it matters greatly what those first-beginnings often are,
With what others, and in what arrangement they are held together,
And what motions they give and receive among themselves.
For the same elements make up the sky, the sea, the lands, the rivers, the sun,
The same make up crops, trees, and living creatures,
But they are mixed together in different ways and different combinations.
Indeed, throughout my very verses you may see
Many elements common to many words,
Though it is necessary to admit that verses and words
Differ from one another in meaning and in sound.
So much can elements accomplish by change of order alone.
But the first-beginnings of things can employ more combinations,
From which all the various things can be created.
Now let us examine the Homoeomeria of Anaxagoras,
Which the Greeks speak of, but which our tongue cannot render,
Since the poverty of our native speech does not permit it —
Yet the thing itself is easy enough to set out in words.
In the first place, what Anaxagoras calls Homoeomeria:
Bones, he says, are formed from tiny, minute
Little bones, and so from tiny, minute
Little pieces of flesh does flesh arise, and blood is created
From many drops of blood coming together,
And gold, he thinks, can be composed of tiny grains of gold,

Gold, and that from small earths the earth grows,
That fire is born when small fires come together among themselves,
That moisture comes from tiny moistures,
And the rest he imagines and supposes by similar reasoning.
Yet he does not grant that there is any void in things anywhere,
Nor that there is any limit to the cutting of bodies.
Therefore it seems to me that in both respects
He errs equally, as do those we mentioned above.
Add to this that he imagines the first elements too weak,
If the first elements, endowed with similar nature
As things themselves, labor equally,
And perish, with nothing to hold them back from destruction.
For what among them will endure under violent pressure,
So as to escape death beneath the very blows of doom?
Fire? or moisture? or air? or which of these their blood? Nay,
Nothing, I think, when all things are equally destroyed to the bone.
So mortal will it be, just as what we plainly see
Perish before our eyes by some force.
But that things cannot fall back to nothing, nor
Grow from nothing, I attest by what has been proved before.
Furthermore, since food increases and nourishes the body,
Whether we say it enters as veins and blood and bones within us,
Or whether they say all foods are mixed within the body
And contain within themselves tiny bodies of nerves,
And bones, and veins throughout, and parts of blood:
It will follow that all food, both dry and liquid itself,
Is held to consist of alien elements,
Of bones, and nerves, and gore, and mixed blood.
Furthermore, whatever bodies grow from the earth,
If they are in the earth, then earth must consist of them.

BOOK [I]

From foreign elements that arise from the earth,
you may transfer the same idea using the same number of words.
If flame lies hidden in wood, along with smoke and ash,
it must be that wood consists of foreign elements.
There remains here a certain slender opportunity for things to hide,
which is what Anaxagoras takes as his principle: that in all things all
things lie mixed and hidden, but that alone appears
of which there are the most parts,
placed most readily at hand and foremost to the eye —
yet this is far removed from true reasoning.
For it would follow that grains, when often broken
by the threatening force of a rock, should give off a sign
of blood, or something that nourishes our bodies,
and that when we grind stone on stone, blood should flow.
By similar reasoning, it would follow that herbs too
should often emit sweet drops of liquid, of like flavor
to the milk such as woolly flocks possess.
Likewise, when clods of earth are crumbled,
kinds of grasses, grains, and foliage should be seen
scattered within, and lying hidden in tiny parts throughout the soil;
and lastly, in wood, ash and smoke should be seen,
and tiny fires lying hidden, when wood is broken apart.
Since manifest reality shows that none of this occurs,
you may know that things are not so mixed within things.
Rather, seeds common to many things must lie
hidden in many ways intermingled within things.
But often, you say, on great mountains it happens
that tall trees rub their topmost branches against each other
when mighty south winds drive them to do so,
until they burst out flowering with flame sprung forth.

And yet fire is not innate in wood,
but there are many seeds of heat, and when rubbing
brings them together, they kindle fires in the forests.
For if so great a flame lay hidden in the forests,
the fires could not be concealed for any time at all,
they would consume the woodlands and burn up the groves.
Do you not see then (as we said a little while ago)
that it matters greatly that these same first-beginnings
are combined with what others, and in what arrangement they are held,
and what motions they give and receive among themselves,
and that the same ones, slightly rearranged among themselves, create
fires from wood — just as words themselves also
differ among themselves by a slight change of elements,
when we distinguish wood and fires by different names?
Finally, whatever you now observe in visible things,
if you suppose it impossible unless you imagine
that the bodies of matter are endowed with a similar nature,
by this reasoning the first-beginnings of things perish for you —
it will come to pass that they shake with trembling laughter and laugh aloud,
and wet their faces and cheeks with salt tears.
Now come, hear what remains, and listen more clearly.
Nor does it escape my mind that these things are obscure; but a great
hope of glory has struck my heart with the sharpest thyrsus,
and at the same time has struck into my breast a sweet love
of the Muses, by which now, with mind alive and vigorous,
I traverse the pathless regions of the Pierides,
trodden by no foot before; it delights me to approach untouched springs
and to drink from them, and to gather new flowers,
and to seek from them a glorious garland for my head,
from which the Muses have before veiled the temples of none.

BOOK.
First, I proceed to teach of great matters, and to free
the mind from the tight knots of religion.
Next, what I compose in such clear verse about an obscure subject,
touching everything with the charm of the Muses,
this too seems to be done for no small reason:
just as doctors, when they try to give children
foul wormwood to drink, first touch the rim
of the cup all around with the sweet golden
liquid of honey, so that the children's
unsuspecting age may be tricked as far as their lips,
and meanwhile drink the bitter juice of wormwood,
and though deceived, not be harmed by it,
but rather, restored by such a treatment, recover their health —
so I now, since this philosophy often seems
too harsh to those who have not encountered it, and
the common crowd shrinks from it, wished to set forth
our reasoning to you in sweet-speaking Pierian verse,
and to touch it, as it were, with the sweet honey of the Muses,
in hopes of holding your attention by such means
through my verses, while you perceive the whole
nature of things, and the form in which it is arranged.
But since I have taught that the most solid bodies of matter
fly about unconquered through all eternity,
come now, hear what is the sum and limit of these things,
let us also unfold this: what void has been found,
or place, or space in which all things move about;
let us see clearly whether the whole is entirely finite,
or stretches immeasurably to the depths below.
Everything that exists, then, is not bounded in any direction
of its paths, for it would have to have an extremity.
But an extremity of nothing seems possible

to exist,

To be, unless there is something beyond to bound it so it seems,
Which nature of the senses follows no further.
Now beyond the sum of things, since nothing must be admitted to exist,
It has no extremity, and therefore lacks an end and limit;
Nor does it matter in which regions of it you stand.
So far indeed, whatever place each person occupies, in all directions
The infinite whole leaves an equal measure of space on every side.
Moreover, if the whole of space that exists were now assumed to be finite,
If someone were to run out to the outermost edges
And hurl a flying javelin with all his force,
Would you have it go, hurled by powerful arms,
Flying far and fast in the direction it was thrown,
Or do you think something could block it and stand in the way?
One or the other you must admit and accept as necessary,
Either of which cuts off your escape and compels you
To grant that space extends beyond all bounds.
For whether something exists that blocks it and prevents
The missile from going where it was sent and settling at its end,
Or whether it flies outward, it did not depart from a boundary.
In this way I will pursue you, and wherever you place
The outermost edges, I will ask what finally becomes of the javelin.
The result will be that a boundary can nowhere stand firm,
And the opportunity for flight will always extend the escape further.
Furthermore, if the whole space of the sum of all things
Were enclosed on every side within fixed borders and were finite,
By now the entire store of matter would have flowed together
By its own weight to the bottom from all sides,
And nothing could be accomplished beneath the canopy of heaven,
Nor would there be any sky at all, nor the light of the sun.
For all matter, heaped up in a mass, would be lying there

BOOK I.

Subsiding from infinite time until now,
Yet surely no rest has ever been granted to the primal bodies,
Since there is nothing whatsoever at the bottom,
To which they might, as it were, flow together and find a resting place.
All things are ever driven along by ceaseless motion,
And from all directions particles of matter are supplied eternally
From the infinite, moving swiftly.
Finally, we see that one thing bounds another before our eyes:
Air surrounds the hills, and mountains bound the air,
Earth bounds the sea, and sea in turn bounds all lands.
But in truth there is nothing outside the universe to bound it.
Therefore there exists a nature of place and a depth of space,
Such that not even the bright lightning bolts traversing it in their course
Through the endless tract of time could complete the journey,
Nor find that the distance to travel grows any less as they go.
So vast and open on all sides is the immense supply of space,
Free of all limits in every direction.
Nature itself prevents the sum of things from being able
To set a limit for itself, since body is bounded by void,
And what is void in turn is bounded by body,
So that by this alternation all things are made infinite,
Or else, if one does not bound the other,
Then simple nature would lie open and immeasurably unbounded.
Neither sea, nor land, nor the bright temples of the sky,
Nor mortal kind, nor the holy bodies of the gods
Could endure even the tiny span of an hour.
For the store of matter, scattered and dissolved from its union,
Would be swept through the great void,
Or rather would never have gathered to create anything at all,
Since once dispersed it could not be brought together again.

For certainly the first beginnings of things did not place themselves in order by design or by keen intelligence, nor did they agree upon what motions each would give. But because, being many and changed in many ways throughout all the infinite, they are driven about and struck by blows, they try every kind of motion and combination, and at last they fall into such arrangements as those by which this sum of things is constituted, and having been preserved through many great years, once set into motions that are mutually fitting, it brings it about that the rivers replenish the greedy sea with generous waves of water, and the earth, warmed by the sun's heat, renews its offspring, and the race of living creatures flourishes and grows, and the gliding fires of the heavens live on — which they could in no way do, unless matter could arise in infinite supply from the infinite, from which whatever is lost may be restored in things. For just as the nature of living creatures, deprived of food, wastes away losing its body, so all things must dissolve as soon as matter fails to supply them, diverted in some way from its path, and blows from without could not in every way preserve the whole of whatever is brought together. They can indeed strike often and hold back a part, while others come, so that the whole may be replenished. But sometimes they are forced to rebound, and at the same time to grant the first-beginnings of things space and time to escape, so that they may move freely away from the union. Therefore it is necessary that many things arise again and again, and yet, so that the blows themselves may also be available,

An infinite supply of matter is needed on all sides.
Flee far from this belief in these matters, Memmius:
that all things press toward the center of the universe,
and that therefore the nature of the world stands without any
external blows, and that the top and bottom cannot be dissolved,
because all things press toward the center —
if you believe that anything can support itself by its own weight,
and that things which lie beneath the earth all press upward again
and rest upon the earth, placed in reverse like reflections
which we now see of objects through water,
and in the same way they contend that animals roam about upside-down,
and that they cannot fall from the earth into the regions of the sky below,
any more than our bodies could spontaneously fly up into the temples of heaven;
and that when those creatures see the sun, we see the stars of night,
and that they share the seasons of the sky with us in alternation,
and divide the nights equally and the days likewise.
But idle error produces all these notions in fools,
embraced by those whose first principles are perverse and blind.
For there can be no center where the void and space are infinite;
and even if there were a center,
nothing could remain there for this reason
any more than it could stay for any other reason.
For every place and space, which we call the void,
must yield alike through the center and through what is not the center
to the motions of weights in whatever direction they move.
Nor is there any place to which bodies, once they have arrived,
can stand in the void having lost the force of their weight.
