Nor should the void support them,
but must keep yielding according to its nature's demand.

Things cannot therefore be held together by such reasoning,
bound in union by desire for the center.
Besides, since they claim not all bodies press
toward the center, but rather those of earth and water,
the moisture of the sea, and waves from great mountains,
and whatever is contained in an earthly body —
yet on the other hand they say the light breezes of air rise outward,
and likewise fires spread away from the center,
and that the whole ether trembles with constellations,
and the sun's flame is fed along the blue paths of the sky,
because heat fleeing from the center gathers its fires there.
Indeed, that mortal generations spring from the earth,
and that trees could not put forth leafy branches at their tops
unless nourishment were fed to each gradually from the earth,
and that the sky above wraps around all things —
lest the walls of the world, swift as flames,
should suddenly dissolve and scatter through the great void,
and lest all other things be carried off in like manner,
lest the deep vaults of the sky crash down from above,
and the earth slip swiftly from beneath our feet, and all bodies,
dissolved amid the mingled ruins of earth and sky,
should pass away through the deep void,
so that in a moment of time nothing remains,
save empty space and the first-beginnings of darkness.
For wherever you suppose that bodies first begin to be lacking,
that region will be the gate of death for all things,
through it the whole mass of matter will pour itself out.
If you grasp these things, led by a little effort,
one truth will illuminate another, and blind night
will not steal away your path — until you see clearly
the deepest truths of nature; so shall understanding kindle its lights upon all things.

TITUS LUCRETIUS CARUS: ON THE NATURE OF THINGS
BOOK TWO

It is sweet, when on the great sea the winds are stirring up
the waters, to watch from land another's great struggle
and toil — not because it is a pleasure that someone is troubled,
but because it is sweet to see from what hardships you yourself are free.
It is sweet also to behold the great contests of war
arrayed across the plains, when you have no share in the danger.
But nothing is sweeter than to occupy the lofty sanctuaries
of the wise, well fortified by calm learning,
from which you may look down on others and see them wandering
everywhere, straying and seeking the path of life —
competing in talent, contending in nobility,
striving night and day with surpassing effort
to rise to the heights of wealth and to seize power.
O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts!
In what darkness of life, in what great dangers,
is spent this little span of time — whatever it is! Do you not see
that nature cries out for nothing other than this:
that the body be free from pain, and that the mind enjoy
a sense of pleasure, removed from care and fear?
Therefore we see that for the body's nature, very little is needed —
only what removes pain entirely —
and also that luxuries need not be many to sustain delight.

Nature herself requires no greater pleasure than this:
if there are no golden statues of young men throughout the halls
holding fiery torches in their right hands,
to supply light for nightly banquets,
if the house does not gleam with silver and shine with gold,
if the gilded, paneled halls do not resound with the lyre —
yet when men lie together on the soft grass
beside a stream of water, under the branches of a tall tree,
they refresh their bodies pleasantly at no great cost,
especially when the weather smiles and the season
sprinkles the green grass with flowers.
No sooner do the burning fevers leave the body
if you toss about on embroidered coverlets with crimson dye
than if you must lie in a common linen garment.
Since, therefore, neither wealth nor noble birth
nor the glory of kingship does anything for our body,
so too for the mind we must reckon they are of no benefit,
unless perhaps you see your legions swarming over the field,
stirring up the phantom of war.
When, with these same things, superstitions flee
from the swollen mind, and fears of death,
then they leave behind a life free of anxiety and care.
But if we see that these things are ridiculous and mockeries,
and that the fears and anxieties of men truly follow them,
and that men fear neither the clash of arms nor savage weapons,
but boldly walk among kings and the mighty rulers of the world,
holding no reverence for the gleam of gold
nor the brilliant splendor of purple robes —
why do you doubt that all of this is poverty of reason?
Especially when all of life struggles in darkness?

Book II

For just as children tremble and fear everything
In the darkness, so we in the light sometimes fear
Things no more worthy of dread than what children
Imagine and dread in the dark.
This terror of the mind, and this darkness,
Must be dispelled not by the rays of the sun,
Nor by the bright shafts of day,
But by the face of nature and her laws.
Now let me explain by what motions the generative
Bodies of matter beget diverse things, and break them down once made,
By what force they are compelled to do so, and what speed
Has been granted them to travel through the vast void —
Be sure to keep these teachings in mind.
For matter does not cling packed tightly together,
Since we see all things diminish little by little,
And as if flowing away over long stretches of time,
Withdrawing their old age from our eyes,
While yet the sum of things seems to remain unharmed.
This is because whatever particles depart
Lessen what they leave, and increase what they go to join,
Causing the one to age, the other to flourish in turn.
Yet they do not linger there; so the sum of things
Is forever renewed, and mortals live by mutual exchange.
Some nations grow, others diminish,
And in a brief span the generations of living creatures change,
Like runners passing on the torch of life.
If you think the first beginnings of things can stop,
And by stopping, generate new motions in things,
You wander far astray from true reasoning.
For since all things wander through the void, it must be
That the first-beginnings of things are carried either by their own weight,

Or by the strong blow of another; for swift from above
They meet head-on, rushing together, so that suddenly apart
They spring back — no wonder, since they are hardest of all things,
And solid weights obstruct nothing from behind.
And that you may see more clearly how all the bodies of matter
Are tossed about, remember that the universe has no bottom,
No resting place exists in the sum of things, nor any ground where
The first bodies might stand, since space is without limit and end.
It extends immeasurably in all directions everywhere,
As I have shown at length and proved by certain reasoning.
Since this is established, clearly no rest is granted
To the first bodies throughout the deep void,
But rather, driven ceaselessly in varied motion,
Some, struck together across great intervals, rebound,
Others are buffeted by blows across short spaces.
And those that are joined in closer combination,
Bound together in small intervals, rebound,
Entangled and held fast by their own interlocking shapes —
These form the strong roots of rock, and the fierce bulk of iron,
And other things of that same kind.
A few wander onward through the great void.
The rest spring far apart and recoil far
Across great intervals — these supply us with thin air
And the bright light of the sun.
And many more besides wander through the great void,
Cast off from combinations of things, unable anywhere
To be received and unite their motions.
Of this, as I shall explain, a likeness and image
Is ever before our eyes and presses upon us:
Observe, when the rays of the sun pour in, and when

Book II

They pour their rays through the dark spaces of houses,
And you will see many tiny bodies in many ways
Mixing through the void in the light of the rays themselves,
And as if in an eternal contest waging battles,
Struggling in troops without pause,
Driven constantly by unions and separations,
So that from this you may gather that the first-beginnings of things
Are always being tossed about in the great void,
To the extent that this small thing can serve as an example
For great matters, and give traces of understanding.
For this reason too it is fitting that you turn your mind to this:
The bodies that are seen to swirl in the sun's rays
Show that such turbulent motions of matter
Lie hidden beneath, unseen.
For you will see many particles there, struck by invisible blows,
Change their course, and, driven back, return,
Now here, now there, in every direction on all sides.
This wandering comes, you may be sure, from the first-beginnings of all things.
For the first-beginnings of things move first by themselves,
Then those small bodies that are, as it were, nearest
In size to the power of the first-beginnings,
Are struck and set in motion by their invisible blows,
And they in turn strike those that are a little larger,
Thus motion rises up from the first-beginnings and emerges
Little by little to reach our senses, so that those particles too are moved
Which we can perceive in the sunlight,
Though the blows by which they are struck do not appear openly.
Now, Memmius, from this you may learn in a few words
What speed of motion has been given to the particles of matter.
First, when the dawn scatters new light upon the earth,

And the various birds, haunting the remote groves,
Fill the soft air of those places with their liquid voices.
How suddenly the sun, rising at such a time,
Is wont to clothe all things, suffusing them with its own light,
Is plain and manifest to all of us.
But the vapor which the sun sends forth, and its clear radiance,
Does not travel through empty void, because it is compelled
To go more slowly, since the sun strikes apart the waves of air,
Nor do the particles of vapor travel one by one,
But bound together they move among themselves, clumped in masses.
Therefore they hinder one another simultaneously, and from without
Are impeded, so that they are forced to move more slowly.
But those first-beginnings which are solid in their simplicity,
When they move through empty void, and nothing outside delays them,
And they themselves, from all their own parts united
Into one mass, are carried together to the one place they have aimed for,
Must surely excel in swiftness of motion,
And be carried far more quickly than the light of the sun,
And traverse many times over the same span of space
In the time that the lightning flashes of the sun stream through the sky.
For they need not wait, held back by deliberate purpose,
Nor need individual first-beginnings be sought out one by one,
To see by what reasoning each thing is carried on.
But some men, ignorant of these matters, suppose that without the power of gods
Nature cannot, with such great effect, conform herself to human reason,
Change the seasons of the year, and bring forth crops,
And do all the other things that divine pleasure, leader of life,
Persuades mortals to approach and undertake,
And itself leads them, so that through the charms of Venus they propagate the generations.

BOOK [II]

Lest the human race should perish — for whose sake they pretend the gods created all things — yet in all matters they seem to have strayed far from true reason. For though one might not know what the first principles of things are, this much I would dare to affirm from the very logic of the heavens and from many other considerations: that the nature of the world was not created for us by divine power, so great are the faults with which it is endowed — faults which we shall later make plain to you, Memmius. Now we shall deal with what remains, concerning motion. Now is the place (I think) in these matters to confirm this point for you as well: that no corporeal thing can be carried upward by its own force, or travel upward — lest the bodies of flames deceive you on this score. For plants grow upward and take on increase, and bright crops and orchards grow upward too. Yet when all heavy things fall downward according to their weight, and when fires leap up to the rooftops of houses and swift flame licks at beams and timbers, we must not suppose this happens of its own accord without some force acting below. Just as when blood is discharged from our body it leaps up high and sprays its stream. Do you not also see with what force beams and timbers resist the push of water? For the more we thrust them straight down and press them hard with great force, the more eagerly the water thrusts them back upward and releases them, so that more than half of them spring forth and leap out. Yet in all this we do not doubt, I think, that all things in themselves would fall downward through the void. Thus flames too must be able to pass through the air...

Air, pressed upward, rises to take the place above, though its own weight strives to draw it downward.
Do you not see the nocturnal torches of the sky flying aloft,
trailing long streaks of flame across wherever nature has opened passages?
Do you not see stars and constellations falling to earth?
The sun too scatters all its heat from its high place in the heavens,
and sows its light across the fields.
So the sun's fire also bends down toward the earth,
and you see lightning bolts fly sideways through the rain.
Now here, now there, fires burst from the clouds
and rush together; their fiery force strikes the earth below.
This too, in these matters, we wish you to understand:
when bodies fall straight down through the void,
they are carried by their own weight at uncertain times,
and swerve a little from their course in uncertain places—
just enough that you might call it a change of direction.
For if they did not swerve, all things would fall straight down
like drops of rain through the deep void,
and no collision would arise, no blow be struck
among the first-beginnings, and nature would have created nothing.
But if someone thinks that heavier bodies,
moving more swiftly straight through the void,
could fall upon lighter ones from above and so produce
the blows that might give rise to generative motions,
he strays very far from the path of true reason.
For whatever falls through water and through air downward,
these things must accelerate their fall in proportion to their weight,
because the body of water and the thin nature of air
cannot equally delay each thing for equally long.

BOOK II.

But the heavier ones, being overcome, yield more quickly.
On the other hand, from no place and at no time
Can empty void persist anywhere in matter,
Without its nature yielding what it seeks to yield.
Therefore all things must be carried through the quiet void,
Driven together though unequal in their weights.
Thus the heavier cannot fall upon the lighter from above
And of themselves generate blows
That produce the varying motions by which nature conducts things.
Therefore bodies must swerve just a little —
No more than the minimum — lest we seem to invent
Oblique motions, and the truth of things refute us.
For this we see plainly and manifestly before us:
That weights, as far as in them lies, cannot travel obliquely
When they plunge downward — as anyone can observe.
But that nothing at all swerves from the straight path,
Who is there that could perceive such a swerve?
Next, if every motion is always linked in chain,
And new motion always arises from old in fixed order,
And the atoms by their swerving do not create
Some first beginning that might break the bonds of fate,
So that cause does not follow cause from infinity —
Whence comes this free will that living creatures possess throughout the world,
Whence is this will torn free from fate?
By which we move forward wherever our will leads us.
We also swerve our movements, not at a fixed time,
Nor at a fixed point in space, but where the mind itself directs.
For beyond doubt, in these matters, each person's own will
Provides the beginning, and from this motion spreads through the limbs.
Do you not see also, at the very instant when the gates of time are opened —

From the starting gates, the eager force of horses cannot burst forth all at once, though the mind itself desires it. For the entire supply of matter throughout the body must be gathered and set in motion through all the limbs, so that, joined together, it may follow the mind's impulse. Thus you may see that motion originates from the heart, and proceeds first from the will of the mind, then spreads from there throughout the body and limbs. It is not the same as when we are driven forward by the blow of another's great force and great impact. For then it is clear that the entire matter of the body moves against our will and is swept away, until the will reins it back through the limbs. Do you not see, then, that even though an external force drives many people and compels them to move against their will, and sweeps them headlong, there is nevertheless something in our chest that can fight against it and resist it? At its command, the supply of matter throughout the limbs and body is sometimes compelled to change course, and, though thrust forward, is reined back and comes to rest again. Therefore in seeds too you must acknowledge there is another cause of motion besides blows and weight, from which this power is born in us — since we see that nothing can come from nothing. For weight prevents all things from happening through blows, as if by an external force; but so that the mind itself not be compelled by an internal necessity in all its actions, driven as it were and forced to endure passively, it is the tiny swerve of the first-beginnings that brings this about — at no fixed place and no fixed time.

Book II

Nor was the store of matter ever more densely packed,
Nor spread across wider intervals than now;
For nothing is added to it, nor does any part of it perish.
Therefore, in whatever motion the bodies of first-beginnings
Move now, they moved in that same way in ages past,
And they will always be carried on in the same manner hereafter.
What has been accustomed to be born will be born under the same
Conditions, and will exist and grow and flourish,
As far as is allotted to each by the laws of nature.
No force can alter the sum total of things.
For there is no place outside the whole into which any kind of matter
Could escape, nor can any new force burst in from outside
To change the nature of all things and overturn their motions.
It is not surprising in this regard
That, though all the first-beginnings of things are in motion,
The whole nevertheless appears to stand perfectly still,
Except when something moves with its own individual body.
For the nature of first-beginnings lies far below
Our senses; and so, since you cannot perceive them,
Their motions too must escape you —
Especially since things we can perceive often conceal
Their motions when separated over distances of space.
For often on a hillside, woolly sheep cropping rich grass
Creep slowly on, drawn wherever the dewy fresh grass
Calls them with its gleaming invitation,
And the full-fed lambs frisk and play and sparkle —
All of which, seen from afar, blurs together for us,
Like a white shimmer resting upon a green hill.
Moreover, great legions filling the plains with their running march...

They fill the plains, rousing the spectacles of war,
Lightning there lifts itself to the sky, and all around
The earth gleams with bronze, the tramp of men's feet
Stirs a sound beneath, shouts make the mountains
Echo voices back to the stars of the sky.
Horsemen wheel around and suddenly charge
Through the middle, shaking the fields with violent force.
And yet there is some high place among the mountains from which
They seem to stand still, and the lightning to rest upon the plains.
Come now, learn in turn the first beginnings of all things,
What they are like, how widely they differ in their forms,
How varied they are in their many different shapes:
Not that many are endowed with a very similar appearance,
But because they are not all equal to all in common measure,
Nor is this a wonder, for since their supply is so great
That neither end nor sum of them exists (as I have shown),
It follows that not all of them are in every way exactly
Of equal thread, or shaped with identical form.
Moreover, the human race, the swimming creatures of changing kind,
The scaly fish, and the glad herds, and the wild beasts,
And the varied birds, those that haunt the joyful places of water
And throng the banks and springs and lakes,
And those that flit through pathless groves,
Take any one of these kinds and you will find
That among themselves they still differ in their shapes.
In no other way could a child recognize its mother,
Nor a mother her child — which we see they can do —
Nor less so, that men are known among themselves.
For often before the glorious shrines of the gods, a calf
Slaughtered beside the incense-burning altars falls,

A warm river of blood breathing out from the chest.
But the mother, bereaved, roaming the green pastures,
Leaves on the ground the imprints pressed by her cloven hooves,
Scanning every place with her eyes, if she might anywhere
Catch sight of her lost calf, and she fills with her laments
The leafy grove, returning again and again
To the stall, pierced with longing for the young bullock.
Neither the tender willows, nor the herbs fresh with dew,
Nor any rivers gliding along their banks
Can delight her spirit or suddenly turn aside her grief.
Nor can the sight of other calves in the happy pastures
Divert her mind or ease her sorrow —
So greatly does she seek something known and her own.
Moreover, the tender kids with their trembling voices
Know their horned mothers, and the frisky lambs
Know the bleating of the flock — as nature requires —
And each runs to its own udder for milk.
Finally, any grain, though not every grain alike,
You will see is similar within its own kind,
Yet some difference in form always runs through them.
Similarly we observe the race of shells
Painting the lap of the earth where the gentle waves
Of the curved shore wash the thirsty sand.
Therefore, again and again, by the same reasoning, it must be
That, since things consist of nature and are not made by hand,
The primordia of things fly about
In forms somewhat unlike one another for a single fixed shape —
This is easy for us to work out by reason of the mind.
Therefore lightning's fire flows much more penetratingly
Than fire born from our earthly torches.

For you might say that the celestial fire of lightning
Is composed of finer and smaller particles,
And therefore passes through openings that our fire,
Born from wood and created from earth, cannot traverse.
Moreover, light passes through a horn, while rain
Is repelled. Why? Unless the particles of light are smaller
Than those of which the nourishing liquid of water is made.
And though we see wine flow suddenly through a strainer,
Olive oil, by contrast, trickles slowly and lingers.
Either because its elements are larger,
Or more hooked together and intertwined with each other,
And therefore the individual first-beginnings cannot
Be drawn apart so quickly from one another
To pass individually through each opening.
Add to this that the liquids of honey and milk
Are handled with pleasant sensation by the tongue in the mouth,
While the foul nature of wormwood and bitter
Centaury twist the mouth with a hideous taste.
So you may easily understand that what can touch
The senses pleasantly consists of smooth and round particles,
While all things that seem bitter and harsh
Are held together by more hooked particles intertwined,
And for this reason tend to tear open pathways
In our senses and to break into the body at their entry.
Finally, all things good to the senses and harmful to the touch
Conflict with each other, fashioned of dissimilar shapes.
Do not suppose that the harsh, grating horror
Of a screeching saw consists of elements as smooth
As the musical melodies that musicians shape upon the strings,
Awakened by their skilled fingers.

Do not think that the first-beginnings of matter enter the nostrils of men with the same form when putrid corpses rot and reek, or when the stage is freshly sprinkled with Cilician saffron, and a nearby altar breathes out Panchaean perfumes. Do not assume that the good colors of things, which can delight the eyes, are made of the same seeds as those which sting the sight and force out tears, or those which appear foul and repulsive in their ugly form. For every sensation that soothes and pleases the senses either arises from a somewhat smoother first principle, or else, on the contrary, whatever is troublesome, harsh, and unpleasant is found to arise from matter that has some roughness in it. There are also things which rightly seem neither smooth nor entirely hooked with curved points, but rather have projections that are somewhat small and gentle — things that tickle the senses more than hurt them. Of this kind are tartar sediment and the taste of wine. Then again, hot fire and cold frost prick the senses in different ways — this is made clear to us by the sense of touch in each case. For touch — touch, oh sacred powers of the gods! — is the sense of the body, whether when something external insinuates itself into it, or when something born within the body harms it, or when something pleasurable issues forth through the paths of Venus, or when the seeds, stirred up within the body itself by collision, are thrown into disorder and confuse sensation. As if by chance you were to strike any part of your own body with your hand and thereby put it to the test.

Therefore the shapes of first-beginnings must differ widely,
Since they can produce varied sensations.
Further, those things which seem to us dense and hard
Must be made of particles more hooked together,
And held in place as though by interlocking branches.
In this category above all stand the adamantine rocks,
Which are accustomed to resist blows and stand firm,
And hard flints, and the tough substance of iron,
And bronze, which cries out in protest when struck and confined.
These things ought to consist of elements more smooth and round
That flow together in liquid form with fluid body.
For poppy seeds pour out easily, as does water,
And their gathered clusters do not hold together.
And its course on a downward slope is freely rolling.
Finally, all things which you see in a moment of time
Scatter — like smoke, clouds, and flames — must be so,
If not entirely of smooth and rounded elements,
Yet not so tangled as to be held back,
So that they can sting the body and penetrate rocks,
Yet not cling together, as we perceive each
To be given to the senses — so you may easily understand
They come not from tangled, but from sharp elements.
That bitter things you see, the same that flow as liquid,
Like the brine of the sea, need not be thought surprising.
For what is fluid is made of smooth and rounded particles,
Yet mixed with them are painful jagged bodies,
Nor need these be hooked to hold together —
They are evidently globular as well, though rough in texture,
So they can roll along yet injure the senses.
And so that the mixture of rougher with smoother may be

From where comes the harsh body of Neptune's realm,
There is a method of separating and seeing each apart.
Where sweet moisture more frequently percolates through the earth,
So that it flows into a hollow and becomes gentle,
It leaves behind the rough primordia of bitter matter
That are more able to cling in the soil.
Since I have shown this, I will continue to connect the point which
From this may fittingly lead to belief: that the primordia of things
Vary their shapes in a finite number of kinds.
For if this were not so, then certain seeds
Would have to be of infinite bodily size,
Since within the short span of any single body,
The shapes cannot vary greatly among themselves,
Given that the first bodies are made of minimal parts —
Take three parts, or add a few more.
For when you place all the parts of a single body,
Top and bottom, and pass them smoothly through your hand,
Having tried every arrangement, seeing what order each gives
To the appearance of the whole body's shape —
When that is done, if you wish to vary the shapes further,
You will need to add other parts, and from that it will follow
That you need still others, in like manner, as order demands,
If you again wish to vary the forms.
Therefore novelty of shapes follows upon increase of body.
So you cannot rightly believe
That seeds differ in infinitely varied forms,
Lest you be forced to make some of immense, boundless size —
Which, as I have already shown, cannot be proven possible.
Now before you stand barbarian robes and Meliboean purple gleaming,
Dyed with the color of Thessalian conch-shells,

The golden beauty of peacocks, glowing with charm,
Which things surpassed in color would lie neglected,
And the scorned scent of myrrh, and the taste of honey,
And the swan's song, and the intricate melodies of Phoebus
Fashioned on strings, would likewise be silenced, suppressed.
For always something more excellent would arise over another.
All things could likewise fall back into the worse,
Just as we said, into the better in the same way,
For to others something else in turn would seem more foul
To nose, to ears, to eyes, and to the taste of the mouth.
Since these things are not so rendered in reality, and a fixed
Limit holds the sum on each side, you must admit
That matter also differs in finite shapes.
Likewise, from fires to the cold frosts of winter
The range is finite, and measured back again by equal reckoning.
For heat is the limit, and cold, and the middle warmth
Lies between the two, filling out the sum in order.
Therefore created things differ within a finite range,
Since they are marked at both ends by a double boundary,
On one side by flames, on the other beset by rigid frosts.
Since I have demonstrated this, I will proceed to connect the argument
Which from this point fittingly draws proof concerning the first-beginnings of things,
Those which are perfected in similar shape to one another.
Since the varieties of shapes, though infinite in distance, must be finite,
Those that are alike must be infinite in number,
Or else the sum of matter must be finite —
Which I have already proved is not the case.
Since I have shown this, come now, in a few sweetly spoken
Verses I will demonstrate that the particles of matter
Hold together the sum of things from infinity throughout.

LIB.

On every side the succession of blows is unbroken.
For where you see that certain animals are rare,
And you observe that nature is more fertile in those regions,
Yet in some distant land and remote territories
Many of their kind may exist and fill their numbers,
As we see is the case above all with four-footed creatures:
Among these we count the elephants with their serpentine trunks, in whose India
Many thousands form a rampart of ivory,
So that it cannot be penetrated at all, so great is the force
Of those beasts, of which we ourselves see very few examples.
Yet even granting that, let it be as you wish:
Suppose some unique thing exists, singular in its native body,
To which nothing similar exists in all the world —
Still, unless the supply of matter is infinite,
From which it might be conceived and brought into being,
It could not come to be, nor could whatever remains of it grow further.
For consider: if eyes could take in only a finite number
Of the generative particles of a single thing scattered through all the world,
From where, and by what force, and by what chance would they come together
And unite in so vast a sea of matter, so alien a confusion?
They have no means, I think, of coming together,
But just as in a great shipwreck, when winds and whirlpools
Cause the great sea to scatter thwarts, keel,
Yards, prow, masts, and floating oars,
So that along all the shores of the world the drifting wreckage appears
And gives warning to mortals, bearing witness
To the treacherous snares of the sea, its strength and its deceit,
So that men may avoid them and never at any time trust it
When it smiles with the beguiling calm of a placid sea —
So too, if the first-beginnings of things were once finite for you...

You will establish that scattered through all of eternity
The heats of different matter must sweep apart,
Never able to be driven together into union,
Nor linger in union, nor grow by accumulation —
Both of which facts the plain evidence of things makes manifest:
That things are generated, and that things once born can grow.
It is therefore clear that in every kind of thing the first-beginnings
Are infinite, from which all things are supplied,
And that destructive motions cannot altogether prevail forever,
Nor bury life's preservation for eternity.
Nor again can the life-giving and growth-bringing
Motion forever preserve created things.
Thus in equal combat the war of first-beginnings
Is waged, drawn out from infinite time,
Now here, now there the life-forces of things prevail,
And in turn are overcome; mingled with death is the wailing cry
Which children raise as they look upon the shores of light.
Nor has any night followed upon a day, nor any dawn upon a night,
That has not heard, mixed with the sickly wailings,
The laments that attend death and grim burial.
It is fitting also to hold this truth sealed firm among these matters,
And to keep it committed to mindful memory:
That nothing whose nature appears before us
Consists of a single kind of first-beginnings,
Nor is anything made up without a mingling of seeds.
And the more powers and forces any thing possesses within itself,
So much the more does it show that the first-beginnings within it
Are of many kinds and of varied shapes.
First, the earth holds within itself primary bodies,
From which the vast sea, the rolling rivers, the springs —

BOOK II.

They constantly vomit forth, having fires from which they arise.
For the floors of the earth burn, set alight in many places.
From its depths the force of Etna rages with fires.
Then furthermore it has the means to raise up bright crops and joyful groves
For the peoples of mankind.
From it too may flow liquid leaves and glad pasture
To provide for the mountain-wandering race of wild beasts.
Therefore the great mother of the gods, and mother of wild beasts,
And sole author of our body, has been given this name.
The learned poets of ancient Greece sang of her
Driving a pair of lions yoked to her chariot,
Teaching that the great Earth hangs in the space of air
And that earth cannot rest upon earth.
They joined wild beasts to her, because offspring, however fierce,
Must be tamed and conquered by the dutiful care of parents.
They crowned the top of her head with a mural crown,
Because, fortified in key places, she sustains cities.
Adorned with this emblem, the image of the divine mother
Is now carried in awesome procession through great lands.
Various peoples, following the ancient rite of sacred custom,
Call her the Idaean mother, and give her Phrygian bands
As companions, because from those regions first
The growing of crops throughout the world is said to have begun.
They assign Galli to her, because those who have violated the divine power
Of the Mother, and been found ungrateful to their parents,
Are meant to be shown as unworthy to be considered fit
To bring living offspring into the shores of light.
Taut drums thunder under palms, and hollow cymbals crash around,
And horns threaten with their raucous song,
And the hollow Phrygian flute stirs the mind with its rhythm.

They carry weapons, violent signs of fury,
To terrify with the goddess's power the ungrateful minds and impious hearts of the common people.
And so when she is first borne through great cities,
She silently bestows her blessing of health upon mortals,
They strew her path with bronze and silver, enriching all around
With generous gifts, and shower rose blossoms,
Shadowing the mother with flowers, and the crowds of her companions.
Here an armed band (whom the Greeks call Curetes,
Said to be Phrygians) vigorously sport among themselves in competing bands,
Leaping joyfully to the rhythm, glad with blood,
Shaking their fearsome helmet-crests with divine power.
They represent the Dictaean Curetes, who are said
To have once hidden the infant cry of Jupiter in Crete,
While as boys they danced in swift chorus around the boy-child,
Armed, keeping time in swift chorus,
Armed, clashing bronze upon bronze in rhythm,
Lest Saturn, having caught him, consign him to destruction
And deal an everlasting wound to the mother's heart.
For this reason armed men attend the Great Mother,
Or because they signify that the goddess proclaims that men should be willing
To defend their native land with arms and courage,
And be a protection and an ornament to their parents.
Yet though these things are told well and splendidly,
They are far removed from true reason.
For the whole nature of the gods must of necessity
Enjoy immortal life in supreme peace,
Far removed from our affairs and separated far from them.
For free from all pain, free from dangers,
Powerful in its own resources, it needs nothing from us,

Book II.

It is not well seized upon for its merits, nor touched by anger.
The earth indeed lacks all sensation at all times,
And because it holds the first-beginnings of many things,
It brings forth many things in many ways into the light of the sun.
If anyone here wishes to call the sea Neptune, and grain Ceres,
And prefers to misuse the name of Bacchus
Rather than to give the liquid its proper name,
Let us grant that he proclaims this world to be the mother of the gods,
So long as in truth the thing itself be not so.
Often therefore, cropping the grass from one field,
The wool-bearing flocks and the war-like offspring of horses,
And herds of cattle, under the same canopy of sky,
Slaking their thirst from one and the same stream,
Live yet with different appearance, and each preserves
The nature of its parents, and imitates their ways in kind.
So great is the diversity of material in any kind of plant,
So great likewise in any stream.
Hence furthermore any single living creature from all its parts —
Bones, blood, veins, heat, moisture, organs, sinews —
Are made up of elements that are far apart from one another,
Perfected by the dissimilar shapes of their first-beginnings.
Then furthermore, whatever things are set aflame and burned by fire,
If they convey nothing else within their body
Whence they might throw out fire and send forth light,
And scatter sparks, and spread cinders far and wide?
Pursuing other things with similar reasoning of mind,
You will therefore find the seeds of many things
Conceal bodies within themselves, and hold various shapes.
Finally you see many things that have both odor and taste together,
And when desire is ready to touch them with the tooth —

These things are given back when offerings burn, the many gifts first among them.
These therefore must consist of varied shapes,
For vapor penetrates where juice does not enter the limbs.
Likewise juice moves separately, and the flavor of things seeps into
The senses, so you may know they differ in their primary shapes.
Unlike forms therefore gather into one mass,
And things hold together with a fixed seed.
Indeed throughout our own verses
You see many elements common to many words,
Yet you must acknowledge that verse and word differ
In that they are composed of different arrangements of elements.
Not because few letters are shared in common,
Nor that no two are identical among all,
But because they do not all equally match in all positions.
So likewise in other things many elements are shared,
Yet when the first-beginnings of many things are considered,
Their combinations can differ greatly from one another,
So that rightly from different elements are said to be composed
The human race, grain, and the flourishing groves.
Yet it must not be thought that all things can be joined
In any way at all, for then you would see monstrosities everywhere:
Half-beast forms of humans coming into being,
And tall branches sometimes sprouting from a living body,
And many limbs of land creatures joined to those of sea creatures,
And fire-breathing Chimaeras with terrible jaws
Feeding on nature throughout the all-producing lands.
But it is clear that none of these things occur, since we see
That all things, created from fixed seeds by a fixed mother,
Preserve their kind as they grow;
And it follows that this must happen by a fixed law of nature.

For from all foods, the particles proper to each spread inward through the limbs,
And joining with compatible parts, produce their motions.
But we see nature casting foreign particles back to the earth,
And many flee from the body, driven out by blind blows,
Which could not unite with any part, nor within
Conform to the vital motions and imitate them.
But do not think that only animals are governed
By these laws — a certain principle distinguishes all things.
For just as all things born are unlike one another throughout nature,
So it is necessary that they consist of primary particles of dissimilar shape.
Not because many do not share a similar form,
But because not all things are uniformly equal in all respects.
Since seeds differ from one another, it must follow that they differ
In their intervals, paths, connections, weights, and blows,
Their collisions and motions — which not only separate animal bodies
But distinguish lands from the whole sea,
And hold the sky apart from the earth entirely.
Now then, take in what I have sought out with sweet labor,
And do not suppose that white things you see before your eyes
Arise from white first-principles,
Or that things which are black were born from black seed,
Or that whatever color things are stained with,
You should believe the bodies of matter are tinted with that same color.
For the bodies of matter have no color whatsoever —
Neither like nor unlike the things they compose.
If it seems to you that no perception of the mind can enter into these bodies, you are wandering far from the path.

For those born blind who have never seen the light of the sun
can nonetheless recognize bodies by touch,
having known from the earliest age no color bound to them —
thus we may understand that our minds too can form
knowledge of things clothed in no color of their own.
Again, whatever we ourselves touch in the blind dark
we feel to be tinged with no color at all,
and this is what I shall now prove can indeed be so.
For every color changes entirely into all others,
yet the first-beginnings of things must not do this,
for something unchangeable must persist,
lest all things be utterly reduced to nothing.
For whatever passes beyond its own boundaries by changing
immediately becomes the death of what it was before.
Therefore, take care not to tinge the seeds of things with color,
lest all things be utterly reduced to nothing for you.
Moreover, if no color has been assigned
to the nature of first-beginnings, yet they are endowed with varied shapes,
from which they produce and vary all colors of every kind —
it matters greatly, therefore, which seeds combine with which,
in what arrangement they are held together,
and what motions they give to and receive from one another,
so that you may readily explain by example
why that which was dark in color just before
can suddenly become as white as marble —
as the sea, when great winds have stirred its surface,
turns to white-crested waves with gleaming marble brightness.
For you might say: what we often see as black
is so because its matter is disordered within it,
its arrangement among the first-beginnings altered, some added, some removed.

BOOK II.

This happens continuously, so that it appears glowing and white.
For if the waters of the sea were made of blue-colored seeds,
they could in no way turn white.
For however you may disturb them, whatever blue things there are,
they can never migrate to a marble-white color.
But if the seeds that make up the one pure brightness of the sea
are tinged with different and varying colors,
just as from other forms and various shapes
something square is often made, with a single figure,
so it would follow that, just as we see dissimilar forms in a square,
we should likewise see in the expanse of the sea,
even in any one place of pure brightness,
colors widely different from one another.
Moreover, dissimilar shapes do not hinder or obstruct
a square from being square in spite of them.
But varied colors of things hinder and prevent
the whole object from having a single brilliance.
Furthermore, the reasoning that leads us to attribute color to first-principles
falls apart, since white things are not created from white,
nor do things that appear black arise from black, but vary from other colors.
Indeed, white things arise far more easily from no color at all
than from black, or from any other color that fights against and opposes whiteness.
Moreover, since colors cannot exist without light,
and since the first-beginnings of things do not come forth into the light,
we may know that they are cloaked in no color.
For what color could exist in blind darkness?
Color is changed by light itself, because it shines differently
when struck by light directly or at an angle —
as with a feather...

How the feathers of doves appear in sunlight,
those that sit around their necks and crown their throats:
sometimes they flash red like bright fire-opal,
sometimes they seem, to the senses, to mingle
blue-green and emerald together.
And the peacock's tail, filled with abundant light,
changes its colors in like fashion as it turns.
Since these colors are produced by a certain stroke of light,
we must understand they cannot exist without it.
And since the pupil of the eye, when it perceives
what is called white color, receives a certain kind of impact,
and perceives another kind when it perceives black and the rest,
it does not matter what color the things you touch may have,
but rather what kind of shape best suits them.
Know then that the first-beginnings have no need of color,
but by their varied forms produce varied sensations of touch.
Moreover, since no particular color belongs to particular shapes,
and all the formations of first-beginnings can exist in any hue,
why are the things composed of them not equally suffused
with all manner of colors throughout every kind?
For then it would follow that ravens in flight
should often flash white color from white feathers,
and that black swans should be born from black seed,
or of any single or varied color whatsoever.
Furthermore, the more a thing is divided into tiny parts,
the more you may observe its color fading gradually away,
as happens when gold is torn apart into small pieces.
Purple — and the Phoenician red, brightest of all by far —

Book II.

When something is scattered and dispersed thread by thread into nothing,
you may understand from this that it first exhales all its color,
its particles dispersing toward the seeds of things.
Finally, since you grant that not all bodies emit voice
or odor, it follows from this
that you should not attribute sounds and odors to all things.
So too with the eyes: since we cannot see all things,
we may know that some things exist stripped of color,
just as some exist without any odor, remote from sound.
A keen mind can recognize these things
no less than it recognizes what is lacking in other respects.
But do not suppose that bodies stripped only of color
remain as first principles — they are also
free of warmth, and altogether of cold, and of hot vapor,
and they move about sterile of sound and bare of moisture,
and they cast no odor from their own body —
just as when you set about making the smooth liquid
of marjoram, or the nectar of spikenard's flowers, which breathe into the nostrils,
among the first things to seek is,
as far as one can find, the nature of odorless olive oil,
which sends no scent to the nostrils —
so that it may least carry into the compound the odors
already mixed and blended with its own strength.
Therefore, ultimately, the first beginnings of things
must not contribute their own odor to the things they produce,
nor sound, since they can send nothing forth from themselves,
nor likewise any flavor whatsoever,
nor cold, nor likewise heat, nor warm vapor.
And since all other things are such that they form mortal matter —
soft, pliant, crumbling, hollow-rotting, with an open body —

It is necessary that all things be separated from their first principles,
if we wish to place immortal foundations beneath things,
on which the highest preservation may rest,
so that all things do not return utterly to nothing for you.
Now those things which we see to have sensation must necessarily
be acknowledged to arise from things without sensation,
consisting of first principles — and plain evidence does not refute this,
nor do known facts at hand fight against it,
but rather they lead us by the hand and compel belief
that animals are born, as I say, from things without sensation.
For indeed one may see living worms emerge
from foul dung, when the damp earth, having caught a stench,
is soaked by untimely rains.
Moreover, all things transform into one another:
rivers turn into leafy plants and rich pastures,
pastures turn into cattle, cattle into our bodies,
and from our bodies the strength of wild beasts
and the bodies of winged creatures often increase.
Therefore nature turns all foods into living bodies
and from this produces all sensation in living things —
by no different reasoning than dry wood
bursts into flame and burns everything in fire.
Do you not see then how much depends on the arrangement
of the first elements of things, in what order they are placed,
and mixed together, what motions they give and receive?
What then is it that strikes the mind itself,
that moves it and compels it to express its various sensations?
Unless you believe that what is sentient is born from what is without sensation —
for surely stones and wood and earth mixed together
cannot render back vital sensation.

This above all in these matters it will be fitting to remember:
That not from all things indiscriminately, from whatever things create matter,
Can something capable of sensation be produced, or senses brought forth.
But it matters greatly, first, how small are the elements that make up things,
What shapes those that produce sensation possess,
What their motions, arrangements, and positions are —
None of which we see in wood or clods of earth.
And yet when these are rotted through by rain,
They give birth to little worms, because the bodies of matter,
Stirred from their ancient arrangements by something new,
Are combined in such a way that living creatures must be born.
Then those who hold that sensation can be created from sensate elements,
Making them in turn from others accustomed to feeling,
Things that make soft tissue — for all sensation is joined
To viscera, nerves, and veins, which we see everywhere
Consist of soft matter created in a mortal body —
But even grant that these could last forever,
They must still either possess the sensation of a part,
Or be thought similar to whole living creatures.
But parts cannot feel on their own — that is necessary.
For the hand cut off from us, and no other
Single part of the body, can hold sensation alone.
It follows then that they must be likened only to living creatures,
So that they can share in vital sensation throughout.
How then can the first-beginnings of things be called living,
And avoid the paths of death, when they are animals?
And that they should be one and the same as mortal animals?
Yet if they could do this through combination and union,
They will produce nothing beyond a crowd and throng of living things.

Just as humans, cattle, and wild beasts cannot
By coming together generate any thing among themselves,
So too must those things that are smallest be capable of sensation.
But if they chance to shed their own sense from their body
And take on another, what was the point of assigning what
Is then taken away — and besides, we avoid that very conclusion.
Since we see living things transformed into chicks,
And worms teeming from the earth,
When putrefaction has begun after untimely rains,
We may know that sensation can arise from what has no sensation.
But if someone should say that sensation arises
Not from sense itself, but from mobility of sense,
Before the creature is born and brought forth into the world,
It will be enough to make this point plain and to demonstrate:
That a creature is not formed except from a prior union,
And that nothing is changed without a coming-together.
In the first place, no body can possess
Sensation before the very nature of the living creature is born.
For the matter is scattered and held apart
In air, in rivers, in earth, and in created flames,
And has not yet come together in life-giving union,
Nor contributed among itself those motions by which,
Guarding all things, the senses tend the living creature.
Furthermore, when a blow greater than its nature can bear
Suddenly strikes a living creature and confounds
All the senses of the body and of the mind,
The arrangements of the first-elements are dissolved,
And the vital motions are hindered deep within,
Until the matter, shaken throughout the limbs,
Loosens the vital knots of the soul from the body.

These very things must themselves consist of elements,

For you would say I follow any argument, laughing at me.
And that wisdom arises from these same things that produce it.
But if we see these ideas as mad and senseless,

Why then can those things not exist which we see sense,

In short, we are all born of heavenly seed;

And, made fertile, brings forth bright grain and joyful orchards,
And the human race, and brings forth all generations of wild beasts,
Providing the food on which all bodies are nourished
And lead a sweet life, and propagate their offspring.
Therefore she has rightly received the name of Mother.
Likewise, what was once of earth returns back
Into the earth, and what was sent from the shores of the sky
The shining temples of heaven receive back again.
Nor does death so destroy things that it annihilates
The bodies of matter, but scatters their union,
Then joins one thing to another, and causes all things
To change their forms and alter their colors,
And to acquire senses, and yield them up in a moment of time.
So that you may know how to trace the first beginnings of things,
With what elements they are combined and in what arrangement held,
And what motions they exchange among themselves and produce.
And do not think that things eternal could have rested long unchanged.

(Book II)

We see the primary particles floating on the surface of things, and sometimes born and suddenly perishing. Indeed it matters in our verses too, with which elements and in what order each is placed. For the same letters signify sky, sea, lands, rivers, sun; they signify crops, trees, living creatures — if not all things, then by far the greatest part is alike, yet it is their arrangement that makes things differ. So likewise in things themselves, the intervals, paths, connections, weights, blows, collisions, motions, order, position, and shapes of matter — when these are changed, things themselves must also change.

Now give your mind attentively to true reasoning, for a strikingly new understanding is striving to reach your ears and reveal a new appearance of things. Yet nothing is so easy that it is not, at first, more difficult to believe; and likewise nothing is so great and so wonderful that all people do not gradually cease to marvel at it.

Consider first the clear and pure color of the sky, and all that the wandering stars hold within it on every side, the moon, and the sun with its brilliant splendor — if all these were now appearing to mortals for the first time, suddenly presented as if unexpected, what could be called more marvelous than these things? What would people previously have dared to believe could exist? Nothing, I think, would have been so worthy of wonder. Yet now, no one, wearied and sated with seeing, deigns to look up at the bright quarters of the sky. Therefore, cease to be terrified by the mere novelty of things —

It shakes things with its thunder, hurls lightning bolts, and often

And many things, after the world's generative age, and the primal day

From which the sea and lands could grow, and from which

For from all directions the proper bodies are distributed

Moisture flows to moisture, earth grows by earthly matter,
Fire is hammered out by fires, and aether by aether.
And finally, nature the creator of things leads everything
To the uttermost limit of growth,
So that there comes a point where no more is taken in
Through the vital veins than flows and passes away —
At that point, age must stand still for all things.
Here nature reins in growth with her own forces.
For whatever you see growing cheerfully toward increase,
And climbing step by step the grades of mature age,
Takes in more bodies than it sends out,
So long as food is easily absorbed into the veins, and so long
As things are not yet so widely spread that they release much
And spend more than the age can consume.
For certainly we must concede that many bodies
Flow away and retreat from things, but more must come in,
Until they have touched the highest peak of growth.

BOOK II.

From that point on, little by little, strength and the vigor of full growth
Are broken, and age melts away toward its worse portion.
For the greater the mass of a thing, once its augmentation is taken away,
And the more widely spread it is in all directions,
The more it scatters its particles abroad and sends bodies away from itself,
Nor does all nourishment easily spread through its veins,
Nor is there thirst sufficient to seethe with its broad heat,
So that it can produce and supply as much
As is needed, and as much as nature requires to renew itself.
Rightly, therefore, all things perish, when, worn thin by the flowing away,
They are overcome by blows from without,
Since in great old age food at last fails.
Nor do the bodies that beat upon things from without cease
To wear them away and overcome them with hostile blows.
So too the great walls of the world, when they have been stormed,
Shall all give way to ruin and crumbling decay.
For food must renew all things by its restoring,
And food must prop all things and sustain them—
All in vain, since the veins cannot hold
What is sufficient, nor does nature supply as much as is needed.
And now so worn out is the age, and so worn out is the earth,
That it can scarcely create small creatures, it that once created all the ages
And gave birth to the enormous bodies of wild beasts.
For it was not, I think, by a golden rope let down from heaven above
That mortal generations were lowered into the fields.
Nor did the sea nor the waves beating on the rocks create them,
But the same earth that now feeds them from herself gave them birth.
Moreover, bright crops and the joyous vines
She first created by herself of her own accord for mortals,
She herself gave sweet fruits and rich pastures.

Who utterly disrupts human life from its depths,

For shameful contempt and bitter poverty

BOOK III.

Hence men, driven by false terror, though they wish to have fled far, far away, stir up strife with civil bloodshed and greedily heap up riches, piling slaughter upon slaughter. Cruelly they rejoice at a brother's bitter death, and hate and fear the tables of their own kin. By the same reasoning, from this same fear, envy gnaws at them when they see another man of power before their eyes, and another admired who walks in bright honor, while they themselves complain of wallowing in darkness and filth. Some perish for the sake of statues and a name; and often, so great is their dread of death, hatred of life and the sight of the light seizes men, so that with grieving heart they bring death upon themselves, forgetting that this fear is the very source of all their cares. This fear drives men to violate honor, to break the bonds of friendship, and in short, to overturn all piety. Many have already betrayed their homeland and their dear parents, seeking to escape the halls of Acheron. For just as children tremble and fear everything in blind darkness, so we sometimes fear in the light things no more worthy of fear than what children shudder at in the dark and imagine will come to pass. This terror of the mind, then, and this darkness must be scattered not by the rays of the sun nor the bright shafts of day, but by the face and reasoning of nature. First, I say that the mind — which we often call the intellect — in which dwells the guidance and governance of life, is nonetheless a part of a human being, just as the hand, the foot, and the eyes are parts of the whole living creature.

Although many in the crowd of wise men have believed
that the sensation of the mind is not fixed in any one place,
but is rather a certain vital disposition of the body,
which the Greeks call harmony, and which makes us
live with sensation, though the mind resides in no single part,
just as good health is often said to exist
in the body, yet is itself no part of the healthy person,
so they do not place the mind's sensation in any fixed part —
in this they seem to me to err greatly.
Often enough a body is visibly sick,
yet we take pleasure in some other part that is well;

Moreover, when the limbs are given over to gentle sleep,

Now, so that you may also understand that the soul exists within the limbs,

Yet we must not suppose this nature to be simple.
For a thin breath departs from the dying, mixed with vapor,

Nor is there any heat that does not have air mixed with it.
Since its nature is rare, it must be
that many particles of air move among it.
So the nature of the mind has now been found to be threefold,
yet even all these together are not enough to produce sensation,
since none of these can be the source of
the sense-bearing motions that the mind turns over within itself.
Therefore a fourth nature must be assigned to these,
one entirely without a name,
than which nothing more mobile or more fine exists,
nor anything made of smaller or smoother elements —
it was this that first distributed sense-bearing motions through the limbs.
For it is set in motion first, being composed of tiny perfect shapes.

From there heat gets its motion, and the blind force of the winds,

Now how these things are mixed together among themselves,

Yet I will touch on it as best I can, in summary.
For the first-beginnings of the elements run among each other
In their motions so that no single one can be separated out,
Nor can their power exist divided in space,
But they exist as if multiple parts of one single body.
Just as in any living creature one may commonly observe
Odor and a certain warmth and flavor, and yet from all
These together there is one complete bodily growth.
So heat and air and the blind force of the winds,
Being mingled, create one nature, and that mobile

Is the source from which feeling-bearing motion first arises through the organs.
For this nature lies hidden deep within, and underlies all,
Nor is there anything deeper than this in our body.
And the anima is moreover the soul of the whole mind itself.
Just as in our limbs and in the whole body

The hidden power of the mind is a blended force, the soul's own capacity,
because it is created from small and few particles.
So this force, lacking a name, made of tiny
bodies, spreads widely, and the mind is, as it were, the whole of itself

By similar reasoning, wind, and air,

There is also that heat which the mind takes on in anger,

There is also the abundant cold air that accompanies fear,
