There is also that calm condition of air
which comes with a tranquil breast and a serene expression.
But those whose hearts are fierce have more of the hot element,
and their passionate minds readily boil over in anger.
Of this kind above all is the violent nature of lions,
who often burst their chests with roaring and groaning,
and cannot contain the surging floods of rage within their breasts.
But the cold mind of deer is more full of wind,
and more quickly stirs icy currents through their vitals,
which cause a trembling motion to arise in their limbs.
But the nature of cattle lives by a calmer air,
and the smoky torch of rage, spreading the shadows of blind darkness,
never strikes them too fiercely beneath its yoke,
nor are they frozen stiff, pierced by the icy darts of fear.
They stand between the two — between the deer and the savage lions.

BOOK III.

Such is the nature of humankind: although education
May refine certain people equally, it still leaves behind
The first traces of each person's natural character,
And one must not think that faults can be uprooted entirely.
One person tends more readily to fall into sharp anger,
Another is somewhat more quickly touched by fear, while yet another
Takes certain things more calmly than is right.
In many other respects, people must necessarily differ —
The varied natures of men, and the habits that follow from them.
The hidden causes of these differences I cannot now set out,
Nor can I find names enough for all the shapes of atoms
From which this variety of things originates.
One thing I can affirm about these matters:
The traces of natural character left behind are so small
That reason cannot drive them out by argument,
So that nothing prevents one from living a life worthy of the gods.
This nature, then, is held within the body on all sides,
And is itself the body's guardian and the source of its health.
For soul and spirit cling together by common roots,
And cannot be torn apart without destruction to both.
Just as it is not easy to extract the scent from lumps of frankincense
Without destroying its very nature in the process,
So it is not easy to draw the nature of mind and spirit
Wholly from the body without everything dissolving,
So interwoven are they from their first origin,
That they share a life bound together in partnership,
And neither the power of body nor that of mind
Seems able, apart from the other, to feel anything on its own.
Rather, sensation — kindled for us through our vitals —
Is stirred up from the motions common to them both.

Besides, the body is never by itself brought into being,
Nor does it grow, nor seem to endure after death.
For as water does not often lose its flavor,
Which was given to it, nor is the vessel itself disrupted by this cause,
But remains unharmed — not so, I say, can the limbs left behind
Bear the separation of the soul,
But they wholly perish when torn apart, and rot away together.
From the very beginning of life, body and soul
Learn together the vital interactions of motion,
Even while sheltered in the mother's womb and belly,
So that their separation cannot occur without destruction and ruin,
So that you may see, since the cause of health is joined,
That their natures too exist in conjunction.
As for the remaining argument, if anyone denies that the body feels,
And believes that the soul, blended throughout the body,
Takes up that motion which we call sensation,
He struggles against what is plain and evident and true.
For who would claim what it is for the body to feel,
If not what experience itself has made plain and taught us?
But when the soul is gone, the body lacks all sensation everywhere.
For it loses what was not its own property in life,
And loses much else besides when the soul is expelled.
To say furthermore that the eyes can see nothing of themselves,
But that the mind sees through them, as through open doors —
This is difficult to maintain, when the very senses lead the other way.
For the sense itself draws us, and drives our sight toward the objects,
Especially since we often cannot look upon brilliant lights
With our own eyes, because they are overpowered by them —
Which does not happen with doors, for the doorways thrown open
Do not themselves suffer any difficulty from what we see through them.

BOOK III.

Besides, if our eyes serve as windows before the door,
it would seem the mind should see things more clearly
with the posts themselves removed when the eyes are taken away.
You could by no means accept that view in these matters
which the revered opinion of Democritus sets forth:
that the first elements of body and mind are placed
alternately, one by one, joined together and binding the limbs.
For since the elements of the soul are much smaller
than those of which our body and inner organs consist,
they also yield in number, and are scattered sparsely through the limbs —
so much so that you may only promise this:
that the primary particles, being so tiny, thrown into us, can stir
sensory motions in the body of such magnitude
as the intervals that the first beginnings of the soul hold apart.
For we do not feel the dust clinging to our body,
nor chalk striking and settling on our limbs,
nor mist at night, nor the spider's thin threads
that we encounter as we walk into them,
nor a worn garment fallen upon our head,
nor feathers of birds, nor floating seeds of plants,
which fall more often than not with their excessive lightness.
Nor do we feel the sudden movement of any creature whatsoever,
nor the individual footprints which gnats and the rest
place upon our body.
So greatly must many seeds first be stirred within us,
mixed throughout our body in our limbs,
before the first beginnings of the soul, shaken, begin to feel it,
and before, jostling across such great intervals, they can
rush together, collide, and spring apart in turn.
And the mind is more the keeper of the stronghold of life.

And more dominant for life, whatever the animating force may be.
For without mind and spirit, no part of the soul can reside
Even a brief moment of time throughout the limbs,
But follows as a companion, and easily departs into the air,
And leaves the cold limbs in the chill of death.
But he remains in life whose mind and spirit have stayed,
Even though, cut all around, he is mangled in his limbs,
A trunk, with the soul stripped away on all sides and limbs removed,
He lives, and breathes the vital airs of the sky,
If not with all, yet with a great part of the soul;
Deprived of it, he nevertheless lingers unwillingly and holds on.
Just as when the eye is lacerated all around, if the pupil remains
Unharmed, the living power of sight remains intact,
Provided you do not destroy the whole orb of light,
But trim the visual field and leave it alone —
For even that will not happen without harm to them.
But if that tiny central part of the eye is eaten away,
Though the orb is otherwise unharmed and bright,
The light immediately fails, and darkness follows.
By such a bond are soul and spirit always joined together.
Come now, so that you may understand that living creatures have
Minds and souls that are by nature mortal and light,
I shall proceed to set forth verses worthy of your life,
Long sought and found with sweet labor.
See that you join both under one name,
And when I proceed to speak of the anima, calling it mortal,
Understand that I mean the animus as well,
Insofar as they are one thing between them, joined together.
First, since I have shown that it is composed of minute
And very much smaller bodies,

Book III.

Made of first-beginnings, as liquid water's moisture,
Or as mist, or smoke — for it far surpasses in mobility,
And is more readily moved by a slight cause,
Since it is moved by images of smoke and mist.
Just as in sleep, when drowsy, we perceive altars
Exhaling vapor on high, and carrying smoke —
For without doubt, these images are carried to us from afar.
Now therefore, since when vessels are shattered on every side
You see the moisture flow away and the liquid depart,
And since mist and smoke depart into the air,
Believe that the soul too is spread abroad and perishes
Much more quickly, and its primal particles dissolve sooner,
Once it has withdrawn from all the limbs together.
For if the body, which served as its vessel,
Cannot contain it when shattered by some cause,
And when thinned by the withdrawal of blood from the veins —
How could you believe that air, which is more rarified than our body, could contain it?
Moreover, we perceive that the mind is born together with the body, and grows with it,
And equally grows old along with it.
For just as children wander about with a weak and tender body,
So the judgment of the mind follows, slight and frail.
Then when age has grown strong with robust powers,
The counsel too is greater, and the strength of the mind increases.
But afterward, when the body has been battered by the powerful forces of time
And the limbs have fallen with their strength blunted,
The intellect limps, the tongue rambles, and the mind wanders,
All faculties fail and give out at the same time.
It follows therefore that the entire nature of the soul also dissolves,
Like smoke, into the high winds of the air.

Since we see that mind and body are born together, and grow together, and (as I have shown) together wear out with age, there is this further point: we see that the body itself takes on terrible diseases and hard toil, and likewise the mind suffers sharp anxieties, grief, and fear. It follows therefore that the mind must share in death as well. Moreover, in the wandering byways of bodily disease the mind often goes astray; for madness comes upon it and it raves. At times, under heavy lethargy, it is carried into a deep and eternal sleep, with eyes and face drooping. There it can no longer hear voices, nor recognize the faces of those who stand around weeping, their cheeks wet with tears, calling it back to life. Therefore you must acknowledge that the mind too is dissolved, since the contagion of disease penetrates into it. For pain and disease are both architects of death — as we have learned well from the destruction of many — and since we see that the mind can be healed, just as a sick body, and bent by medicine in like manner. Moreover, when the sharp power of wine has penetrated a man and its fire has spread into his veins, heaviness of limbs follows, his staggering legs give way, his tongue grows slow, his mind soaks, his eyes swim, shouting, hiccuping, and quarreling break out. And all the other things of this kind that follow — why do they occur? Only because the violent force of wine is accustomed to disturb the soul while still within the body. But whatever things can be disturbed and impeded show, if a somewhat more powerful cause presses in, that they will perish, robbed of their future life.

Moreover, someone in our sight is often struck down suddenly by the violent force of disease, as if by a thunderbolt — he falls, foams at the mouth, groans, his limbs tremble, he loses his reason, his muscles stretch taut, he writhes and gasps, and tosses his limbs about without rest. This happens because the force of disease, spread through his limbs, churns the soul as storms stir the salt-foaming waves with the powerful strength of winds. A groan is wrung out because his limbs are racked with pain, and because the seeds of voice are driven out and hurled in a mass through the mouth along their accustomed and well-worn path. Derangement follows because the power of mind and soul is thrown into turmoil and, as I have shown, torn apart and scattered by that same poison. Then, when the cause of the disease has turned back and the sharp corrupted humor retreats into its hiding places in the body, the sufferer first rises staggering, and then gradually returns to his senses and recovers his soul. Since, therefore, mind and soul suffer such great disturbances within the body itself, and are torn and tormented in such wretched ways, why do you believe they could survive outside the body, in the open air, amid the buffeting winds for an age? And since we observe the mind being healed, just as a sick body can be, and see that medicine can alter it, this too foretells that the mind lives a mortal life. For whoever undertakes to add parts to the mind, or to transpose their order, or to take anything away from the whole, or to alter a person's disposition, seeks to bend its very nature or any other nature whatsoever.

It does not wish to have any part of itself transferred away or diminished — that which is immortal does not wish to lose even a drop. For whatever changes and passes beyond its own boundaries, that is immediately the death of what it was before. Therefore if the soul either sickens and shows signs of mortality, or is altered by medicine, this sufficiently proves to one who examines it that false reasoning appears to encounter true things, and to block every avenue of escape, and to refute with two-edged argument what is false.

Moreover, it is often the case that a person dies gradually, limb by limb, losing vital sensation piece by piece. First the toes and nails of the feet grow livid, then the feet and legs die, then afterward the cold traces of death creep step by step through the other limbs. Since the nature of the soul is thus divided and does not exist whole at one moment, it must be considered mortal.

But if perhaps you suppose that the soul can draw itself inward through the limbs and gather its parts into one, and thereby concentrate sensation in all members — yet that place where so great a store of soul is gathered ought then to appear to have greater sensation. Since this is nowhere the case, the soul is clearly scattered abroad and perishes.

Furthermore, even if one were willing to grant what is false — that the soul can be gathered together in the body of those who are dying one part at a time — still, you must admit that the soul is mortal. Nor does it matter whether it perishes scattered through the winds or shrinks together from its own parts and grows numb. As the senses more and more from every side abandon the whole man...

BOOK III.

Life diminishes and grows less from all sides,
And since the mind is one part of a human being, fixed
In a certain place, just as the ears and eyes are,
And the other senses that govern life throughout,
And just as a hand, or an eye, or a nostril, separated
From us, cannot sense or exist on its own,
But still perishes in a brief time,
So the mind by itself cannot exist without the body, and without
The person himself, whose very essence it seems to be,
Or whatever else one might more fittingly imagine,
Since the body is bound to it by connection.
The living power of body and mind together
Joined as one, enjoy life and its vitality,
Nor can the nature of the mind alone, without the body,
Produce vital motions, nor can the body
Without the soul endure and make use of the senses.
Just as an eye, torn from its roots, cannot
Perceive anything when separated from the whole body,
So the soul and mind seem able to do nothing on their own.
Because they are mixed throughout veins and organs,
Through nerves and bones, held by the whole body,
And their first elements cannot leap freely
Across great intervals; thus, enclosed, they will produce
Sense-carrying motions, which once cast out beyond the body
Into the breezes of air after death they cannot produce,
Because they are not held together in the same way.
For air strikes the body and the spirits equally, if the soul
Can contain itself and enclose within them those motions
Which it formerly drove through nerves and in the body itself.
Therefore, again and again, once the entire covering of the body

Once the vital breath has been expelled from the body's shelter, it must be admitted that the senses of the mind dissolve, since the cause is joined to both body and soul. And since the body cannot endure the separation from the soul without rotting away in foul odor, why do you doubt that the soul's power has streamed out and dispersed like smoke, rising up from the very depths? And so the body, transformed by so great a rotting ruin, has utterly collapsed, because the foundations of the soul have moved out through the limbs, flowing along all the winding channels within the body and through its pores. In many ways you may understand that the nature of the soul has been scattered through the limbs, and was already torn apart within the body itself before it slipped out and swam into the breezes of the air. Indeed, even while life still turns within its limits, often some part of the soul seems weakened by some cause, and the face seems to languish as if in its final hour, and all the limbs fall limp and drained from the body. This is what people describe as the mind being struck ill, or the soul slipping away when alarm spreads and everyone strives to recall its last strength. For then the mind and all the power of the soul are shaken, and they collapse together with the body itself, so that a somewhat greater cause can bring about dissolution. Why do you doubt, then, that the soul, once driven outside the body, exposed and helpless in the open air without its shelter, not only cannot endure through all eternity, but cannot persist even for the briefest moment? For no one who is dying seems to feel it himself.

Book III.

The soul goes out unharmed from the whole body,
Not first approaching the throat and upper airways,
But rather failing in the region where it is located,
So that each sense dissolves in its own part.
But if our mind were immortal,
It would not lament so much, at death, its dissolution,
But would rather go outward, like a snake shedding its skin,
Or an old stag rejoicing in the shedding of its long horns.
Why, too, does the mind's power, thought, and reason
Come to be in the head, not in the feet or hands, but fixed
In one seat and in certain regions throughout,
Unless specific places are assigned to each thing for its birth,
And where each created thing can endure,
And thus exist in so many ways throughout all the limbs,
So that no disordered arrangement ever arises —
To such a degree does one thing follow from another, and flame is not
Normally born from rivers, nor cold generated in fire.
Moreover, if the nature of the soul is immortal,
And it can feel apart and separate from our body,
We must suppose it to be endowed with the five senses —
There is no other way we can imagine
That the souls in the underworld are called up from Acheron.
And so painters, and earlier generations of writers,
Have thus depicted souls as endowed with senses.
But neither eyes alone, nor nostrils, nor hands themselves
Can be the soul, nor tongue separate from it, nor ears
Can on their own perceive hearing, or exist independently.
And since throughout the whole body we feel
A vital sense to be present, and we see the whole to be animate,
If suddenly a swift blow were to cut through the middle

Some force separates each part from the other,
The vital power too is scattered and dispersed,
And being torn apart, it is cast away along with the body.
But that which is divided and parts into any fragments
Thereby denies itself an eternal nature.
They tell how scythe-bearing chariots cut off limbs
So suddenly in the hot confusion of battle,
That the severed part is seen trembling on the ground,
While yet the mind and vital force of the man,
Through the swiftness of the blow, cannot feel the pain,
And the mind, intent upon the passion of the fight,
Continues battle and slaughter with the remaining body,
And does not notice the missing left arm, taken away
With its shield among the wheels and the swooping scythes,
Nor that another has lost his right arm as he climbs and presses on.
Then another tries to rise though his leg is gone,
While the dying foot twitches its toes upon the ground,
And the head cut from the warm and living trunk
Keeps upon the ground a living expression, with eyes wide open,
Until it has surrendered all the remnants of the soul.
Moreover, if you should choose to cut with iron
A snake with flickering tongue and long sinuous body
Into many parts,
You will see each piece writhing separately from the fresh wound,
And spattering the ground with gore,
The front part seeking back with its mouth toward the rear part
In its burning pain, to press the struck place with its bite.
Shall we then say that whole souls exist in all
Those particles? But then it would follow
That one living creature had many souls within one body.

Therefore that which was one together with the body is divided, and so both must be considered mortal, since it is split into many parts equally.
Furthermore, if the nature of the soul is immortal and enters into a body at birth, why are we unable to remember the time before, why can we not recall having perished before, and that what now exists was only now created? Why do we retain no traces of things previously done?
For if the power of the mind has been so greatly changed that all recollection of past deeds has fallen away, that, I think, is not far removed from death.
Therefore you must admit that what existed before has perished, and that what now exists has only now been created.
Moreover, if the living power of the soul is customarily implanted in us only when our body is already fully formed — at the moment we are born and cross the threshold of life — then it would not be fitting for it to seem to grow together with the body and the limbs in the very blood itself, but rather it would be fitting for it to live alone by itself, as if in a cage, while the whole body nevertheless is flooded with sensation.
Therefore souls must be considered not free from origin, nor released from the law of death.
For it cannot be thought that souls, infused from outside into our bodies, could be so firmly bound — the whole of reality shows clearly that this is the opposite of what happens.
For the soul is so bound throughout veins, viscera, nerves, and bones, that even the teeth share in sensation, as disease shows, and the chill of cold water, and the sharp sensation of a stone pressing suddenly through soft food. And yet, so interwoven as they are, the souls do not appear able to depart...

That they can remain intact and withdraw themselves safely
From all the nerves, bones, and joints.
But if you think that the soul, breathed in from outside,
Normally flows through our limbs to remain within,
Then all the more will it perish, poured through the body.
For what permeates is dissolved — and so it perishes.
Distributed through all the passages of the body,
Just as food, when spread through limbs and members, is dispersed
And gives rise to another nature from itself,
So too the soul and mind, though they enter the body
Whole and fresh, are nonetheless dissolved in flowing through,
While their particles are distributed, as through passages, into the limbs —
The particles from which this nature of the mind is formed,
Which now rules within our body, born
From that soul which then perished, distributed through the limbs.
Therefore the nature of the soul does not appear to be
Without a birthday, nor is it exempt from death.
Furthermore, do seeds of the soul remain or not
In a lifeless body? If they remain and are present,
Then it cannot rightly be considered immortal,
Since it departed diminished, having lost some parts.
But if it fled away with all its members intact,
Leaving no parts of itself behind in the body,
From where do corpses breathe forth worms from rotting flesh,
And from where does such a mass of living creatures
Surge, boneless and bloodless, through the swollen limbs?
But if you believe that souls are breathed in from outside
Into the worms, and can come individually into bodies,
And do not consider why many thousands of souls
Should gather where only one departed — yet this remains, that

Book III.

We must inquire, and bring this into question:
Whether souls hunt out seeds of worms at last
And fashion them for themselves wherever they may be,
Or whether they slip into bodies already formed and perfect.
But neither can it be shown why they would act or labor thus,
Since without a body they have no way to do so;
Yet if disembodied, they would be tormented by disease, cold, and hunger.
For the body suffers more from these afflictions,
And the mind too endures many contagions from it.
Yet even granting that it is useful for them to fashion a body,
No way appears by which they could manage it.
Therefore souls do not make bodies and limbs for themselves,
Nor yet can it be that they slip into fully formed bodies,
For they could not be subtly interwoven with them,
Nor would shared sensation result.
Again, why does the fierce violence of lions
Follow their seed, and cunning follow foxes, and flight follow deer?
These traits come down from their fathers, and a father's fear spurs their limbs,
And all other such traits of this kind — why do all these things
From the earliest age grow up together with the body, mind and all,
If it is not because a fixed force of mind
Grows equally with the body from its own specific seed?
But if the soul were immortal and accustomed to change bodies,
Living creatures would have their natures all mixed together:
The hound of Hyrcanian breed would often flee
The charge of the antlered stag, and the hawk would tremble through the air
Fleeing the approach of the dove;
Men would lack reason, and wild beasts would have wisdom.
For it is argued on false reasoning that
An immortal soul is changed by the change of body.

For what changes, dissolves, and therefore perishes.
For the parts are transported and migrate in order,
And therefore they must be able to dissolve throughout the limbs,
So that all may perish together with the body.
But if they say that human souls always pass into human
Bodies, still you will ask why from a wise man
A fool can be born, and why no child is prudent,
And why the foal of a mare is not as learned as the strength of its sire.
If it is not because, from its own fixed seed,
The power of the mind grows together with the body.
Clearly they would have the mind grow tender in the tender body,
Which, if it now happens, you must confess
That the soul is mortal, since changed throughout the limbs
It so greatly loses its former life and sense.
For how will the power of the mind be able equally with the body
To reach the desired flower of age, confirmed in strength,
Unless it is a partner from the very first origin?
Or why does it wish to go forth outside the aging limbs?
Does it fear to remain shut in a rotting body,
Lest the house, worn out by the long span of age, fall upon it?
But there are no dangers for an immortal thing.
Again, that souls stand ready at the unions of Venus and the births of wild creatures
Seems ridiculous,
And that immortal souls should watch over mortal limbs,
Competing in number upon number, hastily racing
Among themselves to see which first and most powerfully insinuates itself.
Unless perhaps the compacts of souls are so arranged
That whichever arrives first flying, shall enter first,
And that they do not contend among themselves in strength at all.
Finally, in the air no tree, and in the deep sea

Clouds can exist, and fish cannot live in the open air,
Nor can blood be found in wood, nor sap in rocks.
It is fixed and determined where each thing may grow and be present.
So the nature of the mind cannot arise without the body,
Nor exist alone, apart from nerves and blood.
For if it could, the mind's power would much sooner
Be found in the head, or the shoulders, or the lowest heels,
And could grow up in any part it pleased,
Yet still remain in the same man, in the same vessel.
But since it is established that it consists in our body,
And it appears determined where the soul and mind can exist and grow,
We must all the more deny that they can endure
Outside the body as a whole.
Therefore, when the body has perished, we must admit
That the soul, scattered throughout the body, has likewise perished.
Indeed, to join the mortal with the eternal, and to think
They can act together and share mutual functions,
Is foolishness. For what could be more at odds,
More incompatible and discordant,
Than the mortal joined with the immortal and everlasting,
Together enduring savage storms in union?
Furthermore, whatever things remain eternal must either,
Because they exist with solid body, repel blows,
And allow nothing to penetrate that might more deeply
Dissolve their inner parts — as the bodies of matter
Whose nature we have shown before —
Or they must be able to endure through all time
Because they are free from blows, as the void is,
Which remains untouched and is not struck by any blow,
Or because there is no space available around them.

By what means things can separate and dissolve,
Just as the sum of sums is eternal, and beyond it
There is no place to which bodies might flee, nor are there bodies
That could strike and powerfully shatter it with a blow.
Moreover (as I have taught) the nature of the mind
Is not solid in body, since void is mixed among things.
Yet neither is it like the void, nor are bodies lacking
From the infinite, which might by chance arise
And overwhelm this mass of mind with violent force,
Or bring some other disaster and peril,
Nor does the extent of space and the depth of the void
Fail, in which the vital force might scatter,
Or be struck by any other force and perish.
Therefore the door of death is not closed to the mind.
But if it is thought to be immortal for this reason,
That it is protected and held fast by vital forces,
This is clearly far removed from true reasoning.
Either because things that come are not wholly full of health,
Or because what comes recedes for some reason,
Driven back before we can feel what harms us.
For besides the fact that there is sickness when the limbs ail,
There comes upon the mind that which torments it concerning future things,
And wears it with fear, and wearies it with cares,
And past sins and admitted wrongs gnaw at it.
Add to this the mind's own madness, and forgetfulness of things,
Add that it sinks into the black waves of lethargy.
Therefore death is nothing to us, nor concerns us at all,
Since the nature of the mind is held to be mortal,
And just as in time past we felt no distress,
When foes came from every side to join in battle,

When all things were shaken by the trembling uproar of war,
And shuddered horribly beneath the high breezes of the sky,
And it was uncertain under whose dominion, of either side, all human peoples
And lands and seas were to fall,
So too, when we are no more, when the separation
Of body and spirit has occurred — those two which joined us together as one —
Nothing at all, since we shall not exist,
Will be able to happen to us or stir our senses,
Not even if earth mingles with sea, and sea with sky.
And even if, after our body has ceased to feel, the nature
And power of the mind is torn away,
Yet this is nothing to us who are joined together as one
In the union of body and soul;
Nor, if time were to gather our matter together again
After death and restore it to its present arrangement,
And if the light of life were given to us once more,
Would even that concern us at all,
Once the continuity of our self has been broken.
And now those former selves we were are nothing to us,
Nor does anguish over those whom time will bring forth
From our matter trouble us any longer.
For when you look back over all the immeasurable span
Of past time, and consider how varied are the motions of matter,
You can easily believe that these same seeds
Have often been arranged in the same order as now,
Yet we cannot recover the memory of it in our minds,
For between then and now a break in life has intervened,
And all the motions of the senses have wandered and strayed.
For the man who is to suffer misery in the future must himself exist
At that future time, in order that ill may befall him.

Since death removes all this and forbids
those ills from gathering for the one who suffers,
we must know that the very same conditions
in which we now lie sick existed before we were born,
and that there is nothing to fear for us in death.
Nor can one who does not exist be wretched, nor does it matter
at all whether one was never born at any time,
when immortal death has taken away mortal life.
Therefore, when you see a man indignantly protest
that after death his body will rot away in the ground,
or be destroyed by flames, or by the jaws of wild beasts,
know that his words do not ring true, and that beneath them
lies some hidden sting in his heart, however much he denies
that he believes he will have any sensation in death.
He does not fully grant what he claims to grant,
nor does he truly uproot himself from life and cast himself away,
but unconsciously he imagines some part of himself still survives.
For when each person alive imagines his future,
that birds and beasts will tear his body apart in death,
he pities himself — for he does not truly separate himself at all,
nor does he sufficiently remove himself from that abandoned body,
but imagines himself standing there, tainting it with his own senses.
Hence he is indignant that he was born mortal,
and does not see that in true death there will be no other self
who could, while still alive, mourn his own destruction,
or stand and grieve that he lies there, being torn or burned.
For if it is evil in death to be mangled by the jaws of wild beasts,
I cannot see why it is not equally bitter
to be placed on flames and scorched by burning fire,
or to be suffocated, buried in honey, and to stiffen with cold
while lying on the surface of a frozen stone.

BOOK.

To be pressed and crushed beneath the weight of earth above.
No longer will your joyful home receive you, nor your devoted wife,
Nor will your dear children run to snatch the first kiss
And touch your heart with quiet sweetness.
No longer can you prosper in your flourishing deeds, nor be
A protection to your own — one cursed day, they say wretchedly,
Has taken all life's rewards from you.
But this they do not add: that no longing
For these things will remain within you any more.
If they could truly see this with the mind and follow through in speech,
They would free themselves from great anguish of spirit and fear.
You, as you now lie at rest in sleep, will be
For all remaining time freed from all bitter pains.
But we shall mourn you, burned to ash beside the dreadful pyre,
Insatiably, forever,
And no day will lift the grief from our hearts.
So this question must be asked: if all comes back to sleep and rest,
What is so bitter in it that anyone should waste away in endless grief?
People do this too, when they recline at table and hold
Their cups, and shade their faces with garlands,
And say sincerely: "Brief is this pleasure for poor mortals,
Soon it will be gone, and never can be called back again."
As though the greatest evil in death were this for them,
That thirst should burn the wretched, or dry heat scorch them,
Or longing for some other thing should settle upon them.
Yet no one then will miss himself or his life,
When mind and body alike lie still in sleep together.
For though we may sleep forever through all eternity,
No longing for ourselves afflicts us then.

And yet at that time those first-beginnings wander far through our limbs,
Far from the sense-bearing movements,
Until the man seized from sleep collects himself again.
Death, therefore, must be thought to matter even less to us,
If it can matter less, than what we see is nothing.
For a greater scattering of matter's mass follows upon death,
And no one awakens thereafter,
Once the cold pause of life has overtaken him.
And if nature herself should suddenly raise her voice
And rebuke one of us in these words:
"What ails you so greatly, mortal, that you indulge in excessive
Grief and lamentation? Why do you groan at death and weep?
Did not your past life flow freely before you,
And were not all its pleasures gathered as if into a leaking vessel,
Running through and away, ungrateful, lost?
Why do you not withdraw like a guest satisfied with life's feast?
Why not take your rest, fool, with a calm and peaceful mind?
But if all you have enjoyed has been squandered and lost,
And life itself is a burden, why seek to add more,
Only to have it perish badly and pass away thanklessly?
Why not rather make an end of life and toil?
For there is nothing more I can devise or find for you to enjoy:
All things remain forever the same.
If your body does not yet wither with years and your limbs
Are not yet worn out, still all things remain the same,
Even if you were to outlive all ages by living on,
And all the more so if you were never to die."
What can we answer, except that nature rightfully brings this charge
And sets forth the true cause in words?
But as for one who laments his death more than is right,

Does he not rightly cry out more loudly, and rebuke with sharp voice:
"Take away your tears, you fool, and restrain your complaints.
If one even older complains here,
Having enjoyed all the rewards of life, you wither away.
But because you always long for what is absent and scorn what is present,
Your life has slipped away incomplete and ungrateful to you,
And death has stood unexpected at your head
Before you could depart satisfied and full of life's pleasures.
Now set aside all things foreign to your age,
Come, with calm spirit yield to others — it must be so.
He rebukes rightly, in my view, and rightly reproaches and chides."
For old things are always driven out by the novelty of new things,
And it is always necessary to restore one thing from others.
No one is cast down into the pit or into dark Tartarus;
Matter is needed so that future generations may grow.
Yet all these things, once your life is done, will follow you.
No less than you, those before fell, and those after will fall.
Thus one thing after another will never cease to arise.
Life is given to no one as a possession, but to all on loan.
Look back and see how the ancient past of eternal time,
Before we were born, means nothing to us.
This, then, nature holds up as a mirror of future time
After our death — does anything terrible appear there?
Does anything seem grim? Is it not more peaceful than any sleep?
And indeed all the souls said to exist in deep Acheron
Are present for us in life itself.
No wretched Tantalus, as the story goes, fears the great rock
Hanging over him in the air, paralyzed by empty dread —
But rather in life an empty fear of the gods presses harder upon us.

Mortals fear chance, whatever fate may bring to each.
Nor do the birds haunt Tityos lying in the underworld,
Nor could they find anything to probe beneath his great chest
For all eternity, however vast the body he might display,
Though he spread his limbs across not merely nine acres
But across the whole circle of all the earth —
He still could not endure eternal pain,
Nor provide food from his own body forever.
But our Tityos is he who lies prostrate in love,
Whom the birds tear apart, and gnawing anxiety consumes,
Or whom cares rend asunder with whatever torment they bring.
Sisyphus too is before our eyes in this life —
He who seeks from the people the rods and cruel axes of power,
And always returns defeated and grim.
For to seek power that is empty and never truly granted,
And in that pursuit always to endure harsh labor —
This is to strain against the slope and push the boulder up the mountain,
Which yet from the very summit rolls back down again
And swiftly seeks the flat expanse of the plain below.
Then to feed forever the ungrateful nature of the mind,
To fill it with good things and satisfy it — never —
Which the seasons of the years do for us, coming round again,
Bringing their fruits and their varied pleasures —
Yet we are never filled with the fruits of life.
This, I think, is what the story means of maidens in the flower of youth
Who are said to pour water into a vessel full of holes,
Which yet can by no means ever be filled.
As for Cerberus, the Furies, the sunless void,
And Tartarus belching horrifying heat from its jaws —

These things are nowhere, nor can they truly exist.
But in life the fear of punishment for evil deeds
Is conspicuous among the conspicuous, and the atonement for crime:
Prison, and the dreadful hurling of men from the rock,
The lash, the executioners, the rack, the pitch, the iron plate, the torches —
And yet even if these are absent, the mind conscious of its own deed,
Fearing beforehand, applies goads to itself and scorches itself with whips,
And sees no end in the meantime that can be the boundary of its evils,
Nor what limit there can be to its punishments,
And fears all the more lest these torments grow heavier after death —
Thus in the end the life of fools becomes a hell on earth.
This too you might sometimes say to yourself:
Even good Ancus left the light of the sun,
Who was better in many things than you, scoundrel.
Then many other kings and rulers of affairs
Have fallen, who once held sway over great nations.
Even he who once laid a road across the great sea
And gave his legions a path to march over the deep,
And taught them to walk on foot over the salt lagoons,
And scorned the roaring of the waves, spurring his horses over the sea —
He too, his light taken away, poured out his soul from his dying body.
Scipio, the thunderbolt of war, the terror of Carthage,
Gave his bones to the earth, as if he had been the lowest of servants.
Add the discoverers of the arts and sciences, and of wit and charm.
Add the companions of the Heliconian Muses, of whom Homer alone
Having won the scepter, sleeps the same sleep as the rest.
And Democritus, when ripe old age
Warned him that the motions of his memory and mind were failing,
Went of his own accord to meet death and offered up his life.
Epicurus himself died when the light of his life had run its course.

Who

Who surpassed the human race in genius, and extinguished
All the stars as the heavenly sun rises.
Will you then hesitate, and feel indignant at dying?
You whose life is nearly dead already, though you yet live and see?
You who waste the greater part of your years in sleep,
And snore while waking, and never cease to see dreams,
And carry a mind burdened with empty dread,
And cannot find what it is that so often ails you, when
Wretched, you are pressed on all sides by countless cares while drunk,
And drift wandering with an uncertain mind in error?
If people could perceive, as clearly as they seem to feel,
That there is a weight upon the mind that wears it down with its heaviness,
And could understand the causes of it, and from where
So great and heavy a mass of trouble settles in the heart,
They would not live their lives as now we mostly see them do —
Each not knowing what he wants, and always seeking
To change his place, as if he could lay down a burden.
He who is bored at home often rushes out of his great house,
And then suddenly returns,
Since he feels no better outside.
He races his horses headlong out to his country villa,
As if rushing to bring help to a house on fire,
Then yawns the moment he has crossed the villa's threshold,
Or sinks into heavy sleep, seeking forgetfulness,
Or hurries back again to town and revisits it.
In this way each man flees from himself, yet since,
As must be, he cannot truly escape, he clings with greater bitterness and torment,
Because the sick man does not grasp the cause of his disease.
How well it would be, if each man, setting all else aside,
Would first strive to understand the nature of things.

Since of eternal time no single hour
Is granted us to know what state awaits
All mortals after death, however long they linger,
Why do we tremble so in doubtful dangers?
What great desire for life drives us to these evils?
Certainly the end of life stands fixed for mortals,
And death cannot be avoided — we must all meet it.
Moreover we revolve in the same round, endlessly,
And no new pleasure is forged for us by living on.
But while what we desire is absent, it seems to surpass all else;
Then once we have it, we desire something new,
And an equal thirst for life holds us ever open-mouthed.
And uncertain is what fortune the future years will bring,
What chance will carry to us, or what end looms near.
Nor by prolonging life do we subtract one moment
From the time of death, nor can we whittle down
How long we shall have perished by fate.
So though you live through as many ages as you will,
Eternal death will nonetheless await you still,
And no less long will he be gone from this day's light
Who made an end of life today, than he
Who perished many months and years before.

BOOK LVIII.
TITUS LUCRETIUS CARUS: ON THE NATURE OF THINGS
BOOK FOUR.

I wander through the pathless haunts of the Muses,
trodden by no foot before,
I love to approach untouched springs and drink from them,
I love to pluck fresh flowers
and seek for my head a glorious crown
from fields where the Muses have never yet wreathed any brow.
First, because I teach of great matters, and strive
to free the mind from the tight knots of superstition;
then, because I shed such clear light on dark subjects,
touching everything with the charm of the Muses.
For this too seems not without good reason.
Just as doctors, when they try to give
foul-tasting wormwood to children,
first coat the rim of the cup all around
with the sweet golden liquid of honey,
so that the unsuspecting age of childhood is tricked
at the lips, and meanwhile drinks down the bitter
draught of wormwood, and though deceived is not harmed,
but rather by such means is restored to health:
so I now, since this philosophy
tends to seem rather grim to those unused to it,
and the common people shrink back from it,
have wished to set forth our reasoning to you
in sweet-speaking Pierian verse,
and as it were touch it with the sweet honey of the Muses,
in hopes that by this means I might hold your attention

BOOK VI

In my verses I could, while you take in the whole
Nature of things, and perceive its usefulness.
But since I have taught the beginnings of all things,
What they are like, and how they differ in their varied forms,
How they fly about of their own accord, stirred by alternating motion,
And in what way each thing can be created from these elements,
And since I have taught what the nature of the mind is,
And from what elements it is joined together with the body to thrive,
And in what way, when torn apart, it returns to its first beginnings,
Now I shall begin to treat for you what is of great importance to these matters:
That there exist what we call images of things,
Which, like thin membranes stripped from the outermost surface of things,
Fly back and forth through the air.
These same images terrify our waking minds,
And often in sleep we behold strange forms,
Phantoms of those lacking light,
Which have often startled us in horrifying fashion as we lie in languid slumber,
Lest we think that souls escape from Acheron
Or that shades flutter among the living,
Or that something of us can remain after death,
When body and the nature of mind alike have been destroyed
And each has returned to its own first beginnings.
I say therefore that likenesses and thin shapes of things
Are sent out from things, from their outermost surface,
Which may be called, as it were, membranes or a kind of skin,
Because the image carries the same appearance and form
As whatever body it may roam abroad from, shed from it.
This you may learn from plain examples, dull of mind though you be.
First, since in plain sight many things give off bodies, partly scattered and dissolved,

Oak trees send out heat as their summit, and fires and vapor,
And partly more densely woven and compressed, as once
When cicadas in summer shed their old tunics,
And calves when at birth they send membranes from their body's surface,
And likewise when the slippery serpent
Strips its garment on the thorns. For we often see
The brambles enriched with their flying spoils.
Since these things happen, a thin image too must
Be sent off from the outermost surface of things.
For why those heavier films fall away and depart from objects,
Rather than those that are thin, no reason can be shown.
Especially since there are in the surfaces of things
Many tiny bodies which can be cast in the same order
As they were, and preserve their form and shape,
And much more swiftly, the less they can be impeded,
Being few and placed on the very outermost surface.
For certainly we see many things hurled and thrown,
Not only from deep below, as we said before,
But also from the very surface — above all, color itself —
As yellow and red awnings commonly do,
And dark-colored ones stretched with great poles in the theatres,
Spread along the masts and beams that hold them round about.
For there below they tint the whole assembly of the crowd, and all
The scenic show of fathers, mothers, and gods,
And compel them to flow with their own color.
And the more the walls of the theatre are enclosed around,
The more all within, bathed in that charm,
Smiles, flooded with the light of day.
Therefore, just as linen cloths send out their dye from their surface,
So too all images must send out their thin films.

BOOK IV.

Since all things hurl their surfaces from their utmost layer in both directions,
there exist already definite traces of forms,
which float about endowed with a subtle thread,
and cannot be perceived individually as separate things.
Moreover, every odor, smoke, vapor, and all similar things
abound diffused from bodies for this reason:
because while arising from outside and coming from afar,
they are broken apart along their winding path, and there are no straight
gateways through which they press to emerge together.
But on the contrary, the thin film of surface color,
when it is cast off, nothing is at hand to tear it apart,
since it lies positioned at the very front surface.
Finally, in mirrors, in water, and in every gleaming surface,
whatever images appear to us, it must be the case,
since they are endowed with a similar appearance to things,
that they exist, and consist of images sent forth from those things.
For there is no way to show why bodies should fall away
and recede from objects more than those thin forms
which objects that radiate from their open surface emit.
Therefore there exist thin likenesses of forms, dissimilar one to another,
images which no one can perceive individually,
yet by continuous and frequent reflection
they are thrown back and produce the appearance seen from the flat surface of mirrors,
nor can they be preserved in any other way
so as to render back so faithfully the likeness of each figure.
Now come, learn of what nature an image consists,
and first, since their first elements are so far below our senses, so much smaller
than what the eyes first found themselves unable to see:
yet now this too, so that I may confirm the beginnings of things

Book IV, [line] 60.
Grasp in a few words how fine all these things are.
First, animals exist that are so tiny
That a third part of them cannot be seen by any means.
What must one think of any intestine of these creatures?
What of the globe of the heart, or the eyes? the limbs? the joints?
How small are they? What then of the first-beginnings of each thing?
It is necessary to understand whence the soul and the nature of the mind consist.
Do you not see how fine they are, how minute?
Moreover, whatever things breathe out a sharp scent from their body —
all-heal, bitter wormwood,
and heavy southernwood, and gloomy centaury —
if you lightly touch any one of these,
straightway the images of things waft forth in abundance
in many ways, without force, and scatter through the senses.
How small a part of them is any single image, no one can say,
nor render account of it in words.
But lest you think that only those images wander
that withdraw from things,
there are also those that arise of their own accord, and are themselves
formed in this sky that is called the air,
as we see clouds easily gather on high at times
and mar the calm face of the sky,
carried aloft, formed in many shapes,
stroking the air as they move. For often the faces of giants
seem to fly past and trail shadow far and wide,
and sometimes great mountains and rocks torn from mountains
pass before the sun and follow after it.
Then other shapes draw along clouds of storm-beasts,
and the flowing forms cease not to change their appearance
and turn into faces of every kind.

Book IV.

Now, so that these things may proceed with ease and swift motion,
and flow perpetually from objects, gliding and giving way:
For always whatever is uppermost in things overflows,
and what is cast off, when it reaches other things,
passes through cloth first, but where it meets rough stone
or the substance of wood, there it is
broken up, so that it can render no image.
But when dense, bright things are placed opposite,
dense as a mirror especially, none of this happens.
For the images can neither pass through like cloth, nor be
broken up, since the smoothness preserves their integrity.
Therefore it is that images stream back to us from mirrors.
And however suddenly, at any moment,
you place a thing before a mirror, an image appears,
showing that textures of fine, thin forms
flow ceaselessly from the surface of bodies.
Therefore many images are produced in a brief span of time,
so that their origin is rightly called swift,
and just as the sun must send out many rays in a brief span
so that all things are perpetually filled with light,
so likewise it must be, by similar reasoning,
that images of things are carried in a point of time
in many ways, in all directions everywhere.
For whenever we turn a mirror to face anything,
the objects there respond with like shape and color.
Moreover, when the sky has been most clear and calm,
and then suddenly all around it turns foul and stormy,
as if all the darkness of Acheron had left its realm
and filled the great caverns of the sky —
so dreadful is the night of storm-clouds that has arisen.

The mouths of dark dread hang overhead,
Of which how small a part the image is, no one can say,
No one who could also give a reasoned account in words.
Come now, let me tell by what swift motion the images are carried,
And what mobility is given to them as they swim through the air,
So that a short hour covers a long stretch of space,
And in what direction each tends with its varied course —
I will tell this in sweet-sounding verse rather than in many lines,
As the swan's brief song is better than the clamor of cranes
Scattered through the southern clouds in the upper air.
First, one may often observe that light things,
Made of small particles, move with swift speed —
In this class is now the light of the sun and its heat,
Because they are made of tiny first-beginnings,
Which, as it were, are struck and driven through the intervals of air
And do not hesitate to cross, urged on by blow upon blow.
For light is instantly supplied by light,
And flash after flash is spurred on as if in relay.
Therefore images must likewise be able to cross
An immeasurable expanse of space in a moment of time.
First, because a very small cause from behind is enough
To propel and drive them forward.
Second, because they are sent forth with a texture so rare
That they can easily penetrate any matter,
And as it were seep through the intervening air.
Moreover, if any particles of things are sent down from on high
To earth, as the light and heat of the sun,
These are seen in an instant of the passing day
To spread themselves through the whole expanse of the sky,
And to fly over sea and land and flood the heavens.

What remains: since these things are carried with such swift lightness,
what then are those things that, ready from the very first,
when they are hurled forth and nothing delays their passage —
do you not see that they must travel faster and farther,
and traverse the manifold distance of space in the same
time that the sun's light floods the sky?
This above all seems a true proof of
how swiftly the images of things are carried in their motion:
for as soon as a gleam of water is placed
beneath the open sky, immediately under the starry heavens
the shining constellations of the world appear mirrored in the water.
Do you not see, then, in what a point of time the image
from the regions of the sky falls down to the regions of earth?
Therefore one must admit that there are exceedingly small
bodies that strike the eyes and assail our vision,
flowing perpetually forth from certain things as they arise —
as cold flows from rivers, heat from the sun, spray from the waves
of the sea, which eats away the walls along the shore.
And again, a salty taste of flavor often comes into the mouth
when we wander near the sea; and when we watch
absinthe being mixed, a bitter sensation touches us.
So universally from all things each particular thing flows forth
and is sent in all directions on every side,
with no pause, no rest granted to the flowing,
since we continually feel and can always
see, smell, and hear sounds.
Nor do varying voices cease to flit through the air.
Moreover, since a shape handled by the hands in darkness
is recognized to be the same as
what is seen in light and clear brightness, it must follow that...

For similar reason touch and sight are moved alike.
Now then, if we try a square shape, and it stirs us
in darkness, what can happen in the light to its appearance,
if not its image, square as it is?
Therefore there seems to be a cause for seeing
in these images, and without them nothing can be seen.
Now those things I call the films of objects are carried
everywhere, cast about in all directions.
But since we can perceive only with our eyes,
it follows that, wherever we turn our gaze, all things
there strike it with their form and color.
And how far each thing is from us, the image
makes us see, and enables us to distinguish distances.
For when it is sent out, it immediately drives and stirs
the air that lies between it and our eyes.
Thus it glides through all our sight,
and as it were brushes our pupils, and so passes on.
Therefore it comes about that we see how far off
each thing is, and the more air is driven before it,
and the longer the current that brushes our eyes,
the more distant each object appears to be.
Of course these things happen with exceeding swiftness,
so that we see at once what it is and how far away.
Nor should this be thought at all wonderful in these matters:
why, though the individual images that strike our eyes
cannot be seen, the objects themselves are perceived clearly.
For when the wind too beats upon us bit by bit, and when
the cold strikes us with its sharp air, we do not usually feel
each individual particle of wind or of cold,
but rather we perceive it as a whole, and we see it happening
as though the blows were being dealt within us.

Book IV.

When blows strike our body, as if some thing
Were striking us, and gave the sensation of its own body from outside.
Moreover, when we strike a stone with our finger,
We touch the outermost surface of the rock, its topmost color,
Yet we do not feel that through touch, but rather
We feel the hardness of the stone deep within.
Now come, understand why the image appears
Beyond the mirror — for it certainly seems far removed within.
Just as those things outside that are truly seen through transparent objects:
When a door gives an open view through itself,
It causes many things outside the house to be seen.
That vision too is produced by a double and twin air.
First the air on this side of the doorposts is seen,
Then the doors themselves follow, right and left,
Then the light from outside reaches the eyes, and another
Air, and those things outside that are truly seen through.
So when the image of the mirror first projects itself,
As it comes to our line of sight, it drives and stirs
The air that lies between itself and our eyes,
And causes us to perceive all that air first,
Before the mirror itself; but when we have sensed the mirror too,
At once the image that travels from us toward it
Arrives, and reflected, revisits our eyes,
And rolling before it drives another air,
And causes us to see that air before the mirror itself, and so
It appears to be set apart, at that same distance from the mirror.
Therefore it is not at all surprising
In those things that return a view from the smooth surface of mirrors
Along lines of air, since the thing is accomplished by both together.
Now as to which part of our body is the right hand side —

In mirrors it happens that the left appears on the right, because when an image meets and strikes the flat surface of the mirror, it is not turned back intact, but straight backward. So it is driven back, as if someone, before it dried, pressed a plaster mask against a pillar or beam. And if that image, preserving its frontal shape, then presses itself out reflected in reverse, the result is that what was the right eye is now the left, and what was the left is now correspondingly the right. Bright things, moreover, the eyes flee and refuse to look upon. The sun even blinds, if you try to gaze straight at it, because its power is great, and images fall heavily from on high through the pure air, striking the eyes and disturbing their structure. Furthermore, any intense brilliance burns the eyes often, because it possesses seeds of fire that cause pain by working their way into the eyes. Whatever jaundiced people look at turns yellow, because many seeds from the jaundice in their bodies flow out to meet the images of things and mix with what is in their eyes, and their contagion colors everything with pallor. What lies in darkness we see from light, because the nearer air of the shadow enters the eyes first and takes possession of them while open, and then the clear bright air quickly follows, which as it were cleanses them and dispels the dark shadows of the former air, for this air is in many respects more mobile, finer, and more potent. As soon as it has filled the pathways of the eyes with light,

And it laid open what the dark air had before blocked,
The images of things, now revealed, follow in succession,
Those that exist in the light press upon us so that we see.
This we cannot do against the darkness from the light,
Because the denser air of darkness comes after,
Thicker, filling all the passages,
Blocking the pathways of the eyes, so that no images
Of any objects, cast together, can be moved.
It happens also that from mirror to mirror an image is passed,
And as many as five or even six images may be produced,
For whatever things lie hidden in the inner recesses behind,
Yet however winding and deeply remote,
All can be drawn out through the winding passages and seen
By these mirrors as if present in the house.
So thoroughly does the image pass from mirror to mirror,
And when the left is presented, it becomes the right,
Then turns back again and returns to the same.
Moreover, whatever small curved sides the mirrors have,
Endowed with a curvature like our own flank,
Send back to us images leaning to the right,
Either because the image is transferred from mirror to mirror
And flies to us having been struck twice, or else
It is turned around as the image arrives, because
The curved shape of the mirror teaches it to turn toward us.
And when we see the square towers of a city from afar,
It happens that they often appear to be rounded,
Because every angle, seen from a distance, appears blunted,
Or rather is not seen at all, and its impact
Is lost, and the blow does not reach our eyes,
Because while the images are carried through much air,

The air forces objects to become blurred through repeated collisions,
and from there, once every angle of perception has escaped us,
it comes about as if things made of stone were shaped on a lathe,
yet not truly round as they would appear up close,
but rather seem faintly shadowed imitations.
Images appear to walk alongside us step by step,
and you might think they place their feet with ours and mimic our gestures,
because from whatever part of the mirror you withdraw,
the images cannot be reflected back from that spot —
for nature compels all things to be returned
and to rebound from surfaces at equal angles.
A shadow likewise appears to us to move in the sunlight,
and to follow our footsteps and mimic our gestures,
if you believe that air, deprived of light, can
follow the movements of people and mimic their gestures.
For nothing else can exist except air struck by light,
which is what we commonly call a shadow.
Indeed, because the earth in certain places in order
is deprived of the sun's light as we pass through blocking it,
and the part we have left is filled again with light —
for this reason, what was the shadow of the body
seems to have followed us from the same position.
For new rays of light are always pouring forth,
and the first ones perish, as if wool were being drawn along an edge.
Therefore the earth is easily stripped of light
and refilled, and washes away its dark shadows from itself.
Yet we do not grant that the eyes are deceived in the least by this.
For wherever there is light and shadow, it belongs to those things to observe
whether the lights are the same or not,
and whether the shadow that forms here passes across to there.

BOOK IV.

Or rather it happens as we said a little before.
The reasoning of the mind alone must discern this,
For the eyes cannot perceive the true nature of things;
So do not attribute this fault of the mind to the eyes.
The ship on which we sail seems to stand still, while it moves.
That which remains at anchor seems to glide past us,
And the hills and fields appear to flee toward the stern
As we drive our ship past them, flying under sail.
The stars seem motionless, fixed in their ethereal vaults,
Yet all things are in constant motion,
Since they return to their rising after long settings,
Having swept the sky with their clear light.
The sun likewise seems to stay still, and the moon
Appears at rest in that position, which the very motion of things contradicts.
And mountains rising far off from the midst of the sea,
Between which there lies open a free passage for fleets,
Appear separated and far apart from one another, though a great
Island formed from these same joined peaks appears as one.
Halls seem to spin and columns to race about
To such a degree that children, when they themselves
Have stopped turning, can scarcely bring themselves to believe
That the whole roof above is not threatening to fall upon them.
And when nature begins to raise the red and trembling gleam of fire on high
And lift it above the mountains,
Those mountains over which the sun then seems to be,
Touching them close at hand with its burning fire,
Are scarce two thousand arrow-shots away from us,
Scarce even five hundred javelin-casts lie
Between them and the sun, while the vast plains of the sea
Lie spread beneath the great shores of the sky,
Interspersed between them.

Though many thousands of miles of lands lie stretched between,
Which various peoples hold, and ages of wild beasts.
Yet a pool of water no higher than a finger's breadth,
That settles between the paving-stones of roads,
Offers a view down beneath the earth so vast
As the high expanse of heaven opens above the earth —
So that you seem to look down upon clouds and sky,
And bodies wondrously placed beneath the earth in the heavens.
Again, when our keen horse has halted mid-stream,
And we have looked down upon the swift waters of the river,
The force seems to carry the horse's body sideways
And thrust it rapidly against the current.
And wherever we turn our eyes, all things seem
To be moving and flowing past us in the same way.
A colonnade, though it runs in equal line,
Standing forever supported on equal columns,
Yet when seen along its full length from one end,
It gradually draws together into the narrow peak of a cone,
Joining roof to floor, until it brings everything
On the right and left together into the cone's dark point.
To sailors on the open sea, the sun rising from the waves
Seems to set back into the waves and hide its light.
For since they see nothing but water and sky,
Do not lightly think that the senses are all deceived.
But to those who do not know the sea, in harbor ships appear
To be limping, straining against the broken waves.
For whatever part of the oars rises above the salt spray
Is straight, and appears straight from above,
But the parts that are plunged beneath the water seem broken and bent,

And reflected, floating near the surface of the water.
And when winds carry clouds across the sky,
At night the bright constellations seem
To glide against the clouds, moving upward
And far in a different direction from where they actually travel.
And if by chance a hand placed beneath one eye
Presses it, by a certain sensation it happens that
Everything we see appears doubled in our sight,
The twin flames of burning lamps,
And all the furniture doubled throughout the house,
And faces of people doubled, and bodies two.
Then when sleep binds the limbs in gentle slumber
And the whole body lies in deepest rest,
Yet we seem to ourselves to be awake, moving our limbs,
And in the blind darkness of night
We think we see the sun and the light of day,
And enclosed in some space, we seem to see the sky, the sea, rivers, mountains
Changing, and we seem to cross over plains on foot,
And to hear sounds — though the stern silence of night
Prevails everywhere — and to speak words while silent.
Many other marvels of this kind we observe,
Which all seem to challenge the reliability of the senses.
In vain — since most of these illusions arise
From the opinions of the mind which we ourselves add,
So that things seem present which the senses have not seen.
For nothing is harder than to separate clear facts
From those doubtful things which the mind promptly adds on its own.
Furthermore, if anyone thinks nothing can be known, he does not know this either —
Whether it can be known, since he admits he knows nothing.
Against such a person, then, I shall refrain from arguing the case,

Who himself set his own footsteps backwards,
And yet, even granting that he knows this much, I will ask:
Since he has seen nothing true in the nature of things before,
How does he know what it is to know, and likewise not to know?
What thing has created the knowledge of truth, and of falsehoods,
And what has proved that doubt differs from certainty?
You will find that knowledge of truth is created
First from the senses, and that the senses cannot be refuted.
For that must be found with greater trust
Which by its own power can overcome falsehood with truth.
What then deserves to be held with greater trust than the senses?
Shall reason, sprung from a false sense, prevail
To speak against them — reason which is itself wholly sprung from the senses?
If the senses are not true, then all reason becomes false as well.
Can the ears refute the eyes? Can touch refute the ears?
Can taste argue against touch from the mouth?
Can the nostrils confute, or the eyes disprove?
Not so, I think. For each sense has its power
Divided apart, each its own proper force; and therefore it must be
That what is soft, or lukewarm, or hot, is perceived as such,
And that the varied colors of things are perceived separately,
And whatever is joined to colors must likewise be perceived.
Taste has its power apart in the mouth, odors theirs separately,
Sounds arise separately; and therefore it must be
That the senses cannot refute one another.
Nor will they be able to refute themselves,
Since equal trust must always be given to each at all times.
Therefore, whatever has appeared to each sense at any given time is true.
And if reason cannot resolve the cause
Of why things that were square close up appear round from a distance,

Yet it is better, when things appear round, to offer a faulty explanation of why each shape looks as it does to a mind lacking reason, than to let slip from one's grasp what is plainly evident, and to violate the primary trust, and to overturn all the foundations upon which life and safety rest. For not only would all reason collapse, but life itself would fall at once, unless you dare to trust the senses. Avoid precipitous places, and all other things of this kind that are to be shunned, and follow their opposites. All that store of words, therefore, is empty that has been marshaled and made ready against the senses. And just as in building, if the original rule is crooked, and the square is faulty and deviates from true lines, and if the level is off even a hair's breadth on one side, then everything must be built wrongly, tilted, leaning forward, sloping back, misshapen, so that some parts seem ready to fall and do fall, betrayed by false judgments at the start. So too must your reasoning about things be false and distorted, and whatever arises from deceived senses must itself be false. Now how each of the other senses perceives its own object — no laborious reasoning is left to settle that. First, sound and every voice is heard when they have made their way into the ears and struck sensation with their body. For we must grant that voice and sound are corporeal, since they can strike upon the senses. Moreover, the voice often scrapes the throat as it passes out, and shouting makes the windpipe rough as it goes outward — for the particles that form the beginnings of voice crowd together in too great a mass through the narrow passage and begin to stream forth outside.

And so when the mouth's gateway is filled up,
Hoarseness wears the passages, and harms the way by which the voice travels into the air.
There is therefore no doubt that voices and words are made of bodily particles, so that they can cause harm.
Nor should it escape you what the body loses, and what
Is drawn from the nerves and very strength of men
By continuous speech stretching to the shadow of black night,
Led onward from the rising brilliance of the dawn,
Especially when it has poured forth with the greatest clamor.
Therefore the voice must be composed of bodily matter,
Since one who speaks much loses part from the body.
Nor do the first-beginnings penetrate the ears with the same form
When the trumpet bellows gravely with its deep murmur,
And the barbarous booming rebounds back with a rasp,
And the swans, wrung by cold death from the cave of Helicon,
Pour out their liquid lament with a mournful voice.
These voices, then, we press out from deep within our body,
And send them straight forth through the mouth,
Where the nimble, craft-skilled tongue of the nerves gives them shape,
And the fashioning of the lips further forms them.
The roughness of voice comes from the roughness
Of its first-beginnings, and likewise smoothness is born of smoothness.
And when the space is not long, from which the voice sets out
To reach the ear, the words themselves must necessarily
Be heard plainly and distinguished syllable by syllable,
For the voice preserves its form and retains its shape.
But if the intervening space is longer than usual,
The words must become confused passing through much air,
And the voice disturbed as it flies through the breezes.
Therefore it comes about that you can perceive the sound, but not

To distinguish what meaning the words carry,
the voice comes so confused and entangled.
Besides, a single proclamation often strikes the ears
of all the people, sent forth from the herald's mouth.
Into many voices, therefore, one voice suddenly
scatters, since it divides itself among individual ears,
stamping the shape of words and their clear sound upon them.
But that part of the voices which does not fall directly into the ears
passes by and is lost, scattered uselessly through the air.
The part that strikes solid surfaces and is thrown back returns its sound,
and sometimes is deceived by an echo of the word.
When you see this clearly, you can give an account
to yourself and others of how, in lonely places,
the rocks give back the forms of words one after another.
When among dark mountains we seek
our wandering companions and call them with a great voice,
I have seen six or even seven places give back voices,
when you cast out one — so the hills, bouncing words
from hill to hill, kept repeating what was said back again.
These places the neighboring folk imagine to be held
by goat-footed satyrs and nymphs, and they say
fauns dwell there, by whose nocturnal noise and playful sport
the voiceless silences are commonly said to be broken,
and the sounds of strings to arise, and sweet laments
which the flute pours out when struck by the fingers of players.
And the country folk widely feel this, when Pan,
shaking the pine-leaf covering of his half-beast head,
often runs his curved lip over the gaping reeds,
so that the pipe never ceases to pour forth its woodland song.
All manner of monsters and marvels of this kind they tell of.

Lest people think that deserted places are held
By gods alone, and so spread tales of miracles,
Or are led by some other reasoning, since all
The human race is far too eager for wonders.
What remains is not surprising: to understand why
Sounds reach places where eyes cannot see things clearly,
And strike upon our ears, when we speak
With doors shut closed, as we often observe.
For voice can pass unharmed through the winding passages
Of matter, while images refuse to pass.
They are torn apart unless they travel through straight openings,
Such as the image of glass, which flies through entirely.
Besides, the voice is divided in all directions,
Since new sounds are born from others, once it has
Split apart into many, like a spark of fire
Which often scatters itself among other flames.
And so hidden places fill with voices, all
That lie around are stirred and set resounding.
But images travel only in straight lines,
As they are sent at once; and so no one
Can see beyond a wall, but voices can be caught outside.
Yet even so, as voice passes through the barriers of its path
It is dulled, and enters our ears in confused fashion,
So that we seem to hear sound rather than words.
Nor do the tongue and palate, by which we sense
The taste, have less share in this, but more work to do.
First we sense the taste in the mouth, when we chew
Food and press it out, as one who takes
A full sponge and squeezes and dries it by hand.
Then what we press out flows through all the passages of the palate

It is said that through the winding passages of the tongue's rare pores,
When these are smooth, the flowing bodies of liquid
Gently touch, and gently handle all things,

But on the other hand they sting the senses and tear the heart,
