Then the pleasure comes from the juice at the roof of the palate.
But when it has plunged downward through the throat,
There is no pleasure while it is distributed through all the limbs.
Nor does it matter what food nourishes the body,
Provided you can distribute what you take in, once digested, through your limbs,
And maintain moisture in the stomach's tone.
Now, why different food suits different people, let us see,
I will explain why what is bitter and unpleasant to some,
Can yet seem very sweet to others.
So great is the difference in these matters, and so great the divergence,
That what is food to one person is bitter poison to another.
There is indeed the case of the snake, which, touched by human saliva,
Perishes, and destroys itself by biting.
Moreover, white hellebore is bitter poison to us,
Yet it fattens goats and quails.
That you may know by what means this comes about,
First it is fitting to remember what we said before,
That seeds are held mingled in things in many ways.
Furthermore, all living creatures that take food,
Just as they are unlike in outward appearance, and each kind
Is bounded by its outermost membrane of limbs,
So they are constituted of different seeds, and vary in their structure.
Since moreover the seeds differ, the intervals must differ,
The passages and pores, which we call

In all the limbs, and in the mouth, and on the palate itself,
Some atoms must be smaller, others larger,
Some triangular, others square of necessity,
Many round, in many ways some many-angled,
For as the nature and motion of shapes requires,
Therefore shapes must differ in their pores,
And vary their passages, as the texture demands.
Thus what is sweet to some becomes bitter to others,
For one who finds it sweet, the smoothest bodies must
Glide caressingly into the cavities of the palate.
But on the other hand, for those to whom the same thing is inwardly harsh,
Rough bodies doubtless penetrate and hook the throat.
Now it is easy from these facts to understand each case:
For when someone's fever has arisen with bile in excess,
Or some violent force of disease has been stirred by another cause,
The whole body is then thrown into disorder, and all
The positions of the first-beginnings are changed therein;
So that what bodies before suited the sense,
Now suit it no longer, while others are more fit,
Which when penetrated can produce a bitter sensation,
Both kinds being mixed in the flavor of honey,
As we have already often shown to you before.
Now come, how the impact of smell strikes the nostrils,
I will explain. First, there must be many things
From which a varied flowing stream of odors rolls,
For it must be thought to flow, to spread, and to be scattered widely.
But different odors suit different living creatures,
Dissimilar in form, and so through the air
Bees are drawn from afar by the scent of honey,
And vultures by carcasses; then the cloven tracks of beasts

Wherever the hoof has passed, the keen power of hounds
leads on, and scents the human odor from afar,
as does the white goose, guardian of the Romulan citadel.
So different smells lead different creatures each
to their own food, and compel them to recoil
from foul poison; in this way the generations of wild beasts are preserved.
This very odor, then, whenever it assails the nostrils,
allows one scent to be carried further than another.
Yet none of them is carried as far
as sound, and voice — to say nothing of the things
that strike the eyes and assault the vision.
For odor wanders and comes slowly, and perishes
before it arrives, little by little, easily scattered into the air,
first because it is only faintly emitted from its source.
For it is clear that odors flow deeply out from things
and spread abroad, and that broken things smell stronger,
as do all things ground up or heated by fire.
Next, one may observe that odor is made of larger
particles than voice, since it does not pass through
stone walls, as sound and noise commonly do.
Therefore you will find it not so easy to track
where exactly the source of a smell is located.
For the scent grows cold as it lingers, drifting through the air,
and warm tidings of things do not run swiftly to the senses.
So hounds often go astray and must search for the trail.
Nor does this apply only to odors and to the
realm of tastes: the appearances of things and colors too
do not suit all senses equally for all,
so that some things are sharper to the sight for some.
Indeed, even the cock, clapping his wings in the night,

...accustomed to herald the dawn with its clear call.
Swift lions cannot stand against this creature,
Nor bear to look at it, so quickly do they flee,
Because there are certain seeds within the body of roosters
Which, when cast into the eyes of lions,
Dig into their pupils and cause sharp pain,
So that the fierce beasts cannot endure to face them.
Yet these same things have no power to harm our own eyes,
Either because they do not penetrate, or because, when they do penetrate,
Free passage out through the eyes is allowed, so they cannot
Hurt our sight in any part.
Now then, hear what it is that moves the mind, and from where
These things that come into thought arise — hear it briefly.
First, I say this: images of things wander about
In many ways, in all directions everywhere,
Fine things that easily join together in the air
When they meet, like the web of a spider, or gold leaf.
For indeed these images are far finer in texture
Than those things which strike the eyes and stimulate sight.
Since these penetrate through the body's pores and stir
The fine nature of the mind within, they stimulate sensation.
Thus we see Centaurs, and the limbs of Scyllas,
And the faces of Cerberus's hound-heads, and the images of those
Whose bones the earth embraces in death.
Since images of every kind are carried everywhere,
Some arising spontaneously in the air itself,
Some departing from various objects,
And some formed and composed from the shapes of these,
For certainly no living centaur ever existed,
Since no such nature of animal has ever been.

But when the image of a horse and a man chance to combine,
It easily adheres at once, as we have said before,
Because of the subtle nature and the fine texture of the films.
The rest of things of this kind are created by the same reasoning,
Which, moving with supreme lightness as they are carried along,
As I showed before, any single subtle image easily stirs
The mind in us with a single stroke.
For the mind itself is thin and wonderfully mobile.
That these things happen, as I describe, you can easily understand
Insofar as what we see with the mind resembles
What we see with the eyes, and must arise by a similar process.
Now, since I have shown that lions, for instance,
Are seen through images that assail the eyes wherever they turn,
We may understand that the mind is moved in the same way
By the images of lions and all else that it perceives equally,
No less than the eyes, except that it perceives things somewhat more fine.
Nor for any other reason, when sleep has poured over the limbs,
Does the mind remain awake, unless the same images assail
Our minds that assail them when we are awake,
So completely that we seem to behold one whom death has now reclaimed
And the earth has taken possession of.
Nature compels this to happen because all the senses
Of the body throughout the limbs are at rest,
And cannot refute the false with the true.
Moreover, the mind itself lies still and grows dull with sleep,
And does not distinguish the one long since claimed by death and Lethe,
Whom the mind believes it sees alive.
As for the rest, it is no wonder that the images move
And swing their arms in rhythm, and their other limbs —
For in dreams it seems that the image does just this.

For when the first image perishes, another is at once born in its place,
and so the former pose seems to have changed.
We must reckon that this happens with swift speed,
so great is the mobility, and so great the abundance of things,
so great at any perceptible moment in time
is the supply of particles, that it can keep pace.
Many things in these matters must be sought out, many things
must be made clear to us, if we truly wish to explain them.
First we ask: why, when a desire has come to anyone,
does his mind instantly think of that very thing?
Do images watch over our will,
so that the moment we wish, the image presents itself?
Whether it be the sea, or land, or sky, whatever the heart desires —
gatherings of men, a procession, a banquet, battles —
does nature create and prepare all these at a word?
Especially since in the same region and place
the mind may think on things utterly unlike each other.
What, moreover, when we see images moving in step in our dreams,
and moving their supple limbs?
When they gracefully extend their arms in alternation,
and repeat fitting gestures with eyes, with movement, with step —
surely the images are skilled and wander with art,
so as to perform their shows in the hours of night?
Or is it rather more true that, because at that time
we give ourselves over to it — as when a single voice is uttered,
many things lie hidden in a moment, which reason has discerned —
therefore at any moment whatsoever,
images stand ready in every place,
so great is the mobility, and so great the abundance of things.
When the first perishes, another is at once born in its place.

From animals like these, which are driven by exercise,
Much is pressed out and flows through sweat from deep within,
Much is exhaled through the mouth as they pant with exhaustion.
By these processes the body grows thin, and all
Its nature is undermined; pain follows in the wake of this.
Therefore food is taken in, to prop up the limbs,
And to restore strength, distributed throughout, and spreading
Through the limbs and veins, so as to sustain the desire for eating.
Moisture likewise disperses into all the parts that each place
Demands moisture, and the many massed bodies of vapor
That provide burning heat to our stomach
Are scattered by the incoming liquid, and quenched, as fire
Is quenched, so that dry heat can no longer scorch the limbs.
Thus the panting thirst is washed away from our body,
Thus the hungry craving is satisfied.
Now I will explain how it comes about that we are able to take steps forward
When we wish, and how it is given to us to move our limbs in various ways,
And what force has learned to push forward this great weight
Of our body — you, take in what I say.
I say that first images of motion come to our mind,
And strike upon it, as I said before.
From this arises will. For no one begins to do
Any action before the mind has foreseen what it wishes.
What it foresees is constituted by the image of that thing.
Therefore when the mind stirs itself so as to wish to go
And to step forward, it immediately strikes the vital force
That is spread through the limbs and members throughout the body,
And this is easy to accomplish, since it is held in union with them.
Then that force in turn strikes the body, and so gradually
The whole mass is pushed forward and set in motion.

As it must, since it is always in motion,

And is dispersed to each of the body's tiniest
Parts. And so, for these two reasons,
The body is carried along as a ship is by sails and wind.
Nor is it remarkable that in these matters

For wind, with its fine and subtle body,

Now in what ways sleep pours its quiet through our limbs
And releases the mind's cares from the breast,
I shall set forth in sweet words rather than in many verses,
As the brief song of the swan is better than the cry of cranes

Give me keen ears and a sharp mind,
Lest you deny that what I describe can happen, and

First, sleep comes when the force of the soul is drawn apart through the limbs,

For there is no doubt that the soul's work

Now as for how each of the other senses perceives its own object,

First, sound and every voice is heard when it has made its way

For that voice and sound are corporeal must be admitted,
Since they are able to strike the senses.
Moreover, the voice often scrapes the throat as it passes,
And shouting makes the windpipe raw as it goes out,
Since, when the first-beginnings of voice gather in greater force
Through a narrow passage, as they begin to go forth outward

For when the mouth is full, the door of voice is given back through hoarse passages, and the path is damaged by which the voice travels into the air.
It is therefore not in doubt that voices and words consist of bodily particles, since they are able to cause harm.
And do not let it escape your notice what the voice takes away from the body, and what it subtracts from the sinews and strength of men, when continuous speech is prolonged from the darkness of black night all the way to the gleam of the rising dawn, especially when it pours out with the loudest clamor.
Therefore it must be the case that voice is corporeal in nature, since one who speaks much loses part of his body.

These voices, then, we press out from deep within our body, and send them straight outward through the mouth; the nimble tongue, that craftsman of the sinews, gives them shape, and the fashioning of the lips in turn gives them their form.
The roughness of voice comes from the roughness of its first-beginnings, and likewise its smoothness is produced by their smoothness.
And when the space is not long, from which the voice travels to the ear, it is necessary that the words themselves be clearly heard and distinguished syllable by syllable, for the voice preserves its form and keeps its shape.
But if the intervening space is longer than usual, the words must become confused passing through much air, and the voice disordered as it flies through the breezes.
Thus it comes about that you can hear a sound, but not

How the meaning of words is distinguished,

Moreover, a single edict will strike the ears

Into many voices a single voice suddenly

But that part of the voices which does not reach the ears directly,

When you understand this well, you can explain to yourself

When among the shady mountains we seek

When hills to hills themselves,

The neighboring peoples imagine that these places are held

And say that fauns dwell there,
By whose night-wandering noise and playful reveling

And that the country folk far and wide become aware of it, when Pan,

Often runs his curved lip over the gaping reeds,

The rest of such things they speak of as marvels and portents.

Lest people think that deserted places are held by gods alone,
who therefore boast of miracles in their speech,
or are led by some other reasoning, since all
the human race is far too eager for stories.
As for what remains, it is no wonder, by what reason
sounds reach places where the eyes cannot clearly see things,
and reach through voices, and assail the ears,
when we speak through closed doors, as we often observe.
For a voice can pass unharmed through the winding
channels of matter, while images refuse to pass through.
Images are broken apart unless they travel straight through openings,
such as all the light of glass passes through.
Moreover, a voice is divided in all directions.
Since new sounds are born from old ones, once
it has burst apart into many, as a spark of fire
often scatters its own offspring into other fires.
So hidden places far within are filled with voices,
and all that lies around stirs with sound.
But images all travel in straight paths,
as they were sent at first. Therefore no one
can see beyond a wall, but can catch voices outside.
And yet, even this voice, while passing through the barriers of its way,
is blunted, and enters the ears in confusion,
and we seem to hear sound rather than words.
Nor do those who sense flavor — the tongue and palate
have rather more to do with it, more work involved.
First, we sense flavor in the mouth when we chew food
and press it out, as one who has taken a full sponge of water
and squeezes it forcefully to dry it out.
Then what we press out flows through all the channels of the palate

It spreads through the winding passages of the tongue,
and where the particles of the flowing juice are smooth,
they touch pleasantly and handle everything gently,
moistening the damp precincts of the palate.
But on the other hand, the rougher they are,
the more they prick and tear the senses.
Next, pleasure comes from the juice at the top of the palate.
But when it plunges down through the throat,
there is no more pleasure while it is distributed through all the limbs.
Nor does it matter at all what food nourishes the body,
provided you can distribute what you take in, once digested,
through the organs and maintain the moist balance of the stomach.
Now let me explain why different food suits different creatures,
and why what is bitter and unpleasant to some
may yet seem very sweet to others.
So great is the difference and diversity in these matters
that what is food for one is bitter poison for another.
There is, for example, a snake: touched by human saliva,
it perishes and tears itself apart by biting.
Moreover, hellebore is a sharp poison to us,
but it makes goats and quails grow fat.
So that you may understand how this comes about,
first you must recall what we said before:
that seeds of many kinds are mixed together in things.
Furthermore, all creatures that take food,
just as they are unlike on the outside and in their general form,
which the outermost contour of their limbs encompasses,
are accordingly composed of different seeds and vary in shape.
And since their seeds differ, the intervals, passages, and pores — as we call them — must also differ.

In all the members, and in the mouth, and in the palate itself,
Some bodies must be smaller, others larger,
Some triangular, some necessarily square for others,
Many round, and some many-angled in many ways,
As the nature and movement of shapes requires,
And therefore the shapes must differ in their pores,
And vary their passages, just as the texture constrains them.
Thus what is sweet to some becomes bitter to others,
For those to whom it is sweet, the smoothest bodies
Must stroke their way gently through the hollows of the palate.
But on the contrary, for those to whom the same thing is harsh within,
Rough bodies doubtless penetrate and hook the throat.
Now it is easy to understand from these facts why,
When someone's fever has arisen from an excess of bile,
Or when the force of disease has been stirred up by some other cause,
The entire body is then disturbed, and all
The positions of the primary elements are shifted,
So that what bodies formerly suited the senses
No longer suit them, while others are more fitting,
Those which, once they have penetrated, can produce a bitter sensation,
For both kinds are mingled in the flavor of honey,
As we have often shown you above before.
Now come, I will address how the scent of odors
Strikes the nostrils. First, there must be many things
From which a varied flood of odors flows and rolls.
For odors must be thought to flow, to be emitted, and to scatter.
But one odor is better suited to one creature, another to another,
Because of their unlike shapes, and so through the air
Bees are led by the scent of honey however far away.
And vultures by carrion; and then the split tracks of wild beasts

BOOK IV.

Wherever the hoof has carried its step, the keen power of the hound's
Scent leads it on, and smells from afar the human odor;
The white goose, guardian of the citadel of Romulus's people.
So to each creature a different scent is given, leading each
To its own food, and compelling it to recoil from foul poison,
And in this way the generations of wild beasts are preserved.
This odor itself, then, whatever it is that strikes the nostrils,
Is capable of being carried farther than another.
Yet none of these travels as far
As sound and voice — to say nothing of those things
Which strike the sight and assail the eyes.
For odor wanders and comes slowly, and perishes before long,
Gradually dispersed into the breezes of the air,
First from on high, since it is barely emitted from the source.
For odors flowing deep out of things and spreading forth
Show that broken things smell more strongly,
As do things crushed or scorched by fire.
Moreover, one may observe that odor is composed of larger
First-beginnings than voice, since it does not pass through rocky walls
As voice and sound commonly do.
Therefore you will find it is not so easy to track down
In what region a scent is located.
For the blow cools as it lingers through the air,
And warm tidings of things do not run swiftly to the senses.
So dogs often wander and search for tracks.
Yet this is not so only with odors and the class
Of tastes, but likewise the appearances of things and colors
Do not all equally suit the senses of all creatures alike,
So that some things are not sharper to the sight of some than others.
Indeed, the cock at night, clapping his wings,

They are accustomed to call out to the bright dawn with their voice.
The swift lions cannot stand against this sound,
Nor look upon it, so thoroughly do they remember to flee —
No doubt because there are certain seeds within the body of roosters
Which, when cast into the eyes of lions,
Dig into their pupils and produce sharp pain,
So that fierce as they are, they cannot endure to face them.
Yet these seeds can in no way harm our own eyesight,
Either because they do not penetrate deeply, or because, even when they do penetrate,
A free exit is given to them from the eyes so that they pass through,
And cannot injure the eyes in any part.

Now come, hear what things move the mind and from where they come;
Take in briefly what enters our thoughts.
First, I say that images of things wander abroad
In many ways through all directions on every side,
Fine things that easily join together in the air
When they meet, like spider's web and gold leaf.
For these are far more fine in texture
Than those things which capture the eyes and assail our sight.
Since these pass through the pores of the body and stir
The fine nature of the mind within and assail its senses,
We see Centaurs and the limbs of Scyllas,
And the faces of Cerberus's hounds, and images of those
Whose bones the earth covers over in death.
Since images of every kind are borne everywhere about,
Some forming of their own accord in the air itself,
Some departing from various things at every moment,
And some composed out of the shapes of these combined —
For surely no living image of a centaur is made,
Since no such nature of living creature ever existed.

BOOK IV.

But when the image of a horse and a man chance to combine,
It readily sticks together, as we said before,
Because of their subtle nature and their fine texture.
All other things of this kind are created in the same way,
And since they move with the utmost lightness and speed,
As I showed before, a single subtle image easily stirs
The mind with one stroke.
For the mind itself is fine and wonderfully mobile.
That this happens, as I explain, you may easily understand,
Insofar as what we see with the mind resembles
What we see with the eyes, and must arise by a similar process.
Now, since I have shown that I, perhaps, see lions
Through images that strike the eyes wherever they appear,
We may understand that the mind is moved in a similar way
By images of lions and whatever else it sees equally,
No less than the eyes, except that it perceives still finer images.
And for no other reason, when sleep has subdued the limbs,
Does the mind stay awake — except that the same images
That strike us when we are awake now strike our minds,
So surely that we seem to see the very person whom
Death has already claimed and the earth now holds.
Nature compels this to happen because all the senses
Of the body throughout the limbs are at rest,
And cannot refute the false with the true.
Moreover, the mind itself lies still and grows drowsy with sleep,
And does not recognize that he, long since claimed by death and the waters of Lethe,
Is the one whom the mind believes it sees alive.
As for the rest, it is no wonder that images move
And swing their arms in rhythm, and the other limbs —
For in dreams it appears that the image does exactly this.

For when the first image perishes, another is born in its place,
and so the former posture seems to have changed,
Since this must be thought to happen with swift speed,
so great is the mobility, and so great the abundance of things,
and so great at any given perceptible moment is
the supply of particles, that it can keep replenishing.
Many things in these matters must be sought, and many things
must be made clear, if we truly wish to explain them.
First it is asked: why, when desire for something
comes to anyone, does his mind immediately think of that very thing?
Do images watch over our will?
And as soon as we wish, does the image present itself to us?
Whether it is the sea, the land, or the sky that is in our heart,
assemblies of men, processions, feasts, battles —
does nature create all things at the mere word, and prepare them,
especially since in the same region and place
the mind may think of things altogether different?
What of the fact that when images march in rhythm,
we see them in dreams, moving their supple limbs?
Smoothly and in turn they swing their arms,
and repeat with eyes and gesture and foot in harmony —
Surely the images are skilled by art, and wander trained,
to perform their shows in the hours of night?
Or is it more true that, because in that time
we agree to it, as when a single word is uttered,
many things lie hidden in that moment which reason has shown to exist?
Therefore it comes about that at any moment whatsoever
images stand ready, prepared in whatever places,
so great is the mobility, and so great the abundance of things.
When the first perishes, another is born in its place,

BOOK IV.

From this the prior state of the gesture seems to have changed,
And because they are fine, unless one strains intensely,
The mind cannot perceive them, and so all things that are
Besides perish, unless it itself has prepared them,
It prepares itself further, and anticipates the future,
So that it may see what follows, whatever the thing may be.
Do you not see that the eyes too, when things are fine,
Begin to make them out, and strain and prepare themselves,
And that without this effort we cannot see clearly?
Yet even in matters that are open you may notice,
If you do not direct your attention, it is as if the thing
Were wholly absent and removed far away.
Why then is it strange if the mind loses all else
Besides, when it is wholly given over to something?
We then make inferences about great things from small signs,
And deceive ourselves in vain, all too readily.
It also happens that sometimes the image that comes
Is not of the same kind, but a woman who was there before
Seems in our hands to have turned into a man present with us,
Or one face and one age follows another in succession —
And that we do not wonder at this, sleep and forgetfulness see to.
There is one fault in these matters to be strenuously avoided,
The error of those who reason thus:
That eyes were not made with their clear light
So that we might look ahead, and so that we might stretch out
Tall strides, since the tops of the calves
And the shins are joined below by feet to be bent,
And that arms are fitted to strong muscles,
And hands given as servants on either side,
So that we might do for life what its use required.

The rest of things of this kind, whatever is claimed about them,
Is all backwards and inverted in reasoning.
Nothing in the body came into being so that we might use it,
But rather what came into being creates its own use.
Nor did sight exist before the eyes were born,
Nor did speech come before the tongue was made,
But rather the origin of the tongue long preceded speech,
And ears were created long before sound was heard,
And all limbs existed (I think) before there was any use for them.
Therefore they could not have grown for the sake of being used.
But on the contrary, to join hands in the combat of battle,
And to tear limbs apart, and to defile members with blood,
Existed long before bright weapons flew through the air.
And nature compelled one to avoid a wound
Before the left hand could present a shield as protection through skill.
Likewise, to commit the body to rest and sleep
Is far more ancient than the soft coverings of a bed.
And to quench thirst came before the cup was invented.
These things, therefore, can be believed to have been recognized
As useful from experience, discovered in the course of life.
But all those other things are separate — those which first,
Having come into being themselves, afterward revealed their usefulness.
Of this kind we see, first of all, the senses and the limbs.
Wherefore it is far from possible for you to believe
That they could have been created for the purpose of utility.
Nor is this to be wondered at, that the very nature
Of each living body seeks its own nourishment.
For indeed I have shown that bodies flow and recede from things
In many ways, but most of all they must —

From these animals, which are driven about by exertion,
And many are pressed out from deep within by sweating,
Many things are exhaled through the mouth, when they pant wearily.
By these processes, then, the body grows thin, and the whole
Nature is undermined, and pain follows in the wake of this.
Therefore food is taken, to prop up the limbs,
And to restore their strength at intervals, and spreading widely
Through the limbs and veins, to dull the keen edge of hunger.
Moisture likewise departs into all the places that
Demand moisture, and the many massed bodies of heat
That furnish fires to our stomach
Are scattered by the incoming liquid and quenched, as a flame,
So that the parching heat can no longer burn the limbs.
Thus it is that the breathless thirst is washed away from our body,
Thus the craving of hunger is satisfied.
Now I will tell how it comes about that we are able to take steps forward,
When we wish, and to move our limbs in various ways,
And what force is accustomed to thrust forward so great a mass
Of our body — you listen to what I say.
I say that images of moving first
Come to our mind, and strike upon it, as I said before.
Then the will arises; for no one begins to do
Any action before the mind foresees what it wishes to do.
What it foresees, the image of that thing is established.
Therefore when the mind stirs itself so as to wish to go
And to step forward, it immediately strikes that force of the soul
Which is spread through the limbs and members throughout the whole body,
And this is easily done, since it is held in union with them.
Then that force strikes the body onward, and so the whole
Mass is gradually thrust forward and set in motion.

Furthermore

Besides, at that time the body also grows more rarefied, and the air
As it should, being always mobile,
Enters through the opened passages, and penetrates the pores abundantly,
And is dispersed to the individual tiny parts
Of the body. Thus, from these two causes together,
The body is carried along as a ship is by its sails and the wind.
Nor is it surprising that in these matters
Such tiny particles can twist so great a body
And turn around our whole burden.
For indeed the wind, thin in its subtle body,
Drives and propels a great ship with great force,
And a single hand steers it moving at whatever speed,
And a single rudder turns it wherever one wishes,
And pulleys and drums with great weight
Move things, and the machine lifts them with slight effort.
Now by what means sleep pours its quiet rest through the limbs,
And releases the cares of the mind from the breast,
I will set forth in sweetly-spoken rather than many verses,
As the brief song of the swan surpasses the cry of cranes
Scattered in the southern clouds through the airy sky.
Give me your fine ears and a keen mind,
Lest you deny that what I describe can happen, and push away
True words from your resistant breast,
When the fault lies with yourself, that you cannot see.
First, sleep comes when the power of the soul is scattered through the limbs,
And partly driven out has departed,
And partly has withdrawn compressed more deeply within,
For then at last the limbs relax and flow slack.
For there is no doubt that sensation in us is the work of the soul,
And when sleep hinders it from being present,

BOOK IV.

Then we must suppose that the soul within us is thrown into disorder,
and not all of it cast out, for then the body would lie
chilled forever in the cold of death.
For if no hidden part of the soul remained
in the limbs, as fire lies buried beneath much ash,
from which sensation could suddenly be rekindled throughout the limbs,
as flame rises up from hidden fire —
but by what causes this disturbance is produced, and from where
the soul can be troubled and the body grow faint,
I shall explain; only see that you do not let my words be scattered to the winds.
First, the body must be struck from the outside,
since, being close to the breezes of the air, it is touched by them,
beaten and struck repeatedly by their blows.
And for this reason nearly all things are covered with hide,
or enclosed by skin, or armored with callus, or sheathed in bark.
The air also beats the inner parts as we breathe,
the same air when it is drawn in and breathed out again.
Therefore, since the body is struck on both sides, and since
the blows penetrate through the small passages of our body
to its innermost parts and primal elements,
a kind of gradual ruin spreads through our limbs.
For the arrangements of the first elements
of body and soul are thrown into disorder, so that part of the soul
is driven out, and part hidden deep within retreats,
and part, scattered through the limbs, cannot remain
joined together, nor share in mutual motion,
for nature shuts off and blocks its paths.
Thus sensation departs as the movements are altered deep within.
And since there is nothing, as it were, to prop up the limbs,
the body grows weak, and all the members grow faint.

Arms, eyelids, and knees give way as one lies down to rest,
And often strength itself dissolves and loosens.
Then after food comes sleep, for what the air produces,
The same effects does food cause, when spread through all the veins,
And that heaviest drowsiness overtakes one,
Which the full or the weary person feels, because so many
Bodies are shaken and bruised by great labor.
By the same reasoning the soul is driven deeper within,
And more abundantly pushed outward from itself,
More divided within itself, more scattered inside.
And whatever pursuit each person has chiefly followed,
Or in whatever affairs we have spent much time before,
And in whatever occupation the mind was most engaged,
In dreams we mostly seem to be doing the same things.
Lawyers plead cases and compose laws.
Generals fight and engage in battles.
Sailors wage their contracted war with the winds.
I pursue this work, and seek the nature of things
Always, and set down discoveries in my native pages.
All other pursuits and arts likewise seem
To hold the minds of men captive in dreams, frustrated.
And whoever for many days in succession
Has devoted assiduous effort to the games, we mostly see
That when they have stopped, their senses still dwell on it.
Yet there are pathways open in the mind
By which the same images of things may come.
And so for many days those same things are observed,
So that even while waking before one's eyes
They seem to see dancers moving
And swaying their supple limbs,
And the liquid song of the lyre and its speaking strings.

To receive with the ears, and to see the same man confessing,
And at once to behold the varied splendors of the stage.
So greatly does inclination and desire matter,
And in what pursuits beings have been accustomed to engage —
Not humans alone, but all living creatures.
For you will see horses, when their limbs lie still,
Yet sweating in their dreams, and breathing hard,
And straining as if for the palm of victory at the limit of their strength,
Or starting as if from open starting-gates in their restless sleep.
And hunting dogs in their soft slumber
Still toss their legs suddenly, and utter cries again and again,
And draw rapid breaths through their nostrils,
As if they were tracking the scent of wild beasts they had found,
And when roused they often chase after phantoms,
As though they beheld stags fleeing in full flight,
Until the illusions fade and they return to themselves.
And the gentle brood of house-puppies
Shake themselves and spring up from the ground at once,
As if they saw strange faces and forms before them.
And the wilder the nature of any creature's seed,
The more fiercely must it rage in dreams.
But birds of various kinds take flight, and with their wings suddenly
Disturb the sacred groves of the gods in the night,
If hawks in light slumber seem to pursue battles and fights,
Chasing after prey and seeing them fly.
And what great stirrings move the minds of men?
For often in sleep they do and enact great deeds.
Kings storm cities, are captured, join in battle,
Raise cries as if they were being slaughtered on the spot,
Many fight hard and utter groans in their pain.

And as if by the bite of a panther or savage lion,
they cry out, filling everything with loud shouts.
Many speak in their sleep of great matters,
and have often thus betrayed the evidence of their deeds.
Many meet their death, and many from high mountains
fall headlong to the ground with their whole body,
and are terrified, and as if seized in their minds from sleep,
they scarcely return to themselves, shaken by the body's fever.
One who is thirsty sits beside a river or pleasant spring,
and nearly swallows the whole stream with his throat.
Many, bound in sleep, think they are lifting their garment
beside a pool or shallow tub,
so as to pour out the body's stored moisture,
while they are drenched in the Babylonian splendor of their bedclothes.
Then for those in whom the seed of their age first stirs,
when the ripe day has created it in their limbs,
images come in from without from some body,
heralding a face of great beauty and glowing color.
For one thing or another stirs and provokes them,
and the force of a human being rouses human seed from a human.
And as if the act were fully completed, they pour forth
great floods of the river, and stain their garments.
For that which we have spoken of before is aroused in us:
the seed, when mature age first strengthens the limbs,
which, as soon as it is expelled from its seat,
passes through all the limbs and members of the whole body,
gathering to the proper places of the nerves,
and straightway rouses the genital parts of the body itself.
Those parts swell, irritated by the seed, and pleasure follows.

BOOK IV.

To expel that which fierce desire strains toward.
It inflames and excites the swollen parts with abundant seed,
And the mind seeks the body from which it received love's wound.
For nearly all fall toward their wound, and blood
Leaps in the direction from which the blow struck us,
And if the enemy is close, the red fluid occupies him.
So likewise one who receives the blow of Venus's darts,
Whether a boy with girlish limbs hurls it,
Or a woman casting love from her whole body —
Toward the source of the wound one strains, longing to join,
And to pour the fluid gathered in the body into that body.
For silent desire foretells the pleasure,
This is Venus for us; from this comes the name of love,
From this that first drop of Venus's sweetness trickled
Into the heart, and then burning care followed after.
For even if the beloved is absent, their images are still present,
And their sweet name echoes in the ears.
But one should flee those images and drive away
The food of love, and turn the mind elsewhere,
And discharge the gathered fluid into any bodies at hand,
Not hold fast to it, captivated by love of one alone,
Preserving thereby one's anxiety and certain pain.
For the sore quickens and grows old by feeding it,
And day by day the madness swells and the misery deepens,
Unless you disturb the old wounds with new blows,
And cure the fresh injuries by wandering widely with Venus,
Or can redirect the motions of your mind elsewhere.
Nor does the one who avoids love lack Venus's fruit —
Rather he takes the pleasures that come without penalty;
For the joy derived from this is surely purer and more wholesome for the healthy.

How wretched, for even in the very moment of possession
The lovers' passion wavers with uncertain errors.
They cannot decide what to enjoy first with eyes or hands;
They press tightly what they sought, and cause bodily pain,
And often drive their teeth into tender lips,
And press kisses hard, because the pleasure is not pure
And hidden goads urge them to hurt the very thing
From which those wild furies spring and grow.
But Venus gently breaks the sting of pain amid love,
And mingled pleasure reins in the biting.
For there is hope that from the same body that fires the desire
The flame might also be quenched —
Yet nature shows this runs contrary to how things work.
This is the one thing: the more of it we have,
The more the breast burns with fierce longing.
For food and drink are taken inside the body
And, since they can occupy fixed places,
The desire for water and grain is easily satisfied.
But from a person's face and lovely complexion
Nothing enters the body to be enjoyed but fleeting
Thin images, which the wind so often snatches away.
As when a thirsty man seeks to drink in dreams, and no water
Is given to quench the burning of his limbs,
But he pursues the images of streams and labors in vain,
Drinking while standing in the midst of a rushing river —
So Venus toys with lovers through images in love,
Nor can they satisfy themselves by gazing on bodies face to face,
Nor can they scrape away anything with tender hands
From the soft limbs, wandering uncertain over the whole body.
At last, when they join their limbs with the flower of youth, they enjoy it —

BOOK IV.
While the body already foretells the joys of youth,
and Venus is present to sow the field of womanhood,
they press their bodies together eagerly, joining their saliva
with their lips, and breathing hard, press teeth against mouths —
all in vain, since they can scrape nothing from this,
nor penetrate and pass wholly into the other's body.
For they seem to want to do this, and to strive for it,
so greedily do they cling in Venus's embrace,
while their limbs, undone by pleasure's force, dissolve.
At last, when desire, built up in the nerves, has burst forth,
there comes a brief pause in the violent heat,
then the same madness returns, that frenzy visits again,
when they seek to attain for themselves what they desire.
Nor can they find what remedy might overcome the ill —
so deeply do they waste away with a hidden wound.
Add that they consume their strength and perish with the effort.
Add that life passes at another's beck and call.
Meanwhile their estate slides away, and obligations go unmet,
their duties languish, and their wavering reputation falls ill.
Perfumes and lovely Sicyonian slippers smile on her feet.
Of course great emeralds with their green gleam
are set in gold, and the sea-blue dress wears thin
with constant use, and drinks in the sweat of Venus's labor.
The well-earned wealth of fathers becomes headbands and tiaras,
sometimes turned into robes, fine garments, and Iacchian attire.
Banquets, lavish in dress and fare, games,
frequent cups of wine, perfumes, garlands, and wreaths are made ready —
all in vain, since from the very heart of the spring of delights
something bitter rises up, to torment amid the very flowers,
or when the guilty mind torments itself with remorse.

To waste one's life in idleness and perish through dissipation,
Or because she left a word hanging ambiguously in the air,
Which, fixed in the eager heart, burns like fire.
Or to cast one's eyes about too much, or to gaze at another,
Because he thinks he sees traces of a smile upon her face.
And these evils in love are found in prosperity, at its very height,
But in adversity and poverty they are found as well —
Things you could grasp with your eyes shut,
Innumerable — so that it is better to be on guard beforehand,
As I have taught you to reason and to beware, lest you be ensnared.
For to avoid the snares so that we are not cast into love's net
Is not so difficult as, once caught in the nets themselves,
To escape and break through the strong bonds of Venus.
And yet, even entangled and ensnared, you could
Escape the danger, unless you yourself stand in your own way,
And overlook all the faults of a depraved mind,
And those of the body of the one you pursue and desire.
For men, blinded by passion, usually do this:
They attribute to women qualities which are not truly to their benefit.
Thus we see women who are misshapen and ugly in many ways
Living in luxury and held in the highest honor.
And some mock others and urge them toward Venus,
So that they may find favor, though they are afflicted by base love,
And in their wretchedness they do not look upon their own great ills. Often
A dark woman [μελάγχρους], unclean and foul-smelling [ἄκοσμος],
A grey-eyed one [πολλάδιον] with a birthmark, woody-limbed [δορκάς].
A tiny one, a dwarf, "all charm," "pure wit,"
A large and monstrous one [κετάτω ληξις], "full of dignity."
One who stammers and cannot speak [τραυλίζει] is called "modest."
But one who is hot-tempered, hateful, talkative becomes "a little torch" [λαμπάδιον].
A skinny one [ἐρωμάριον] becomes such when she can barely survive.

(from Book IV of De Rerum Natura)

Wasted by disease — [Greek terms indicating names or epithets] — she is now dead from coughing.
But [another name], monstrous and fierce, is struck hard by Bacchus,
And [another], a glutton — [Greek epithet] — is plump and voluptuous.
The rest of this kind would take too long to describe.
But still, grant her whatever beauty of face you will,
From whose every limb the power of Venus flows —
Surely there are other women too; surely we lived without her before;
Surely she does the same things, and we know she does everything — the ugly one too —
And she fumigates her wretched self with foul odors,
While her maids flee far off and secretly laugh.
But the weeping, locked-out lover often covers her threshold
With flowers and garlands, and anoints her proud doorposts
With marjoram, and the poor wretch presses kisses on the door.
Yet if he were let in, and one breath met him on the way,
He would seek decent reasons to depart,
And his long-rehearsed, high-flown complaint would fall flat,
And he would blame himself for his foolishness in giving her
More than it is right to grant to any mortal.
Nor does this escape our Venuses themselves — which is why they take
Such great pains to hide all the backstage workings of life
From those they wish to hold and keep bound in love.
But all in vain, since you can in your mind draw everything
Into the light and examine all these things for what they are.
And if she is good-natured and not hateful in return,
You can in turn let yourself attend to your ordinary affairs.
Nor does a woman always feign her sighs of love
When she clasps a man's body with her own
And holds him, moistening his lips with her kisses.
For often she acts from the heart, and seeking shared
Pleasures, urges him to run love's full course together.
And for no other reason do birds, cattle, and wild beasts —

And female cattle could yield to males equally.
If nature herself does not burn with their own desire abundantly,
And manage to entwine the Venus of leaping creatures.
Do you not see how those whom sudden mutual pleasure
Has bound together are tormented in their shared bonds?
In crossroads dogs that wished to part
Meanwhile cling fast in the strong bonds of Venus,
Which they would never do, unless they knew mutual joys
That could keep them lying ensnared and held together.
Therefore again and again (as I say) the pleasure is mutual,
And when the strong male seed mingles
With the female, it seizes it suddenly with its force,
And both strive eagerly with all their strength.
Then children are born resembling the mother through maternal seed,
Just as others resemble the father through paternal seed, but those whom you see
Bearing the features of both parents mixed together
Grow from the father's body and the mother's blood,
When the seeds, stirred through the limbs by Venus's goads,
Are met by a mutual ardor conspiring together,
And neither one has conquered the other, nor been conquered.
It also happens that sometimes children can appear like their grandparents,
And often reproduce the features of their great-grandparents,
Because the many first-beginnings in many combinations
Are often hidden mixed within the body of the parents,
Which fathers hand down from fathers, passed along from the lineage.
From these, Venus produces varied forms in turn,
And reproduces the looks, voices, and hair of ancestors.
Since these things come no more from one fixed seed
Than do our faces, bodies, and limbs.
And a female offspring arises from the paternal seed.

Book IV

Children born of mothers take on the bodily traits of their fathers.
For birth always comes from a double seed,
and whichever parent the child more closely resembles,
it has more than an equal share of that parent's traits, as you can plainly see,
whether the offspring is male or whether its origin is female.
Nor do the divine powers withhold from anyone the seed of generation
so that a father may never be called by the sweet name of his children,
and must spend his life in barren love —
as many people believe, and in grief they drench the altars with blood
and burn offerings on the shrines,
hoping to make their wives pregnant with abundant seed,
and they weary the divine power and the fates to no avail.
For those who are sterile are so partly because their seed is too thick,
and partly because it is too thin and watery beyond what is right.
The thin seed, because it cannot attach itself firmly to the proper places,
immediately flows away, and withdrawing, it ends in miscarriage.
The thicker seed, since it is discharged in a more compacted state than is fitting,
either does not travel with sufficient force,
or cannot penetrate the places equally, or having penetrated,
the seed mixes poorly with the female seed.
For the harmonies of love seem to differ greatly,
and some men fill some women more readily, and from others
some women conceive more easily and grow heavy with child.
And many women who were barren through several marriages
have nevertheless afterward found partners
with whom they could conceive children and grow rich with sweet offspring.
And for those whose wives, though fertile at home, had often failed to bear children,
a matched nature has also been found for them,
so that they could secure their old age with children.
So greatly does it matter what seeds are able to

Suited to mingle with the seeds in the act of generation,
Let the thick join with the thin, and the thin with the thick,
And in this it matters by what diet life is sustained.
For in some beings the seeds grow dense in the limbs,
While in others they are thinned and wasted in turn.
And in what manner gentle pleasure itself is handled
Matters greatly as well. For it is thought that wives
Conceive more readily after the fashion of four-footed beasts,
In the manner of animals, because in that position
The seeds can reach the right place, with the breast lowered
And the loins raised. Nor do soft wanton movements
Help wives at all. For a woman prevents her own conception
And fights against it, if in her joy she responds
To the man's thrust with her hips and makes the whole act fluid,
For she deflects the plow from its straight course
And turns the strike of the seed away from its proper furrow.
For this reason prostitutes are accustomed to move thus,
So as not to conceive frequently and lie heavy with child,
And also so that the pleasure might be more pleasing to men —
Which our own wives have no need of whatsoever.
Nor is it by divine power that a woman of lesser beauty
Is sometimes loved more ardently than one of finer form.
For the woman herself sometimes brings it about by her own conduct,
By her accommodating ways and her well-kept person,
That a man easily grows accustomed to spending his life with her.
As for the rest, habit nurtures love.
For that which is struck repeatedly, even lightly,
Is worn down and gives way over a long span of time.
Do you not see that drops of water falling on stones
Will, over a long period, hollow out the rock?

T. LUCRETIUS CARUS, ON THE NATURE OF THINGS
BOOK FIVE

Who can compose a poem worthy of a leaping heart,
adequate to the majesty of the things discovered?
Who has command of words sufficient
to fashion praises fit for his merits — he who gave us
such gifts, sought out and left to us from his own breast?
No one, I think, born of mortal body could do it.
For if we must speak as the known majesty of these things demands,
he was a god, illustrious Memmius, a god indeed —
who first discovered that principle of life which is now called wisdom,
and who through his art rescued our life from such great waves
and such great darkness, and set it in so calm and clear a light.
Compare with this the ancient divine discoveries of others.
For Ceres is said to have introduced grain to mortals,
and Liber the liquid flowing from the vine,
yet life could still have been sustained without these things,
as some peoples are said even now to live without them.
But a good life could not be lived without a pure heart.
All the more reason, then, that this man deserves to be regarded as a god among us,
from whom now throughout great nations there spread
sweet consolations of life that soothe our souls.
But if you think that the deeds of Hercules surpass his,
you are carried far astray from true reasoning.

Book V, line 80.

All these monsters of this kind that have been destroyed —
if they had not been conquered, what harm would they do alive?
None, I think; for even now the earth teems to satiety
with wild beasts, and is filled with trembling dread
through forests, and great mountains, and deep woods —
places which it is largely within our power to avoid.
But unless the mind is cleansed, what battles and dangers
must we, ungrateful, thrust ourselves into?
How many sharp stings of desire tear apart
the troubled man? And how many fears beside?
And pride, filth, and wantonness — what great
disasters do they cause? And luxury, and sloth?
He therefore who has conquered all these things and driven them
from his mind by reason — not by arms — shall he not
be deemed worthy to be counted among the number of the gods?
Especially since he has said many things, and more divinely than the gods themselves...

But to linger no more in our promises of what is to come:
First, look upon the seas and lands and sky,
Whose threefold nature, three bodies, Memmius,

One single day shall deliver them to ruin, and the great mass

Nor does it escape my mind that this is a strange and wondrous thing
For the mind to grasp — that the sky and earth face destruction —
And how hard it will be for me to prove it by words,
As happens when you bring something unfamiliar to ears
That have not heard it before, and yet you cannot
Lay it before their eyes or touch it with the hand,
By which the nearest road leads straight into the human heart
And the temples of the mind.
Yet I will speak it in words, and the facts themselves will give it credence.
Perhaps you will see all things shaken and shattered
By the force of great earthquakes arising in a short time —
Something which nature, guiding all from afar, keeps from us.
And reason, more than the spectacle itself, will persuade you
That all things can be struck down by a terrible, crashing roar.
Before I undertake this, I will pour forth my words on this matter
In a way more sacred and far more certain in its reasoning
Than the Pythia who speaks from Phoebus' tripod, crowned with laurel.

Book V

I will set out for you many consolations in learned words,
lest, restrained by religion, you should perhaps fear
that the earth, sun, sky, sea, stars, and moon
must remain eternal by divine nature,
and therefore think it right, as the giants did,
that they must pay penalties for some monstrous crime,
those who by their reasoning would disturb the walls of the world
and wish to extinguish the brilliant sun in the sky,
marking immortal things with mortal speech.
These things are so far removed from divine power,
and so unworthy to be counted among the gods,
that they are thought rather to give us knowledge
of what is removed from vital motion and from sense.
For it cannot be that with just any body
the nature of mind and understanding can exist,
just as a tree cannot exist in the sky, nor clouds in the salty sea,
nor can fish live in fields,
nor blood be found in wood, nor sap in stones.
It is fixed and determined where each thing grows and exists.
So the nature of the mind cannot arise without the body,
nor exist alone, far from nerves and blood.
For if it could, the power of the mind itself would much sooner
be able to exist in the head, or the shoulders, or the very heels,
and be accustomed to grow in any part whatsoever,
yet remain in the same man and in the same vessel.
Since it is established that even in our body
it has a fixed place where the soul and spirit can be and grow,
we must all the more deny that it can exist entirely outside the body,
forming an animal shape in the rotting clods of the earth or in the sun's fire.

Or to endure in water, or in the high regions of the ether.
They are therefore not endowed with divine sense,
Since they cannot be animated with vital life.
Nor is it possible to believe, furthermore, that
There exist sacred dwelling-places of the gods in any parts of the world.
For the subtle nature of the gods, far removed
From our senses, is scarcely perceived by the mind.
Since it eludes the touch and blow of our hands,
It must touch nothing that is tangible to us.
For that which cannot itself be touched cannot touch anything,
Therefore their dwellings too must be unlike
Our dwellings, subtle as their bodily forms are —
All of which I shall prove to you later at length.
Furthermore, to say that the gods wished to prepare
The glorious nature of the world for the sake of men, and that therefore
It is fitting to praise this praiseworthy work of the gods,
And to think it eternal and immortal,
And that it is sacrilege ever to shake by any force
What was established by ancient divine reason
For the human race to last forever,
Or to assail it with words and overturn it from its foundations,
And to invent other such things and add them, Memmius —
This is madness. For what benefit could our gratitude
Bestow upon immortal and blessed beings,
That they should undertake anything on our behalf?
Or what novelty could have enticed them, so long at rest,
To desire to change their former life?
For he seems likely to rejoice in new things
Whose old condition troubles him; but one to whom nothing painful
Happened in all past time, when life was passing beautifully —

BOOK V.

What could have kindled such a love of novelty?
What evil would there have been for us in not being created?
Surely life lay in darkness and grief,
Until the generative origin of things brought light.
For whoever is born ought to wish to remain
In life, as long as sweet pleasure holds him there.
But one who has never tasted the love of life,
And was never counted among the living — what harm is it that he was not created?
Moreover, the very pattern for bringing things into being,
And the knowledge first implanted in the gods of what men wanted —
How could they know what they wished to do, or conceive it in their minds?
Or in what way, I ask, was the power of first-beginnings made known?
And what things could they do when rearranged in different order,
If nature herself did not give the pattern through her own act of creation?
For in so many ways the primordia of things,
Driven by blows through infinite time,
Carried along by their own weights in constant motion,
Have moved in all manner of ways and tried out everything,
And whatever combinations could produce something by coming together —
It is no wonder that they fell into such arrangements
And came into such pathways
As those by which this sum of things is now maintained through renewal.
But even if I did not know what the first-beginnings of things are,
I would still dare to affirm this from the very workings of the sky,
And to prove it from many other things as well:
That the nature of things was by no means prepared for us by divine will,
So great are the faults with which it stands endowed.
To begin: of all that the vast sweep of the sky covers,
A greedy portion has been seized by mountains and forests full of wild beasts;
Rocks hold their share, and vast marshes,

And the sea, which keeps apart the wide shores of the lands,
From there again nearly two parts the burning heat,
And the constant falling of frost takes away from mortals.
What remains of farmland, nature with its own force
Would cover in thorns, unless human strength resisted,
Accustomed for the sake of life to groan under the strong mattock,
And to cleave the earth with the pressure of the plow,
If by turning the fertile clods with the share,
And working the soil of the earth to promote growth,
They could not of their own accord spring up into the clear air.
And yet sometimes, sought with great labor,
When now over the lands things leaf out and all things flourish,
Either the ethereal sun scorches with excessive heat,
Or sudden rains and icy frosts destroy them,
And the blasts of winds harass them with violent whirlwind.
Moreover, the dreadful race, the nature of wild beasts,
Hostile to the human race, by land and sea —
Why does nature feed and increase them? Why do the seasons bring diseases?
Why does untimely death roam abroad?
Then again the child, like a sailor cast up by savage waves,
Lies naked on the ground, speechless, in need of every
Kind of support for life, when first nature has poured him forth
By the straining of the womb onto the shores of light,
And fills the place with mournful crying, as is fitting,
For one who has so much suffering still left to pass through in life.
But the various cattle, herds, and wild beasts grow up,
Nor do they need rattles, nor must there be provided for each
The soft and broken babbling of a nurturing nurse,
Nor do they seek different garments for the season of the sky.
Nor do they need weapons or high city walls.

Book V (page 131)

Who are protected by their own, when the earth itself generously gives all things to all, the nature of things being so artfully varied?
First, since the body of the earth, and moisture, and the light breath of air, and warm vapors,
from which the sum of all things appears to be composed,
all consist of a natural and mortal body,
the nature of the world must be considered to be the same.
For indeed those things whose parts and members we observe
to have immortal shapes in their native body,
these same things we see are nearly mortal,
and natural at the same time. Therefore, when I see the greatest parts of the world,
its limbs and members consumed and born again,
we may know that the sky and earth too had some original beginning, and will have a future destruction.
Do not think, in these matters, that I have seized upon this point wrongly, Memmius: that earth, fire, and moisture took on mortal forms, I did not doubt, and that the air too perishes, and that these same things are born again and grow once more — this I have said.
First, a part of the earth, scorched by the constant sun and beaten by many a trampling foot, exhales a mist of dust, and clouds of flying particles, which the strong winds scatter through the air in all directions.
Part of the soil is also reclaimed by the floods from rain, and rivers gnaw away their banks.
Moreover, whatever the earth nourishes and increases from its own share is itself worn away, and since it is beyond doubt that the earth is the universal parent, it is likewise the common tomb of all things.
Thus the earth is diminished for you, and then grows back again enriched.
As for the rest: that the sea, rivers, and springs are ever full with new moisture, and that waters flow on perennially — this is plain to see.

No need for words: the great flow of waters
Declares it everywhere; but first, whatever water
Is lifted up, and in sum, so that no moisture overflows,
Partly the strong winds sweeping over the seas
Diminish it, and the ethereal sun unweaving it with his rays,
Partly it is spread abroad beneath the earth through all lands;
The liquid filters through and seeps back,
And all the substance of moisture gathers at the source of rivers,
And thence flows over the lands in a sweet stream,
Along the path which, once cut, it carried its waters with liquid step.

Now I will speak of air, which throughout its whole body
Is changed in countless ways into separate regions;
For whatever always flows from things, all of it
Is carried into the great sea of air, which, unless in turn
It gives back matter to things and replenishes what flows,
All would by now be dissolved and turned into air.

Thus it never ceases to be born from things, and back into things
To fall continually, since it is established that all things flow.

Likewise the generous fountain of flowing light, the ethereal sun,
Continually floods the sky with shining brightness,
And supplies light upon light without pause,
For whatever of its radiance is lost in any direction,
You may know from this:
As soon as clouds begin to pass before the sun,
And as it were break apart its rays of light,
Immediately the lower part of these rays entirely vanishes,
And the earth is shadowed wherever the storm clouds are carried —
So that you may know that things always need new splendor,
And that each first burst of radiance perishes,
And that things can be seen in the sun by no other means.

Do we not see the monuments of great men collapse

Do not boulders torn away tumble down from high mountains,

For surely they would not fall away so suddenly,
if from infinite time past they had been able to endure.
All things are stripped by time's battering assault.
And now look around you, above and below — that which holds
the whole earth in its embrace, which brings forth from itself
all things (as some say) and takes them back when they perish:
all of it, every part, consists of mortal body.
For whatever thing feeds and nourishes other things from itself —

It must be diminished, and renewed when it takes things back.
Besides, if there was no original birth
of lands and sky, and they were always eternal,
why, beyond the Theban war and the fall of Troy,
have other poets not sung of other events?
Where have so many deeds of men so often perished? And nowhere
do they flourish, planted in the eternal monuments of fame?
But (as I think) the sum of things has newness, and the world
is young in nature, and did not begin long ago.
Therefore even now certain arts are being refined,
even now they are growing, and many things have been added to navigation,
musicians lately produced melodious harmonies.
And finally, this rational account of nature was discovered
recently, and I myself am the first among the first to have found it,
who can now render it into the words of my homeland.
But if you should think that all these same things existed before,
yet that generations of men perished in a torrent of fire,
or that cities fell in a great upheaval of the world,
or that rivers, spreading relentlessly from incessant rains,
covered towns and overran the lands,
then all the more must you be compelled to admit
that destruction of the lands and skies will also come.
For when things were assailed by such great diseases and such great dangers,
if some more grievous cause had weighed upon them,
it would have spread ruin far and wide, and great destruction.
And we see that mortals are susceptible in no other way
among ourselves, except that we fall sick from the same diseases
as those whom nature has taken away from life.
Moreover, whatever things remain eternal, it must be either
because, being of solid body, they repel blows,

Book V.

Nor to allow anything that could forcibly
Dissociate its inner parts to penetrate it, as the bodies

Or to endure through all of time because

But also (as I have taught) the nature of the world

Which, arising by chance from the infinite, might

Nor moreover does the nature of space and the depth of the void

Therefore the gate of death is not shut against the heavens,

Therefore it must also be admitted that these same things
Are born of mortal body, since they could not,
From infinite time until now, have withstood
The mighty forces of immeasurable age.
Finally, when the greatest parts of the world
Fight so greatly among themselves, stirred up in impious war,
Do you not see that some long struggle for them

It is possible that an end may come, when the sun and all its vapor,

What they strive to do, though their efforts have not yet prevailed.
So much do rivers supply, and on their own they threaten

Once, meanwhile, fire has had the upper hand,

For fire prevailed, and spreading far, burned much,
When the fierce power of the sun's horses swept Phaethon

But the almighty father, then driven by fierce anger,
Struck down bold Phaethon with a sudden bolt of lightning,
Hurling him from the horses to the earth, while the sun,
Meeting him as he fell, received back the eternal torch of the world,
Gathered the scattered horses, yoked them trembling,
And thence restored all things, guiding them along their proper course —
As the ancient poets of Greece have sung,
Which is far removed from true rational understanding.
For fire can prevail when there are more bodies of matter
Drawn in from infinity;
Then its strength falls back, overcome by some principle,
Or things perish, burned up by the rushing winds.
Likewise, moisture once began to prevail over all things,
As the tradition of mankind holds, when it overwhelmed many cities.

BOOK V.

Then, when that force had withdrawn and retreated by some means,
Whatever had arisen from the infinite
Stood firm: the rains settled, and the rivers diminished their force.
But in what ways that matter, thrown together,
Founded the sky and the earth, and the depths of the sea,
And the courses of sun and moon, I will set forth in order.
For certainly the first-beginnings of things did not
Place themselves each in their own order by design or by keen intelligence,
Nor did they agree upon what motions each would give.
But because the first-beginnings of things, many in many ways,
Driven by blows from infinite time,
Have been accustomed to be carried along, impelled by their own weights,
And to move in every manner, and to try everything,
Whatever they could create by coming together —
For this reason it comes about that, spread through the great ages,
Trying out all kinds of meetings and motions,
At last those things come together which, suddenly united,
Often become the beginnings of great things:
Of earth, of sea, of sky, and of the race of living beings.
At that time here, neither could the sun's wheel, flying high
With its vast light, be seen, nor the stars of the great world,
Nor the sea, nor the sky, nor the earth, nor the air,
Nor anything resembling what we know could be seen.
But a certain new storm, and a mass that had arisen,
Caused the parts of that place to scatter,
And like things to join with like, and to sort out the world,
And to separate its members, and to arrange the great parts —
Drawn from all kinds of first-beginnings, whose discord,
Mixing intervals, paths, connections, weights, blows,
Collisions, and motions, was stirring up conflict.

Because of their unlike shapes and varied forms,
Not all things joined could remain together thus,
Nor could they exchange fitting motions among themselves —
This is why the high sky was separated from the lands,
And the sea lay apart, disclosed by its own moisture,
And likewise the fires of pure and separate aether.
For indeed all the bodies of the earth,
Because they were heavy and entangled, came together
In the middle, and all settled into the lowest places.
The more they intertwined and pressed together,
The more they forced out those elements that make the sea, the stars, the sun,
And the moon, and the great walls of the world.
For all these things are made of smoother and more rounded seeds,
And of far smaller elements, than earth;
And so aether, bursting through the thin pores of the earth,
First raised itself up through its parts,
And being light, carried away with it many fires —
Not unlike what we often see
When first the golden light of the radiant morning sun
Glows red through the dew-gemmed grass at dawn,
And lakes breathe out their mist, and rivers their endless streams,
And the earth itself sometimes seems to be smoking —
All of which, rising upward and gathering on high,
Weave the clouds beneath the sky with their dense mass.
So it was that the light and spreading aether,
Enclosed and girt on all sides by dense matter,
And widely diffused into all quarters everywhere,
Thus wrapped all other things in its eager embrace.
From this came the beginnings of sun and moon,
And between the two globes that revolve in the air,

Which neither earth claimed for itself, nor the great sky above,
Nor were they heavy enough to settle and sink down,
Nor light enough to glide along the highest edges,
Yet between the two they are such that, like living bodies,
They stir and extend as parts of the whole world.
Just as in us certain limbs may remain in place,
While still there are those that move us.
With these matters thus reviewed, the earth suddenly
Sank away where now the broad blue plain of the sea stretches,
And flooded its hollows with the salt surge.
And as day by day the heat of the sky around
And the rays of the sun pressed the earth from every side
With repeated blows toward its outermost limits,
So that, compressed at its center, it grew dense and firm,
All the more did the salt sweat squeezed from its body
Swell the sea as it oozed out, flooding the plains.
And all the more did those many bodies of vapor and air
Fly outward and escape, and far from the earth
Compress the shining vaults of the high sky.
The plains settled, the mountain heights grew tall,
For the rocks could not sink down,
Nor could all parts give way equally and alike.
Thus the weight of the earth, with its body now consolidated,
Settled, and all the world's slime, heavy as dregs,
Flowed down to the bottom and sank utterly like sediment.
From there the sea, from there the air, from there the fire-bearing sky itself,
All left pure with their fluid bodies,
Each lighter than the last, and the most fluid ether,
The lightest of all, leaps up above the airy breezes.
Nor does the fluid body of the disturbing winds of air

Now let us sing of what causes the motions of the stars.

It is also possible that all the sky remains

Or because air flowing in from outside
Drives the fires as it moves, or because the fires themselves can creep
Wherever food calls each one and invites it onward,
