For to establish with certainty what is the case in this world
Is difficult; but what can happen, and what does happen throughout
The various worlds created in various ways —
This I teach, and I go on to set out several causes
For the motions of the stars, which may hold throughout the universe,
One of which must nonetheless be the true cause in our world —
The cause by which motion is sustained among the constellations. But which of these it is —

To fall headlong is not the same as moving forward step by step.
That the earth rests in the middle region of the world,
It is fitting that its weight should gradually fade and diminish,
And that it should have beneath it another nature
Joined from the beginning of time and fitted together with
The airy parts of the world, in which it lives embedded.
For this reason it is not a burden, nor does it press down upon the air,
Just as a man's own limbs have no weight for him,
Nor is the head a burden to the neck, nor do we feel
The whole weight of the body resting on the feet.
But whatever weights come from outside and are placed upon us
Are burdens, and often much smaller ones cause harm —
So much does it matter what each thing is capable of.
Thus the earth was not suddenly brought from elsewhere
And cast down here, alien to different airs,
But was conceived from the first origin of the world,
And a fixed part of it appears to us almost as our own limbs.
Moreover, when the earth is shaken suddenly by a great thunderclap,
Everything above it is shaken by its motion —
Which it could not do by any means, unless it were
Bound to the airy parts of the world and to the heavens.
For they cling together by shared roots,
Joined from the beginning of time and fitted together as one.
Do you not also see how, though of great weight,
The most tenuous force of the soul sustains our body?
This is because it is so joined and fitted together as one.
And finally, who is able to lift the body in a swift leap
Except the force of the soul, which governs the limbs?
Do you not now see how much a tenuous nature can accomplish
When joined with a heavy body — just as air joined together...

Is the power of the mind joined to the earth and to us?
Neither is the disk of the sun larger, nor its heat less
Than it appears to our senses.
For from whatever distances fires can draw their light
And breathe their warm vapor upon our limbs,
They lose nothing of their body's substance but at intervals,
And nothing is more compact in appearance than flame.
Therefore, since the heat of the sun and its abundant light
Reach our senses, and the places shine with it,
The form of the sun too must appear to us from here,
So that you could add nothing more or less to it in truth.
And the moon, whether it travels through the sky with borrowed light,
Or casts its own light from its own body,
Whatever it is, it moves with no greater shape
Than it appears to be to our eyes when we observe it.
For all things that we see at a great distance
Through much air appear confused in appearance,
Down to the smallest thread. Therefore the moon must,
Since it presents a clear appearance and a definite shape,
Exactly as it is marked at its outermost edges,
Appear to us from up there of exactly the size it is.
Finally, all the fires of the aether that you see from here,
Since we observe similar fires on earth,
While their flickering is visible, while their heat is perceived,
Are seen to waver ever so slightly one way or the other,
When the interval of distance is greater,
You may know they could be only slightly smaller
Or slightly larger by a small margin.
Likewise, whatever size the image appears to us from here, such is its size.
Nor is it surprising, by what means

BOOK V.

That so small a body can send forth so much light,
That it fills the seas and all the lands and the sky with its flooding rays,
And bathes all things in its warm vapor.
For though from this single source the whole world's
Abundantly flowing fountain seems to burst and stream with light
From the entire world, where thus the vaporous elements
Gather from all sides, and being thus collected
Flow together, so that from one head the heat may pour forth:
Do you not see how even a small spring of water
Waters the meadows far and wide, and overflows into the fields?
It is also possible that not from a great fire of the sun
The scorching heat seizes the air with its burning intensity.
If the air is well-suited and fit for the purpose,
It can be set ablaze by small strokes of heat.
Just as we sometimes see crops and stubble
Catching fire in all directions from a single spark.
Perhaps too the rosy sun, shining with its lofty torch,
Possesses much fire within its unseen heat,
With no visible glow around it,
So that the heat-bearing sun merely intensifies the force of its rays.
Nor is the path of the sun simple or straightforward,
As to how from summer regions it makes its way
To its winter turnings, and returning thence
Veers to the solstitial limits of Cancer,
And through months seems to traverse that same space,
In which the sun completes its yearly course.
The cause given for these things is not simple, I say;
Whether it seems possible above all that this could happen
As Democritus, that holy man, sets forth in his teaching:
That the nearer the stars are to the earth,

So much less able to be carried along with the whirling of the sky,
for its rapid fires fade away and diminish
beneath its force, and so it is left behind,
while the sun gradually falls back among the later signs,
being so much lower than the fiery constellations.
And still more so the moon: the lower her course
lies far from the sky and nearer to the earth,
the less she can keep pace with the signs in her path,
since the more sluggish the whirl that carries her,
being lower than the sun, the more all the signs
overtake her, moving around and past her.
That is why she appears to turn back more swiftly
to each sign, because the signs return to her.
It may also be that air flowing in alternating streams
from the transverse regions of the world
can drive the sun away from the summer signs
all the way to the winter solstice and its cold,
and then drive him back from the frozen shadows
into the burning regions and the fiery signs.
Likewise, we must suppose that the moon and stars,
which revolve through their great orbits over great years,
can travel by alternate airs from opposite regions.
Do you not see how clouds, driven by different winds,
move in different directions, lower ones against upper ones?
Why should those stars not equally be carried
through the great orbits of the sky in different currents?
But night covers the earth in deep darkness,
either when after its long journey the sun has struck
the outermost regions of the sky and, spent,
breathes out its fires, shaken and weakened by so much air.

Or because the same force that carried the sun's orb above the earth compels it to turn its course beneath the earth,
and at a fixed time Matuta spreads the rosy dawn through the shores of the ether and unveils the light.
Or because the same sun, returning beneath the earth,
tries to set the sky ablaze in anticipation with its rays,
or because fires and many seeds of heat
have grown accustomed to gathering together at a fixed time,
producing ever-new flames of sunlight.
For it is said that on the high Idaean mountains
scattered fires can be seen in the eastern light,
then coalescing into a single globe and forming a sphere.
Yet it should not seem surprising in these matters
that these seeds of fire are able at such a fixed time
to gather together and renew the brilliance of the sun.
For we see many things that happen at a fixed time
in all things: trees flower at a fixed time
and at a fixed time drop their blossoms,
and no less surely does age command teeth to fall
at their time, and youth to clothe itself in soft down,
and the soft beard to descend equally on the cheeks.
Finally, lightning, snow, rains, clouds, and winds
occur in no very uncertain seasons of the year.
For since the first beginnings of causes were thus established,
and the affairs of the world have unfolded from their first origin in this way,
nature follows from a fixed order of things.
Days may grow longer and nights may waste away,
and daylight diminish as nights increase.
Or because the same sun, passing beneath the earth and above
through unequal curves along the shores of the ether,

It divides and splits the heavens into unequal parts,
And what it takes away from one side, it restores,
Moving ever further in the opposite direction,
Until it reaches that sign of the sky where the year's
Node makes the nights equal to the hours of light.
For midway in its course, between the north wind and the south,
It marks the boundaries of heaven with an equal division,
On account of the sign-bearing position of the whole heavens.
The sun, gliding in its yearly course, winds through the seasons,
Illuminating the earth and sky obliquely,
As the reasoning of those who mapped the regions of the sky
And noted all of them adorned with arranged constellations makes clear.
Or because in certain regions the air is denser,
The trembling fire of the sun therefore hesitates below the earth,
And cannot easily penetrate and rise to its rising.
For this reason the nights in winter time are long,
And cease only when the radiant sign of day arrives.
Or again, because in alternating parts of the year
The fires are accustomed to gather more slowly and more swiftly,
Which cause the sun to rise in a fixed quarter —
For this reason these people seem to speak the truth.
The moon can shine when struck by the rays of the sun,
And turn ever more of that light toward us each day
In proportion as it moves away from the sun's orb,
Until it shines fully against it with complete light,
And rising has seen its setting above the heights.
Then little by little it must, as it were, hide its light again,
The nearer it glides back toward the sun's fire
Through the other part of the zodiac across the sky —
As those believe who hold that the moon is like a ball

Book V.

To hold a similar course and path beneath the sun.
There is also reason why the moon may, with its own light,
Turn and give back various forms of brightness.
For another body may exist that moves along
And glides in every way, attending and serving,
Unable to be seen, because it travels without light,
Spinning as if it were a ball, like a sphere,
Half of its surface touched with glowing light,
And by turning the ball it produces changing shapes.
Then whatever part is lit by fire,
It turns toward us to behold with our open eyes,
Then little by little draws back and takes away
The luminous portion of that orb and sphere,
As the Babylonian Chaldean doctrine, being refuted,
Strives to argue against the art of astrologers.
Since it is nearly impossible that what each side contends can both be true,
Why should you embrace one more than the other?
Why, moreover, could not a new moon always be created
In a fixed order of shapes and set figures,
Each creation abolished day by day,
And another restored in its place and position?
It is difficult to prove by reason and overcome with words,
When you see so many things created in such fixed order.
Spring comes, and Venus, and before her Venus's herald,
The winged Zephyr walks in her footsteps,
While mother Flora, strewing the path before them,
Fills everything with fine colors and fragrance.
Then follows dry heat, and with it as companion
Dusty Ceres, and the etesian blasts of the north winds.
Then autumn comes, and with it Bacchus strides forward,

From there other storms follow, and winds,
The high-thundering Vulturnus, and the South Wind mighty with lightning.
At last winter brings snows and restores the chill of cold,
Winter follows, crackling with the accents of frost.
It is no wonder then, if at a fixed time the moon
Is born, and at a fixed time disappears again,
Since so many things can happen at so fixed a time.
Likewise the eclipses of the sun, and the darkenings of the moon,
Must be thought capable of arising from several causes.
For why should the moon be able to shut off the earth from the sun's
Light, and thrust her high head before it,
Casting her dark orb against its burning rays,
While at the same time some other body is thought incapable
Of doing the same, one that always glides without light?
And why should the sun not be able, growing faint, to let slip its fires
At a fixed time, and then renew its light again,
When it has passed through regions in the air hostile to flames,
Which cause its fires to be extinguished and to perish?
And why should the earth not be able in turn to rob the moon of light,
And hold the sun oppressed beneath itself,
While the moon in her monthly course glides through the cone of rigid shadows?
And at the same time some other body could not aid the moon,
Or glide above the orbit of the sun,
So as to interrupt its rays and the outpouring of its light?
And yet if the moon shines with her own brightness,
Why should she not be able to grow dim in a certain region of the sky,
While she passes through places hostile to her own light,
As she glides monthly through the rigid shadows of the cone?
As for what remains, since throughout the blue expanses of the great world
The means by which everything might come to be has been resolved.

LIB.

So that we might know the varied courses of the sun and the paths of the moon,
what force drives them and what cause sets them in motion,
and in what way they are accustomed to pass away with failing light,
and to cover the lands in darkness while we unsuspecting watch,
then, as if winking, to shine again with open light
so that all bright places are seen gleaming with clear radiance —
now I return to the newness of the world and the soft fields of earth,
to its new offspring, and what first the earth strove to bring
to the shores of light, and to entrust to the uncertain winds.
First, the race of grasses and the green splendor
the earth gave forth around the hills and across all the plains;
the flowering meadows shone with green color,
and to the various trees the great contest of growing
was given freely through the air with loosened reins.
Just as feathers, hairs, and bristles first arise
on the limbs of four-footed creatures and the bodies of the winged,
so the young earth then first raised up grasses and shrubs,
and thereafter brought forth mortal generations in their place,
many arising by many means and in varied ways.
For animals cannot have fallen from the sky,
nor can land creatures have emerged from the salt waters.
It remains that the earth rightly earned the name of mother,
since all things have been created from the earth.
And even now many animals arise from the earth,
formed by rains and the warm vapor of the sun.
So it is less surprising if then more and greater creatures arose,
grown to maturity in the new earth and ether.
First, the race of winged things and the varied birds
left their eggs, hatched in the season of spring,
just as now in summer the cicadas leave their rounded husks

Of their own will they leave their food, seeking life.
Then there the earth first gave birth to mortal generations,
For great heat and moisture abounded in the fields.
Wherever each region of the land offered suitable conditions,
Wombs grew in the roots of the earth, fitted for their purpose,
And when time had ripened them and opened them to age,
The infants, fleeing moisture and seeking the air,
Nature turned there the openings of the earth,
And compelled the veins to pour forth a juice
Like milk, just as now every woman,
When she has given birth, is filled with sweet milk, because all
The rush of nourishment is turned toward her breasts.
The earth provided food for the children, warmth for clothing, grass for bedding,
Abounding in much soft down.
But the newness of the world brought on no harsh cold,
Nor excessive heat, nor winds of great force,
For all things grow together and gain their strength alike.
Therefore the earth, having rightly won the name of mother,
Holds it deservedly, since she herself created the human race
And at nearly a fixed time brought forth every animal
That roams widely across the great mountains,
And likewise the birds of the air in their varied forms.
But because she must at some point cease from bearing,
She stopped, like a woman exhausted by the long passage of time.
For time changes the nature of the whole world,
And one state of things must give way to another in all things,
Nothing remains the same as itself, all things migrate,
Nature changes everything and compels all to transform.
For one thing decays and grows feeble with age,
While another grows up and rises from obscurity.

And so the age of the whole world alters nature,
And one state of the earth gives way to another.
What it once could bear, it can bear no longer; what it could not, now it can.
The earth then tried to create many monstrous things,
Born with strange appearance and mismatched limbs:
Androgynous, neither fully one sex nor the other, and removed from both;
Some deprived of feet, some robbed of hands in turn;
Many found without mouths, or blind without faces;
With their limbs fused and clinging across the whole body,
Unable to do anything, or yield to anything,
Unable to avoid harm or take what use requires.
Other monsters and prodigies of this kind she produced in vain,
Since nature blocked their growth,
And they could not reach the longed-for flower of life's prime,
Nor find food, nor join in the ways of Venus.
For we see that many things must come together
If living creatures are to be able to forge offspring by procreation:
First, food must be available for reproduction; then through the limbs
Seeds must be able to flow when the body is relaxed;
And female must be able to join with male — this is necessary —
With mutual pleasures binding them both together.
And so many generations of living things must have perished,
Unable through procreation to forge offspring.
For whatever you see drawing the breath of life,
It is cunning, or strength, or finally swiftness,
That has protected that kind from the beginning of time and preserved it.
And many creatures remain commended to our care through their usefulness to us.
From the start, the fierce race of lions and their savage generations
Have been protected by strength, foxes by cunning, and deer by flight.

Book V, lines XCIIII

But the gentle oxen with faithful hearts,
And every kind born of the ancient seed,
And woolly flocks and cattle of all ages —
All these are placed under the guardianship of men.
For fleeing eagerly from wild beasts, and seeking peace,
They exist, and abundant fodder gained without labor
We give them as reward for the usefulness they provide us.
But those whom nature endowed with none of these qualities,
And who could neither survive on their own accord
Nor offer us any utility — so that we might shelter
Their kind under our protection and keep them safe —
These creatures lay as prey and profit for others,
All ensnared in their own fatal bonds,
Until nature drove that kind to extinction.
But centaurs never existed, nor could there ever be
A creature of double nature and twofold body,
A power compacted of alien limbs from two kinds,
So that parts from each side might be equally matched.
This anyone may understand, however dull of mind.
First, after three years have passed in their prime,
The horse is in full flower — but a boy not at all;
Even then he often still seeks in dreams
The milk-laden breasts of his nursing mother.
Later, when strong limbs fail with advancing old age
And the vital force retreats from the weakening body,
Then at last youthful vigor in its boyish prime
Arrives, and covers his cheeks with soft down.
Do not believe that centaurs could be formed or exist
From human seed mixed with the seed of horses,
Nor Scyllas with their bodies half of ravening hounds
And half of sea-creature, and others of that kind.

LIB.

Among those whose limbs we see are discordant with each other,
which neither flourish alike, nor gain strength
in their bodies, nor benefit from the aging years,
nor are inflamed by the same desire, nor agree in their habits,
nor do they share the same pleasures throughout their frame.
Indeed one may observe that the bearded herds often fatten
on hemlock, which to man is a sharp poison.
And since flame is accustomed to scorch and burn
the tawny bodies of lions, just as it does every kind
of creature on earth, whatever blood it has,
how could the Chimera, joined in a triple body,
with lion in front, serpent behind, and chimera itself in the middle,
fierce of mouth, breathe forth flames from its body?
Therefore, whoever imagines that on a young earth, under a young sky,
such animals could have been born,
relying on this one empty claim of novelty,
may babble many such things with similar reasoning.
He might say that rivers of gold once flowed
commonly across the lands, and that shrubs bloomed with gems,
or that man was born with such great power of limb
that he could stride across the high seas on foot
and spin the whole sky around himself with his hands.
For although there were many seeds of things in the earth
at the time when the land first brought forth animals,
there is still no proof that creatures of different kinds could have been created
intermingled, and the limbs of different living things joined together,
because the things that even now abundantly spring from the earth —
the kinds of grasses and crops and flourishing shrubs —
cannot yet be created intertwined with one another,
but each proceeds in its own manner, so that all things...

By nature's fixed laws they maintained their distinctions.
And that race of humanity was much hardier
In the fields, as was fitting, since the hard earth had made them so,
Built on larger and more solid bones within,
Fitted with strong sinews throughout their flesh.
They were not easily overcome by heat or cold,
Nor by unfamiliar food, nor any failing of the body.
Through many a cycle of the sun rolling through the sky
They led their lives wandering in the manner of wild beasts.
No one was yet a skilled guide of the curved plow,
Nor knew how to work the fields with iron,
Nor how to plant new shoots in the ground, nor cut
The old branches from tall trees with pruning hooks.
What the sun and rains had given, what the earth had produced of itself,
Was gift enough to satisfy their hearts.
They tended their bodies mostly among the acorn-bearing oaks,
And the arbutus berries which you now see in winter
Ripening to a bright crimson color —
The earth then brought forth even more and larger ones.
The youthful freshness of the world then also produced
Many harsh and terrible foods for wretched mortals.
But rivers and springs taught them to quench their thirst,
Just as now the rushing waters down from great mountains
Call the thirsty generations of wild beasts.
Then too they occupied the woodland shrines of the Nymphs,
Known to wanderers, from which the flowing waters
Poured in abundance to wash the wet slippery rocks,
Wet rocks dripping above with green moss,
And in part bubbled up across the level plain.
They did not yet know how to work with fire, nor to make use of it.

BOOK V.

They clothed their bodies with the hides and spoils of wild beasts,
But they lived in groves and hollow hills and forests,
And hid their filthy limbs among the undergrowth,
Compelled to shelter from the lashing winds and rains.
They could not look to the common good, nor did they know
How to govern themselves by customs or by laws.
Whatever prize of prey fortune offered, each man took.
Each was taught by nature to live and thrive alone,
Armed with hurled rocks and the great weight of the club.
And Venus joined the bodies of lovers in the woods;
For either mutual desire drew each together,
Or the man's fierce force and violent passion,
Or a payment of acorns, arbutus-berries, or choice pears.
And trusting in the wondrous strength of their hands and feet,
They would hunt the woodland generations of wild beasts,
Overpowering many, and escaping a few by hiding,
And like bristly swine they would lay their forest-hardened limbs
Naked on the ground when caught by nightfall,
Wrapping themselves in leaves and branches all around.
Nor did they wander in panic through the fields by day
Lamenting the sun, searching through the shadows of night,
But lay silent, buried in sleep,
Until the sun with his rosy torch brought light back to the sky.
For since from childhood they had always seen
That darkness and light were born in alternating time,
There was no reason they should ever wonder at it,
Nor fear that eternal night might hold the earth forever
Once the sun's light was taken away.
But what troubled them more was that the generations of wild beasts
Would often make their rest dangerous and wretched,

Driven from their homes, they fled the rocky dwellings
At the arrival of the foaming boar and mighty lion,
And in the dead of night yielded up in fear
Their leaf-strewn beds to these savage guests.
Nor then did mortal generations leave
The sweet light of life with any greater grief than now.
For then each one who was caught alone
Was seized alive and fed the beasts with his living flesh,
And filled the groves, mountains, and forests with his groaning,
Watching his living entrails buried in a living tomb.
But those whom flight had saved, their bodies half-consumed,
Afterward held their trembling palms over festering wounds
And called upon death with terrible cries,
Until savage parasites robbed them of life,
Helpless and ignorant of what the wounds demanded.
Yet not many thousands of men, led beneath the standards,
Were given over to destruction in a single day,
Nor did the stormy seas dash ships upon the rocks
And drown their crews.
Nor did the sea, stirred up by reckless surging waves,
Often rage in vain and lay aside its idle threats.
The treacherous lure of the calm sea's smiling surface
Could not then deceive men to their ruin.
The wicked art of navigation lay then unknown.
Then scarcity of food gave limbs weakened unto death,
While now abundance overwhelms us.
They in their ignorance often poured poison
Upon themselves; now others give it more skillfully.
Then, once they had built huts, and prepared skins and fire,
And woman joined with man was united with one partner,
And the joys of chaste matrimony in private love were known,

These things became known, and offspring were seen to spring from themselves.
Then the human race first began to grow soft,
For fire ensured that cold bodies
Could no longer bear the chill beneath the canopy of heaven.
And Venus diminished the strength of parents and children alike;
By flattery, their proud spirit was easily broken.
Then neighbors began eagerly to join in friendship,
Wishing neither to harm nor to wrong one another.
They commended children and the female sex to one another,
Expressing with voices and gestures, though haltingly,
That it was right to take pity on the weak.
Yet harmony could not come about in every way,
But a good and great part observed their pacts faithfully,
Or else the whole human race would have perished by then,
And reproduction could not have carried the generations forward.
But nature compelled them to produce various sounds of speech,
And practical need pressed out names for things.
It is not much different from the way
The infancy of language seems to draw children to gesture,
When it causes them to point with a finger at things present before them.
For each creature feels by its own power what it can use.
The horns of a calf appear before they extend from its forehead,
And with them, when angered, it charges and attacks aggressively.
But the cubs of panthers and the whelps of lions
Already fight back with claws and paws and bites,
Scarcely even when their teeth and claws are just formed.
And we see that all the race of winged creatures
Trusts in its wings and seeks trembling refuge in its feathers.
To suppose, therefore, that someone at that time assigned names to things,
And that from this humans learned their first words —
Is foolishness.

It is folly — for why would it be thought impossible that one person could have given names to things and uttered the various sounds of language, while at the same time others could not do the same? Besides, if others had not already used words among themselves, from where would the concept of usefulness have been implanted, and from where would the first capacity for this have been given — to know what he wanted to do and to perceive it in his mind? One person could not have compelled a multitude and overcome them so that they would be willing to learn the names of things; nor could he have taught them by any method, or persuaded the deaf about what needed to be done — for they would not easily have endured it, nor for any reason would they have suffered to have the strange and unheard sounds of speech beat upon their ears to no purpose.

Finally, what is so remarkable about this? If the human race, endowed with voice and tongue, distinguished different things with different sounds according to different feelings — since even mute cattle, and the generations of wild beasts, are accustomed to utter different and varied sounds when fear or pain is present, or when joys begin to swell. Indeed, this can be observed plainly in familiar things. When the large Molossian hounds are angered, their soft lips draw back snarling and baring their hard teeth — with a sound far different from when their rage is restrained and they merely bark, filling everything with their noise. But when they try to lick their cubs gently with their tongue, or toss them with their paws and snap at them playfully, pretending to bite with their teeth held back, they fawn with quite a different whining sound of voice. And when left alone they howl in the house, or when, whimpering, they slink away with lowered body from a beating —

BOOK V.

And so it seems that whinnies also differ,
When among the mares a young stallion in the flower of youth
Is stung by love's spurs and rages,
And at other times when he neighs with trembling limbs,
And snorts his breath through wide nostrils, roused to battle.
Finally the race of winged creatures, the various birds,
Hawks, ospreys, and seabirds that seek their food and life
In the salt waves of the sea,
Utter sounds far different from one another at different times,
When they compete for food and fight over their prey,
And in part the ancient generations of crows change
Their raucous songs along with the weather,
And flocks of ravens, when they are said to call for rain and showers,
And at times to cry out for winds and breezes.
Therefore, if varied feelings drive animals,
Though mute, to produce various sounds,
How much more reasonable is it that mortals at that time were able
To mark different things with different words?
Do not silently wonder about this in these matters:
Lightning brought fire down to earth for mortals,
And from this all the burning of flames is said to derive.
For we see many things kindled by heavenly flames
Blazing, when the region of the sky has bestowed its heat.
And also when a branching tree, shaken by winds and swaying,
Presses and seethes against another tree's branches,
Fire is forced out, rubbed out by the strong friction,
And sometimes the fierce glowing heat flashes forth,
While the branches and trunks rub against each other,
Either of which could have given fire to mortals.
From there, to cook food and to soften it with flame's heat,

The sun taught them, since they saw many things softened
by the blows of its rays and overcome by heat across the fields.
And day by day they were led to change their former
food and way of life for new things, and fire,
those who excelled in intellect and were strong in spirit.
Then kings began to found cities and establish citadels
as strongholds and refuges for themselves.
They divided up the livestock and land, and distributed them
according to each person's appearance, strength, and ability.
For appearance counted for much, and strength flourished.
Later, wealth was discovered and gold found,
which easily stripped honor from the strong and handsome alike.
For people mostly follow the faction of the wealthier man,
however brave or well-formed in body they may be.
But if someone truly governs life by reason,
great wealth for a person lies in living frugally
with a calm mind, for there is never any lack of little things.
Yet men wanted to be famous and powerful,
so that their fortune might rest on a stable foundation
and they might live a peaceful and prosperous life —
all in vain, since striving to rise to the highest honor,
they made the path of life a dangerous road.
And yet, as though struck by lightning from the summit,
envy sometimes casts them down contemptuously into grim Tartarus.
So it is far better to obey and live in quiet
than to want to rule affairs with command and hold kingdoms.
Therefore, let the weary sweat their blood in vain,
struggling along the narrow path of ambition.
For envy, like lightning, scorches those at the top,
and especially whatever stands most prominently in high places.

BOOK V.

Since they think with borrowed minds, and seek
Their knowledge from hearsay rather than their own senses,
And it is no more so now, nor will it be, than it was before.
So when kings were slain, the ancient majesty
Of thrones lay overthrown, and proud scepters fell,
And the glorious crown of the supreme head, stained with blood,
Mourned its great honor beneath the feet of the common mob.
For what was once too greatly feared is now trampled underfoot.
And so affairs sank to the lowest dregs and tumult,
As each man sought supreme power for himself.
Then some among the magistrates taught how to create offices,
And established laws, so that men would willingly live by them.
For the human race, exhausted by living under constant violence,
Was worn down by feuds, and so of its own accord
Fell under the rule of laws and strict ordinances.
For each person, driven by anger, prepared to take
Harsher vengeance than is now permitted by just laws.
For this reason men grew weary of living under constant violence,
And the fear of punishment now stains the rewards of life.
For violence and injury ensnare their perpetrator,
And return most often to the one from whom they sprang.
Nor is it easy to live a calm and peaceful life
For one who breaks by his deeds the common bonds of peace.
For even if he escapes the knowledge of gods and men alike,
He must still forever fear that his deception will be found out.
Indeed, since many are said to talk in their sleep,
Or rave in fever and so betray themselves,
And bring long-hidden sins to light.
Now what cause has spread the divine power of the gods among great nations,
And filled cities with altars,

And they took care to perform solemn sacred rites,
Which now flourish in great matters and in sacred places,
From which even now there is implanted in mortals a sense of dread,
Which raises up new temples to the gods throughout the whole world
Of lands, and compels men to celebrate on feast days —
It is not so difficult to give an account of this in words.
For indeed even then, mortal generations
Would see in their waking minds the outstanding forms of the gods,
And even more so in dreams, with their wondrous bodily stature.
To these beings they therefore attributed sensation, and moreover
Supposed that they moved their limbs, and uttered proud voices
Worthy of their glorious appearance and their great strength,
And they granted them eternal life, because the faces of the gods
Were always being supplied to them, and their form remained.
And yet they thought that beings endowed with such great powers
Could not easily be overcome by any force.
And they thought the gods far surpassed men in fortune,
Because the fear of death did not trouble any of them,
And because in dreams they saw these beings performing many wonderful things
And suffering no labor from it.
Moreover, they observed the movements of the sky in fixed order,
And the changing seasons of the years revolving,
But could not understand by what causes this came about.
Therefore they made it their refuge to entrust all things to the gods,
And to suppose that all things were guided by their nod,
And they placed the dwelling places and temples of the gods in the heavens,
Because through the sky the night and moon are seen to move,
The moon, the day, and the night, and the stern signs of the night,
And the night-wandering torches of the sky and flying flames,
Clouds, the sun, rains, snow, winds, lightning, hail.

And the swift roarings and the great thunderous threats.
O unhappy human race, when it attributed such deeds to the gods and added bitter anger to them —
What groans they brought upon themselves, what wounds upon us,
What tears for those who came after us!
It is no act of piety to be seen turning veiled
Toward a stone, or approaching every altar,
Or to prostrate oneself upon the ground and spread one's palms
Before the shrines of the gods, or to sprinkle altars
With the blood of four-footed beasts, or to pile vow upon vow,
But rather to be able to look upon all things with a mind at peace.
For when we gaze up at the heavenly regions of the great world above,
At the sky fixed with its glittering stars,
And the thought comes to us of the paths of the sun and moon,
Then into a heart already burdened with other troubles
That care too begins to raise its awakened head:
Whether perhaps some immense power of the gods over us
Moves the bright stars in their varied courses.
For the poverty of reason assails the doubting mind:
What was the original birth of the world,
And likewise what limit there may be to the walls of the world,
And whether the silent motions can sustain this labor forever —
Or whether, endowed by divine gift with eternal life,
They may glide through the everlasting course of time
And scorn the mighty forces of endless age.
Besides, whose heart is not gripped with dread of the gods,
Whose limbs do not creep with terror
At the dreadful stroke of lightning, when the parched earth trembles
And rumbles of thunder race across the vast sky?
Do not peoples and nations tremble? And proud kings —

Do the limbs of those struck with fear of the gods tremble?
Lest for some act foully committed, or word spoken arrogantly,
The heavy time for paying penalties has come due,
Even when the supreme force of a violent wind at sea
Sweeps a commander across the waters with his fleet,
Together with his strong legions and their elephants —
Does he not seek the peace of the gods with prayers and vows,
And fearfully beg for favorable winds and fair sailing?
All in vain, since often caught up in a violent whirlwind
He is carried no less swiftly toward the shallows of death.
So thoroughly does some hidden force trample human affairs
And crush the fine rods of office and their cruel axes,
And seem to make sport of them and hold them in mockery.
Again, when the whole earth shakes beneath one's feet,
And cities collapse in ruin and threaten to fall further,
Is it any wonder that mortal generations humble themselves
And yield great powers and extraordinary authority
To divine forces in the world, believing they govern all things?
What remains: bronze and gold and iron were discovered,
And likewise the weight of silver and the use of lead.
When fire had burned the vast forests with its heat
In the great mountains, whether from lightning sent from the sky,
Or because men waging a woodland war among themselves
Had brought fire upon their enemies to spread terror,
Or because, drawn by the goodness of the soil, they wished
To open up rich fields and turn the land to pasture,
Or to hunt wild beasts and enrich themselves with prey —
For the pit-trap and fire came first in the art of hunting
Before the practice of encircling a grove with snares and rousing game with dogs.
Whatever it may be, from whatever cause the flaming heat

With a terrible roar, as it had consumed the tall forests
From their roots, and scorched the earth with fire,
It flowed through glowing veins into the hollow places of the earth,
A river of silver gathering there, and of gold,
And of bronze and lead; and when they saw these, once cooled,
Gleaming afterward with bright color upon the earth,
They were captivated by the smooth and pleasing luster,
And saw that they were shaped in a similar form,
Bearing the impressions of the hollows where each had lain.
Then it came to them that these metals, melted by heat,
Could flow into any shape and form of things,
And that they could be drawn out into points, however sharp and fine,
Into the tips of blades by hammering,
So that they might forge weapons for themselves, and cut down forests,
And work timber, and plane smooth beams,
And bore through things, and pierce and perforate them.
They prepared to do this with silver and gold no less
Than with the first strong force of sturdy bronze,
But to no avail, for the strength of these metals yielded and was overcome,
And they could not equally endure the hard labor.
For bronze was then held in high esteem, while gold lay neglected
As useless, dulled by its blunted edge.
Now bronze lies neglected, and gold has risen to the highest honor.
So does rolling time change the seasons of things:
What was once prized comes to be held in no esteem at all,
While something else rises in its place, emerging from contempt,
And is sought after more each day, and once discovered flourishes
In praise, and is held in wondrous honor among mortals.
Now, Memmius, how the nature of iron was discovered
It is easy enough for you yourself to understand.

The ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth,
And stones, and likewise branches broken from forest trees,
And flame and fire, after these were first discovered,
Then later iron and bronze were found to be useful,
And the use of bronze was known before that of iron,
Because its nature is more workable and its supply greater.
With bronze they worked the soil of the earth, and with bronze they stirred
The waves of war, and spread wide and savage wounds,
And seized cattle and farmlands, for everything unarmed
And defenseless yielded easily to those bearing weapons.
Then gradually the iron sword came into use,
And the shape of the bronze sickle fell into disrepute,
And men began to cut through the soil of the earth with iron,
And the contests of war, ever uncertain, were made equal.
And it came first to mount upon the back of a horse armed,
To guide it with reins and urge it on with the right hand,
Before risking the dangers of battle in a two-horse chariot.
And the two-horse team came before the yoking of four horses together,
And before the invention of mounting scythe-bearing chariots.
Then the Carthaginians taught their grim tower-bodied Lucanian oxen
To endure the wounds of battle with snake-like hands,
And to throw into disorder the great battalions of Mars.
So sad discord bred one thing from another,
To be a horror in arms for the nations of mankind,
And day by day added more to the terrors of war.
They tried bulls too in the service of war,
And attempted to send savage boars against the enemy,
And some sent powerful lions ahead of them
With armed handlers and cruel trainers,
Who might be able to control them and keep them in chains.

Book V.

Since, mingled in the slaughter, the fierce beasts,
Burning with rage, threw the ranks into chaos without distinction,
Shaking their fearsome crests on every side.
The horsemen could not soothe their horses, terrified by the din,
Nor turn their mounts with the reins against the enemy.
The lionesses hurled their bodies in leaping on every side,
And rushed at the faces of those coming toward them,
And tore at those who least expected it from behind,
And grappling, dragged the defeated down to the ground,
Held fast with powerful bites and hooked claws.
The bulls tossed their own men and trampled them underfoot,
And gored the flanks and bellies of horses from below,
And rushed with menacing intent to gore the ground.
The boars cut down their own allies with powerful tusks,
Staining with their own blood the weapons broken in them,
And dealt ruin alike to cavalry and infantry.
For the beasts drove their tusks sideways, slashing fiercely,
Or reared up on their hind legs and struck at the wind,
In vain, since you would see them hamstrung at the tendons,
Collapsing and crashing heavily to the ground.
Those they thought tame enough before, reared at home,
Were seen to boil with fury in the heat of action,
With wounds, uproar, flight, terror, and tumult,
And no part of them could be brought under control.
For every kind of wild creature fled in all directions,
Just as now the elephants of Africa, badly wounded by the sword,
Flee after dealing great savage blows to their own men.
So it was that they acted thus. But I can barely believe
That they did not foresee in their minds beforehand,
And see what a general disaster and foul outcome it would be.

And you could more readily argue this to have happened, Memmius,
In various worlds, created by various means,
Than in any one particular globe of lands.
But they did not do this so much in hope of winning,
As to give the enemy cause for grief, and to perish themselves,
Who lacked confidence in numbers, and were wanting in arms.
Before woven cloth, garments were made of knotted fiber.
Woven cloth came after iron, because looms are made with iron.
Nor can such delicate things be produced by any other means —
The heddles, spindles, shuttles, and the sounding combs.
And nature compelled men to work wool before women,
For the male sex excels far more in skill,
And the whole male kind is far more inventive,
Until the stern farmers, making a point of reproach,
Were willing to yield that work to women's hands,
And themselves equally to endure hard labor,
And in hard work hardened their limbs and hands.
But the model for sowing, and the origin of grafting,
Was nature herself, the first creator of things.
For berries and acorns, falling from the trees,
Would give rise in due season to swarms of seedlings beneath,
From which also it became natural to graft shoots onto branches,
And to plant new slips throughout the fields.
Then they tried one and then another method of tending the sweet plot,
And saw that the wild fruits could be tamed by the earth
Through patient care and gentle cultivation.
And day by day they forced the forests to retreat up the mountain,
And yield the ground below to cultivation.
So that they might have meadows, lakes, streams, crops, and joyful vineyards
On the hills and plains, and groves of olive trees

The blue expanse, distinguishing regions, could run
Across hills and valleys and spreading plains,
Just as you see everything now varied with charm,
Adorned with sweet fruits set among the fields,
And held about with thriving planted groves.
But to imitate with the mouth the liquid songs of birds
Came long before men could celebrate
Smooth verses in song and delight the ear.
And the whistling of Zephyr through the hollow reeds
First taught rustic folk to blow into hollow hemlock stalks.
Then little by little they learned the tender complaints
That the flute pours forth, pressed by the fingers of players,
Found through pathless groves and forests and glades,
Through the lonely haunts of shepherds and their divine leisure.
Thus time draws out each thing gradually
Into the open, and reason brings it to the shores of light.
These things would soothe their minds and give them pleasure
When they had eaten their fill, for then all things are welcome.
Often therefore, lying together on the soft grass
Beside a stream of water, under the branches of a tall tree,
With no great wealth they refreshed their bodies pleasantly.
Especially when the weather smiled and the seasons of the year
Painted the green grass with flowers.
Then jokes, then talk, then sweet laughter
Were their custom, for the rustic muse was vigorous then.
Then joyful wantonness urged them to wreathe their heads
And shoulders with garlands woven of flowers and leaves.
And moving their limbs out of time and step,
Striking the earth hard with heavy foot,
From this arose laughter and sweet merriment.

All these things were then newer and more wonderful,
And for the wakeful there came the comfort of sleep
To draw out voices in many ways, and bend them into song,
And run across the reeds with a single lip.
Hence even now those who keep watch guard these discoveries,
And the race has learned to maintain the measure, yet gains
No greater sweet pleasure from it thereby
Than the wild race of earth-born men once gained.
For what is present and at hand (unless we have known
Something sweeter before) pleases most and seems best,
But then some later discovery, found to be better,
Destroys our taste for the old and changes our feelings about everything.
So began the hatred of the acorn, so that bed
Of strewn leaves was abandoned and heaped with grasses and boughs.
Likewise the wearing of beast-skin fell into contempt —
A discovery I suspect arose from such jealousy
That he who first wore it was slain by ambush and died.
And yet it was torn apart among them with much bloodshed
And could not be turned to any use.
Then it was skins, now gold and purple
That torment human life with cares and weary it with war.
In this, I think, the fault lies more with us.
For cold used to torture the earth-born men, naked without skins,
But it does us no harm to go without a purple robe
Adorned with gold and great emblems,
So long as we have a plain one that can protect us.
So the race of men labors always in vain and to no purpose,
And wastes its life in empty cares,
Because it has not learned what the limit of having is,
And how far true pleasure can genuinely grow.

Gradually it advanced life to greater heights,
And stirred the great storms of war from their depths.
But the watchmen of the great and turning vault of the world,
The sun and moon, circling and illuminating it with their light,
Taught men that the seasons of the years revolve,
And that all things are governed by a sure plan and fixed order.
Already men lived out their days protected by strong towers,
And the land was divided and cultivated in separate portions.
Then the sail-winged sea bloomed with broad ships,
And they had allies and companions bound by treaty,
When poets began to hand down great deeds in verse,
And not long before that were the letters of the alphabet discovered.
Therefore our age cannot look back to see what was done before,
Except where reason shows us traces of the past.
Ships, agriculture, city walls, laws,
Arms, roads, clothing, and all other things of this kind,
Prizes, the pleasures of life too, all of them entirely,
Songs, paintings, and the skillful carving of statues —
All these, practice and the tireless experience of the eager mind
Taught step by step to those who pressed forward gradually.
So time draws forth each thing little by little into the open,
And reason raises it up into the light of day.
For they saw one thing grow clear from another in their minds,
Through the arts, until they reached the highest peak.

TITUS LUCRETIUS CARUS, ON THE NATURE OF THINGS
BOOK SIX

Athens of glorious name first gave to mortal fields
the fruit-bearing crops,
And renewed life, and established laws,
And first gave the sweet consolations of life,
When she brought forth a man of such a heart,
Who once poured forth all things from his truth-telling mouth.
And though he is gone, because of his divine discoveries
His ancient glory, now spread abroad, is carried to the sky.
For when he saw that nearly everything mortals require for sustenance
Was already provided,
And that life could be made secure,
That men of power in wealth, honor, and praise
Could abound, and excel in the good reputation of their children,
And yet that no less did anxious hearts dwell in every home,
And that life was tormented by the mind's ungrateful complaints —
The many things that compel men to serve bitter grievances —
He understood that the vessel itself was causing the flaw,
And that all things were being corrupted within by its defect,
Whatever was brought from outside and whatever benefits came,
Partly because he saw it was leaky and full of holes,
So that it could never be filled by any means,
Partly because whatever it had taken in
He saw it taint, as it were, with a foul taste throughout.

BOOK IV

He therefore cleansed our hearts with truthful words,
And set a limit to desire and fear,
And showed the highest good toward which we all strive,
And pointed out a path along a gentle slope
By which we might travel straight toward that goal,
And what evil pervades the lives of mortals everywhere,
What flows from nature to each person, and comes about
Either by chance or force, as nature arranged it,
And through what gates one may meet each of these things,
And he showed that the human race struggles in vain
Rolling the sad waves of care within their hearts.
For just as children tremble and fear all things
In blind darkness, so we in the light sometimes fear
Things no more worthy of fear than what children dread
And imagine in the dark as future threats.
Therefore this terror of the mind, and this darkness,
Must be dispelled not by the rays of the sun nor the bright shafts of day,
But by the face of nature and her reason,
Which moves me further to weave out my poem in words.
And since I have shown that the mortal quarters of the world
Exist, and that the sky is formed of native matter,
And that whatever happens in it must happen,
Learn now what remains: understand further
That since once the hope of our vows urges us
To mount the glorious chariot, and again
What once stood against us turns to willing favor,
The other things that mortals watch come to pass
On earth and in the sky, when they hang in fearful minds,
Make their souls humble with dread of the gods,
And press them down to the ground, because ignorance

Ignorance of causes compels men to assign
Power to the gods, and to yield them dominion.
The causes of these works they can in no way see by reason,
And so they think all things come to pass by divine will.
For those who have truly learned that the gods lead a carefree life,
If yet they marvel in the meantime at what reason explains
How all things can come to pass, especially in those matters
Which are seen above their heads in the ethereal regions,
Are carried back again to the old religions,
And take on harsh masters, whom in their misery they believe
To have power over all things, not knowing what can be,
What cannot be, and by what law each thing has its
Fixed limit, and its deeply set boundary —
And so, all the more, they are swept along in total error.
Unless you cast these notions from your mind, and put far away
The thoughts unworthy of the gods, and alien to their peace,
The holy divine powers of the gods, touched gently by you,
Will often be present — for the supreme power of the gods cannot
Be violated, so as to drink in fury and seek harsh punishments.
But because you yourself in quiet and placid peace will set aside
The great surging waves of anger,
You will approach the shrines of the gods with a calm heart,
And the images which, carried forth from the holy body,
Enter the minds of men as messengers of divine form —
These you will be unable to receive with the tranquil peace of mind.
From this we may see what manner of life must follow,
Which indeed our truest reasoning drives far from us — although
Much has already proceeded from me,
Yet much remains, and must be adorned in polished
Verses, and the account of the heavens and sky must be maintained.

BOOK IV.

Storms and bright lightning bolts must be sung of,
What they do and from what cause they are carried anywhere,
Lest you go mad with fear when the sky is split apart,
Wondering from where the flying fire came, or to which side
It turned from here, how it made its way through enclosed spaces,
And how, once master, it withdrew itself from there —
The causes of these phenomena people cannot perceive by any reasoning,
And so believe they come about by divine power.
Guide me to the shining paths of your highest teaching,
Cunning Muse, as I run my course show me the way,
Calliope, rest of men and divine delight,
So that led by you I may win a crown with distinguished glory.
First, the blue expanses of the sky are shaken by thunder
Because the clouds that fly on high come together
Against one another, driven by competing winds.
For no sound comes from a clear part of the sky;
But wherever clouds mass in a denser formation,
So much the more does a great rumbling roar arise there.
Moreover, clouds cannot be of such dense substance
As stones and timber, nor yet so thin
As mist and drifting smoke.
For then they would either fall, pressed by their brute weight, like stones,
Or, like smoke, be unable to hold together,
And could not contain cold snows and showers of hail.
They also give out sound across the wide surfaces of the world,
As a canvas awning stretched over a great theater
Snaps and crackles as it is tossed between the masts and beams,
At times, torn through, it rages against the wanton winds,
And imitates the brittle rustling sound of paper.
This kind of sound too you may recognize in thunder.

Or when they toss suspended clothing or flying papers
With their blows and beat them wailing through the air.
For it happens too at times that clouds do not so much
Clash head-on against opposing fronts, but rather move
Sideways, brushing past each other's bodies in different directions,
And that dry sound grazes them and carries on for a long while,
Until it has passed out from the narrow regions.
In this same way all things are often seen to shake
With heavy thunder's concussion, and the vast walls
Of the capacious world seem suddenly to burst apart,
When a storm gathered by powerful winds
Has twisted itself into the clouds, and locked within them,
The whirling vortex ever more and more on every side
Compels the cloud to hollow out with dense body all around.
Then when its force and keen impetus have stirred things up,
It bursts forth with a crashing sound from its release.
No wonder, since a small bladder full of air
Often likewise gives a sharp report when suddenly burst.
There is also this explanation: when winds blow through clouds,
They produce sounds, for we see clouds that are branching
And rough, carried along in many ways;
Just as when the blasts of the northwest wind blow through
A dense forest, the leaves give sound and the branches crash.
It also happens that sometimes the force of powerful winds
Tears through a cloud, breaking it apart with a straight thrust —
For what a blast can do there, plain facts make clear.
Here on earth it is milder, yet even so it uproots
Tall trees, wrenching them from the lowest roots.
There are also waves moving through clouds, which give out
A kind of deep rumbling as they break, as likewise happens on the high

With rivers, and the great sea, when it is shattered by the heat.
It also happens when the fierce force of lightning
Strikes from cloud to cloud, and if that cloud
Has absorbed much moisture, it immediately destroys the fire
With a great roar — just as glowing iron from the hot furnace
Hisses when we plunge it quickly into cold water.
But if a drier cloud receives the fire,
It is instantly set ablaze and burns with a tremendous sound —
As when flame roams through the laurel-haired mountains,
Driven by a whirlwind of winds with great force.
And nothing burns more than the Delphic laurel of Phoebus,
Crackling and consumed by the roaring flame.
Also, often the great cracking of ice and the crashing
Of hail gives a thunderous sound high in the mighty clouds.
For when the wind compresses them, the dense mountains
Of storm-clouds break apart, mingled with hail.
Lightning also flashes when clouds contain many seeds of fire
That are struck together by collision — as when a stone
Strikes a stone, or iron: for then a spark of light
Leaps out, and fire scatters bright sparks.
But thunder reaches our ears after the fact,
While our eyes see the lightning first, because it always
Travels to the ears more slowly than what moves our sight.
You can recognize this also from the following:
If you see someone far off cutting a tree
With a double-edged axe, you see the blow
Before the sound of the strike reaches your ears —
So too we see the lightning before we hear
The thunder, which is sent forth from the same fire,
Born from the same collision and the same cause.
In this way too, swift light tinges places with its gleam.

Clouds, and the storm flashes with trembling force.
When the wind has invaded a cloud, and turning about within
Has caused it, as I explained before, to thicken,
It grows hot by its own movement, so that everything
Heated throughout you see catching fire; but a leaden ball
Even as it rolls through a long course will melt.
So this burning wind, when it has split through the dark cloud,
Scatters, as if forced out suddenly by its own heat,
The seeds which produce the flashing flames of lightning.
Then sound follows, which reaches our ears more slowly
Than the light which arrives at the threshold of our eyes.
Of course this happens with dense clouds, and at the same time
With others piled high one upon another with wondrous force.
Let it not deceive you that we see them from below,
How much broader they are than tall, stretching as they extend.
Observe, for when carried by winds level with mountains,
The clouds will be borne crosswise through the air,
Or when you will see them heaped above great mountains,
Pressing upon others from above, with the winds
Buried on all sides and held in place.
Then you will be able to recognize their great masses,
And to see caves built as if with overhanging rocks,
Which winds, arising with the storm, have filled;
Enclosed, they rage with great murmuring within the clouds,
Threatening after the manner of wild beasts in their dens,
Now here, now there sending their rumblings through the clouds,
And seeking a way out they swirl about, and the seeds of fire
They roll together from the clouds, and so they force
Many things, and whirl the flame within the hollow furnaces,
Until, bursting through, they have flashed forth gleaming from the cloud.

This is also how it happens that the golden heat of liquid fire, swift in its cause, flies down to earth. The seeds of fire must be very numerous in the clouds themselves; for when they are entirely without moisture, the sky is flaming and bright all around. Indeed, they must absorb much from the light of the sun, so that they justly glow red and pour forth fires. When the wind drives these together into one place and compresses them, forcing them tight, they pour out the seeds that make the colors of flame flash. Lightning also flashes when the clouds of the sky thin out as well. For when the wind gently separates them as they move and dissolves them, those seeds which produce the flash must fall apart without terrible thunder or sound, and the lightning shines without any tumult. As for the rest, the nature of thunderbolts is shown by their blows, and by the signs mixed with vapor, and by the heavy reek of burning sulfur — these are signs of fire, not of wind or rain. Moreover, they set fire by themselves to the rooftops of houses, and with swift flame they dominate within homes themselves. This fire, above all things, nature has fashioned from tiny, swift-moving particles, which nothing at all can resist. The powerful thunderbolt passes through the walls of houses, just as the sound of a voice passes through rocks and through the air, and in an instant it liquefies bronze and gold. It also causes wine to flee suddenly from intact vessels, because it easily loosens everything around and thins out all the sides of the vessel.

The heat arriving, as it seeps into the wine itself,
Loosening it nimbly, disperses the first elements of the wine.
The heat of the sun seems unable to accomplish
What this heat does, blazing with its glowing fire,
So much more mobile and dominant is this force.
Now I will explain how thunderbolts are born, and with such force
That they can shatter towers with their strike,
Overturn houses, tear away beams and timbers,
Demolish the monuments of men, and stir up ruin,
Strike men dead, and lay cattle low everywhere.
All these things, and whatever else this force can do,
I will explain; nor will I delay you longer with promises.
Lightning is thought to be born from thick and towering
Clouds drawn up; for none comes from a clear sky,
Nor are they ever sent from thin and scattered clouds.
That this happens is proven beyond any doubt by plain evidence,
Because at such times clouds thicken throughout the air
On all sides, as if all darkness had quit the underworld
And filled the vast caverns of the sky.
So utterly does the dreadful night of storm clouds rise up
And hang its face of black dread from above,
When the tempest begins to forge its thunderbolts.
Moreover a black cloud often sweeps over the sea,
Falling into the waves like a river of pitch
Poured down from heaven, and it moves far off through the dark, drawing behind it
A storm heavy with thunderbolts and gales,
Itself filled above all with fires and winds,
So that even on land people shudder and seek shelter.
Thus we must understand that above our heads
The storm stands at its height; nor in so great a darkness

They would overwhelm the lands, were it not that many clouds, built up on high, are spread above them, blocking the sun from much of the sky. Nor could the rains coming down oppress us so greatly, nor rivers overflow and flood the fields, were the upper air not drawn off high above the clouds. Thus all things are filled with winds and fires, and so everywhere there are rumblings and lightning-flashes. For, as I showed above, the hollow clouds contain very many seeds of heat, and must absorb many more from the rays of the sun and their warmth. When the wind drives these clouds together into one strong place, and squeezes out many seeds of vapor, mixing itself at the same time with that fire, a whirlpool insinuates itself there and spins in the heights, and within it the heat sharpens the thunderbolt in its fiery furnace. For the fire is kindled in two ways: it grows hot by its own swift motion, and by contact with the fire. Then, when the force of the wind has fully heated, or the violent thrust of fire has moved in, the thunderbolt, now fully ripe as it were, suddenly splits the cloud, and the blazing heat, shot forth, illuminates all places with its flashing lights. Then a heavy crash follows, so sudden and loud that the vaults of heaven above seem to be shattered and crush down upon us. Then a tremor shakes the earth violently, and deep rumblings run through the sky; for by then nearly the whole storm shakes with the concussion and quivers with its roaring. From this shaking there follows a heavy and abundant rain, so that all the sky seems to be turning into rain and rushing headlong back to a deluge — such is the storm of wind and the splitting of the clouds.

A sound is sent forth as it flies with burning stroke.
It also happens when a force of wind, driven from outside,
Falls into a dense cloud with a ripened thunderbolt,
And when it splits it, immediately that fiery
Whirlwind falls down, which we call by its native name, the thunderbolt.
The same thing happens in other directions, wherever the force carries it.
It also happens that sometimes a force of wind sent without fire
Yet kindles into flame in its passage through the long path,
While traveling, shedding certain large bodies in its course
That cannot equally penetrate through the air,
And gathering other small particles from the air itself,
Which, being mixed together in flight, produce fire.
Not very differently, just as a leaden ball
Often grows hot in its course, when, shedding many bodies of cold,
It has caught fire in the air.
It also happens that the force of the blow itself excites fire,
When a force of wind sent without fire has struck,
Because, since it strikes with a violent blow,
The elements of heat can flow together from the blow itself,
And likewise from the object that received the blow at that moment,
Just as when we strike a stone with iron, fire flies out.
Nor because the force of iron is cold does it follow that
The seeds of glowing heat come together any less at the stroke.
So likewise a thing must be set on fire by lightning,
If it happened to be suitable and fit for flames.
Nor can the cold force of the wind be reckless or entirely mild,
Sent down from above with such great force,
Without first, if it is not kindled by fire in its course,
Yet arriving warmed and mixed with heat,
And thus the speed of the thunderbolt is produced, and its heavy blow.

And so lightning bolts travel with nearly swift passage,
Gathering into themselves from the clouds all their force first aroused,
And taking up great momentum for their going.
Then when the cloud could not contain the increase of their force,
The energy is squeezed out, and so it flies with wondrous speed,
As projectiles fly when hurled from powerful engines of war.
Add that it is made of small and smooth elements,
And nothing can easily resist such a nature,
For it slips between and penetrates through all hidden passages.
It does not therefore pause, delayed by many obstacles,
But glides on swiftly, flying with rapid force.
Moreover, since all weights in nature by their very nature
Tend downward, and when a blow is added to that motion,
The speed is doubled, and that force grows heavier,
So that whatever stands in the way it strikes more violently and swiftly,
Scattering obstacles with its blows, following its path.
Furthermore, since it comes with long-building force, it must keep gaining
Momentum, ever increasing as it travels on,
Which strengthens its mighty power and reinforces the blow.
For it causes all the seeds that compose it
To be carried as if from a region into one point,
Directing everything into that one rushing course,
And perhaps as it comes it draws from the very air certain
Bodies that increase its momentum by their impacts.
It passes through things unharmed and travels through them whole,
Through many liquid passages, because fire cuts its way through,
And it shatters many things, when the very body of the lightning
Falls upon the fabric of matter wherever things are held together.
Furthermore, it easily dissolves bronze, and melts gold in an instant,
Yet leaves vessels intact, because being made of minute particles

For there is a force in small and smooth elements,

More often in autumn, when the stars shine high,
the house of heaven is shaken on all sides, and all the earth,
and again when the flowering seasons of spring spread open.
For in cold, fires are lacking, and in heat, winds
fail, and clouds are not of so dense a substance.
So when the seasons of heaven stand between both extremes,
then all the varied causes of lightning come together.
For the year itself mingles cold and heat.
Both of these are needed for us to forge lightning bolts,
so that there may be discord among things, and with great tumult
the air, driven mad by fires and winds, may surge.
The first part of heat and the last part of cold
is the season of spring: so it must be that things unlike
each other struggle together and, mixed, are thrown into turmoil,
and extreme heat mixed with early cold
is rolled together when the season called autumn passes,
here too fierce winters clash with summer's heat.
Therefore these are rightly called the wars of the year.
No wonder that in such a time lightning bolts are most frequent,
and stormy weather is stirred in the turbulent sky,
since battle rages on both sides at once,
with flames from one direction, winds and mingled moisture from the other.
This is how to understand the true nature of fire-bearing lightning
and to see by what force it does its work,
rather than vainly unrolling Etruscan prophecies
to seek out the hidden judgments of the gods' minds,
from where the flying fire has come, or to which side it

How it has turned in that direction, by what means it has threaded through enclosed spaces and from there has raised itself to dominance, and what harm the lightning's stroke from the sky can cause. But if Jupiter and the other shining gods shake the heavenly temples with terrifying sound, and hurl their fires wherever each one pleases, why do they not cause those who harbor some foul and abominable wickedness to be struck and blaze with the flame of lightning, pierced through the chest — a sharp lesson for mortals? Why instead does a man with no guilty conscience of any base deed roll unharmed in the flames, and is suddenly caught up and swept away by the heavenly whirlwind and fire? Why do they aim at lonely places and labor in vain? Are they then exercising their arms and strengthening their muscles? Why do they allow the Father's weapon to be blunted against the earth? Why does he permit it, and not spare it against enemies? And why does Jupiter never hurl his bolt from a clear sky down to earth on all sides, sending out his thunders? Does he descend as soon as clouds have gathered, as if to determine the strike of his weapon up close from there? And for what reason does he send it into the sea? What charge has he against the waves, against the liquid mass and the swimming plains? Moreover, if he wishes us to beware the blow of the fierce lightning bolt, why does he hesitate to let us see it coming? If he wishes to strike the unsuspecting with his fire, why does he thunder from that direction, so that we may step aside? Why does he stir up darkness beforehand, and rumblings and roarings? And how can you believe that he hurls it in many directions at once? Or would you dare to contend that this has never happened — that multiple strikes occurred at the same moment?

But it often happens, and must necessarily happen,
that it rains in many regions, and showers fall,
and thus many lightning bolts are produced at one time.
Finally, why does it strike with hostile bolt the sacred shrines of the gods, their glorious seats?
And why does it shatter the gods' own beneficent images, and with violent wound strip honor from their statues?
And why does it mostly strike high places? — for it is on the mountain tops that we most often see the traces of fire.
As for what remains, it is easy to understand from these facts how the waterspouts — which the Greeks named after their nature — descend from above into the sea.
For it happens that sometimes, like a column let down from the sky, it descends into the sea, while the straits around it seethe, stirred up by the fiercely blowing winds, and all the ships that are then caught in that tumult are brought into the greatest danger.
This happens when sometimes the force of the roused wind cannot burst the cloud it has begun to form, but presses it down, so that it is like a column let down from the sky into the sea — gradually, as if something were being pushed by a fist and extended downward by the arms — until it is thrust out into the waves.
When the wind splits it open, it rushes out into the sea and stirs up a wondrous boiling in the waters.
For the whirlwind descends spinning, and draws the cloud down along with it at the same slow pace.
As soon as it thrusts the cloud, heavy with water, down to the surface of the sea, the whirlwind plunges itself suddenly wholly into the water, and stirs up the whole sea with a mighty roar, forcing it to boil.
It also happens that the whirlwind wraps itself in winds from the clouds

A whirlwind, gathering the seeds of cloud from the air,
And as if sent down from the sky imitates a waterspout;
When it descends upon the earth and disperses,
It belches forth the immense force of a storm and squall.
But because this happens rarely, and mountains necessarily
Obstruct it on land, it appears more frequently

Clouds form when many particles flying together
Come suddenly into contact in this space of sky above,
Rougher particles that can be bound together
By small interlockings, held compressed against each other.
These first cause small clouds to form and stand;
Then these catch hold of one another and gather together,

It also happens that mountain peaks close to the sky,
The higher each one is, the more it smokes unceasingly
