This is because when clouds first come together,
Before the eyes can see such thin masses, the winds
Carry them and force them to the mountain summits.
Then at last it comes about that as a greater mass gathers
And condenses tightly, it appears, and seems to rise
From the very peak of the mountain into the sky.
For the facts themselves confirm to our senses that
The high places are exposed to windy conditions
When we climb to lofty mountain heights.
Moreover, that garments hung along the shore
By the sea take up moisture shows that the sea
Lifts many particles from its entire surface —
All of which seems to contribute greatly to the growth of clouds.

It is also possible for vapor to rise from the salt expanse of the sea.
For the sluggish principle is then absent from the moisture.
Moreover, from all rivers, and at the same time we see
Mists rising from the earth itself and its heat,
Which, expelled upward like breath, are carried aloft,
And spread their darkness over the sky, and gradually
Build up the high clouds as they gather together.
For the heat of the star-bearing ether presses from above,
And as if by condensing, a blue mass of clouds arises.
It also happens that bodies come into this assembly from without,
Those bodies that form clouds and flying storm-clouds.
For I have shown that the number from the deep is beyond counting,
And the sum of things infinite, and how swiftly
Bodies fly through space, and how suddenly
They are accustomed to cross unimaginable distances.
It is no wonder, then, if in a short time
Storms and darkness so often cover the great mountains
And the seas and lands, pressing down from above
On all sides, since through all the vents of the ether,
And as it were around the breathing-holes of the great world,
There is passage for elements both in and out.
Come now, let me explain how rain-moisture thickens
In the high clouds, and falls upon the lands as a shower.
First, I will show that the seeds of water
Rise up in great number together with the clouds themselves
From all things, and that both grow together equally—
Both the clouds and the water contained within them—
Just as our body grows together with our blood.
Likewise sweat, and whatever moisture is dense in the limbs,
They also often take up a great deal of sea water.

Moisture, like wool hanging in fleeces,
is carried by the winds above the great sea in clouds.
In like manner, moisture is drawn up from all rivers
into the clouds; when the seeds of water have gathered
in great numbers from many sources and increased from every side,
the packed clouds strive to release it by the force of the wind
in two ways: for the force of the wind compresses them, and the very
abundance of storm-clouds, massed in greater throng,
presses and weighs from above, and causes rain to flow out.
Moreover, when clouds are thinned out by winds,
or dissolved by the heat of the sun striking upon them,
they shed their moisture drop by drop, as wax placed
over hot flame melts away abundantly.
But a violent rainstorm occurs when clouds are
pressed hard on both sides by their accumulated mass and the force of the wind.
Rains are accustomed to linger long and remain for a great while
wherever the seeds of water were many,
and cloud after cloud, dripping with storm-showers,
are carried along one above another from every direction,
and the whole earth exhales moisture like smoke.
When here the sun has shone with its rays amid the dark of storms,
striking against the spray of rain-clouds,
then the color of the rainbow appears in the dark clouds.
All other things that grow upward and are created above,
and all that condense together in the clouds —
such as snow, winds, hail, and icy frosts,
the great force of ice, the great hardening of water,
and the check that slows rivers everywhere as they flow —
it is quite easy to discover all these things and to perceive in one's mind

when one has understood well...

When you have come to understand well what the elements are and what they produce,

Understand first that you should consider the earth to be hollow beneath,
just as described above, filled everywhere with winds,
bearing in its bosom many lakes and pools,
cliffs and shattered rocks,
and many rivers flowing hidden beneath the earth's back,
rolling their surging waves, with submerged rocks — so we must believe.

With these things, then, connected and established below,

when time undermines vast caverns underground.
Indeed whole mountains fall, and suddenly from the great shock
tremors spread wide and tear them apart;
and rightly so, since buildings along the road tremble
when shaken by wagons of no great weight.
No less do they leap when iron-rimmed wheels
send the shock of the horsemen's chariots rattling on either side.
It also happens that when a vast and massive clod of earth
rolls from age into great and wide pools,
the water is tossed and surges, and the ground wavers too,
just as a vessel cannot stand still
unless the liquid inside has ceased to be shaken about in its uncertain motion.
Moreover, when wind, gathering through the hollow places beneath the earth,
throws itself from one side and presses hard,
straining with great force against the high caverns,
the earth leans in the direction toward which the force of wind presses it downward.
Then all the structures built above the ground —
and the higher each one is raised toward the sky —
lean and threaten to topple, tilted in that same direction.

And beams dragged along impede the passage of those ready to go.
They fear to believe that the nature of the great world
Will retain some destructive time and catastrophe,

Unless the winds breathe freely, nothing can restrain

Now because they breathe in turns, and grow heavy,
And, as if gathered, return and yield when repelled,
More often the earth threatens ruin from this cause

For this reason all rooftops waver,
The highest more than the middle, the middle more than the lowest, and the lowest most of all.
This too is the same great cause of trembling,
When wind and a sudden great force of air,
Arising either from outside or from the earth itself,
Hurls itself into hollow places in the ground, and there
Among vast caverns with a roaring tumult,
Is carried round and round, and then when the force is roused
Is driven out and at the same time splits the deep
Earth asunder and causes a great chasm.
This happened in Syrian Sidon, and it was so at Aegae
In the Peloponnese, where this outburst of air
Threw things into turmoil, and an earthquake arose.
And many walls besides have fallen in great
Upheavals of the earth, and many cities have sunk
To the bottom of the sea together with their citizens.
But if the force does not burst out, still the very impulse of the air
And the fierce violence of wind is distributed
Through the many pores of the earth, spreading horror and shaking it from within.

When cold penetrates deep into our limbs,
It shakes us unwilling, forcing us to tremble and stir.
So people tremble with twofold terror throughout the cities,
Fearing the rooftops above, dreading the caverns below the earth,
Lest nature suddenly dissolve the lands,
And, torn apart, spread wide its gaping chasm,
And in its confusion wish to fill it with its own ruins.
Yet though men may maintain that heaven and earth
Are destined to remain uncorrupted for eternal safety,
Still sometimes the immediate force of danger itself
Plants this spur of fear in some part of the mind:
That the ground, swiftly pulled from beneath their feet, may be swept
Into the abyss, and the sum of all things, betrayed, may follow
Down to the depths, and the world become a confused ruin.
Now we must explain why the sea does not grow larger.
First, men wonder that nature does not make the sea greater,
Given the great rushing flow of waters,
And all the rivers that come from every direction.
Add to this the wandering rains and powerful storms
That scatter over all seas and lands and drench them;
Add the springs themselves. Yet all these together, measured against the sea's fullness,
Will scarcely amount to the equivalent of a single drop of increase.
It is therefore less surprising that the great sea does not grow.
Besides, the sun draws off a great portion with its heat;
For we see that the sun dries out moisture-soaked garments
With its burning rays.
And we see the seas are vast and spread out wide.
Therefore, though the sun may draw but a small measure of moisture
From the sea's surface at any one spot,
Yet over so great an expanse it will carry away much from the waves.

Furthermore, the winds can also carry off a great part
of moisture, sweeping across the surfaces of the sea,
since we often see in the course of a single night the roads
dry out and soft muddy crusts harden.
Moreover, I have shown that clouds also carry off much
moisture gathered from the vast expanse of the sea,
and scatter it everywhere across the whole world,
when it rains on the lands and winds carry the clouds along.
Finally, since the earth has a porous body and lies
joined all around bordering the shores of the sea on every side,
just as moisture from the lands flows into the sea,
so it must seep back into the lands from the salt sea.
For the brine is filtered through, and the moisture
trickles back, and all streams gather at their source,
and from there return over the lands in a sweet current,
along the channel that once guided the flow with liquid foot.
Now I will explain what causes fires to breathe forth
at times with such great force through the throat of Mount Etna,
for it was no small storm of flame that, ruling over the Sicilian fields,
turned toward itself the faces of neighboring peoples,
as they watched the vaults of heaven glittering with smoke
and filled their fearful hearts with dread,
wondering what new thing nature was bringing about.
In these matters you must look widely and deeply,
and survey all directions from afar,
so that you may recall how profound is the sum of things,
and see how the sky is but one small part of the whole universe,
how tiny a fraction it represents among countless parts.
Nor is man but one small quota-part of all the earth.

If you would clearly contemplate what has been well proposed,
And see it plainly, you would cease to marvel at many things.
For who among us is surprised when someone's limbs
Have caught a fever kindled by burning heat?
Or when any other pain of disease spreads through the body?
For a foot suddenly swells, sharp pain
Often seizes the teeth, and invades the very eyes.
The sacred fire breaks out and, like a serpent, burns through the body,
Creeping over whatever part it has seized, spreading through the limbs —
Because, of course, there are seeds of many things,
And this earth and sky bring us enough of evil,
From which the force of enormous disease can grow.
So it must be thought that for all the sky and earth
Everything is supplied in sufficient quantity from the infinite,
From which the shaken earth can suddenly move,
And a swift whirlwind race across seas and lands,
And Etnaean fire overflow, and the sky blaze with flame —
For this too happens, and the celestial vaults catch fire —
And storms of rain come with heavier onset
When the seeds of waters have chanced to gather so.
But the turbulent force of the conflagration is immense,
As is the river that appears greatest to one
Who has never seen a larger, and the huge
Tree, and mankind, and all things of every kind —
Whatever each person has seen that seemed largest, they imagine as vast.
Yet all things together, with sky and earth and sea,
Are nothing compared to the sum total of the universe entire.
Now I will explain by what means, suddenly stirred,
The flame bursts forth from Etna's vast furnaces.
First, the hollow beneath the whole mountain

The Nile rises in summer and overflows the fields.

The Nile is the one river of all Egypt's land,
It waters Egypt's heart through scorching heat again and again.
Or because in summer the north winds blow against its mouth,

For without doubt these blasts are carried upstream,

That river comes from the region of the hot south wind,

When they have gathered toward the middle region of the day,

Perhaps the river swells from deep among the high mountains of Ethiopia,

Now come, let me explain to you what Avernian places and lakes there are,
And of what nature they consist.
First, the name Avernus is given from the thing itself,
Imposed because they are hostile to all birds,
In that when flying creatures come to those regions,

Forgetful of their oars, they let the sails hang slack,

All these things are governed by natural causes,

Lest it be thought that the gate of Hades is situated there,

How far removed this is from true reason, take heed,
For I now attempt to speak of the matter itself.
First, I say this, as I have often said before:
In the earth there exist particles of every kind —
Many that are life-sustaining as food, and many that can bring disease
And accelerate death.

And we have shown before that different things are more suited
to different living creatures for the purpose of life,
because of their unlike nature and unlike
textures among themselves, and their primary shapes.
Much that is hostile passes through the ears, and much
creeps in through the nostrils, troublesome and harsh to the touch.
Nor are many things to be avoided as unpleasant to the touch, or to be
shunned as unpleasant to the sight, or bitter in taste.
Next one may observe how many things are
intensely offensive to the senses of man, foul and repulsive.
Certain trees cast a heavy shade,
so much so that they often cause headaches
if anyone has lain stretched out beneath them in the grass.
There is also on the great mountains of Helicon a tree
accustomed to kill a man with the foul odor of its flower.
All these things grow from the earth because the earth
contains seeds of many things in many ways,
since it holds them mixed together and distributes them separately.
And when a lamp newly extinguished at night offends
the nostrils with its sharp fumes, it brings sleep on the spot —
sleep such as brings down one whom disease is wont to lay low,
and the woman overcome falls back with her limbs relaxed,
and from her tender hands the bright work slips away,
if at the time she has smelled it when her monthly flow is due.
And many things besides loosen the languid limbs throughout the body
and shake the soul from its seat within.
Likewise, if when you refresh yourself in a hot bath
you linger too long, how easily does it happen that you faint?
And the heavy force and odor of charcoal creeps in...

How easily it reaches the brain, unless we have first taken water.
But when the scorching heat has seized and mastered the limbs,
then the smell of wine strikes like a deadly blow.
Do you not also see that the earth itself generates sulphur

And then, when men follow the veins of silver and gold,

What harm do they cause, what do the golden metals exhale?
What faces do they give back to men, what complexions?
Do you not see and hear how quickly they perish,

All these exhalations the earth steams forth as heat,
and breathes them out into the open air and the clear sky.
So too the Avernian places must send forth to birds
a death-bearing force that rises from the earth into the air,
poisoning a certain region of the sky.
As soon as a bird glides in on its wings,
it is seized and stopped by the invisible poison,
and falls in that region where the heat directs it.
When it has fallen there, that same force of heat
strips away the remnants of life from all its limbs.
For first it stirs up in them a kind of heat,
and afterward, when they have fallen into the very sources of the poison,
there too must life be vomited forth,
because so great a supply of evil gathers around.
It also happens sometimes that this force and the heat of Avernus
disperses the air that lies between the birds and the earth,
so that the space here is left nearly empty.

When birds flying there come from a place in line with it,
Their useless wing-strokes at once falter and fail,
And all the effort of both wings is spent in vain;
There, where they cannot maintain themselves upon their wings,
Nature compels them to sink down to the earth by their own weight,
And, lying nearly helpless through the void nearby,
They scatter their life-breath through all the pores of the body.
Moreover, water in wells becomes cooler in summer,
Because the earth grows dry with heat, and whatever seeds
Of vapor it may have, it quickly releases into the air.
The more the earth is exhausted and burned out by heat,
So too the moisture hidden within the earth grows colder,
When all the earth is compressed and squeezed by cold and contracts,
And as it were congeals — in doing so, of course,
It squeezes out into the wells whatever warmth it holds.
Near the shrine of Hammon there is said to be a spring
Cold in the light of day, but warm in the hours of night.
People marvel greatly at this spring, and suppose
That it boils up beneath the earth, stirred by the fierce sun,
When night covers the lands with its terrible darkness —
Which is far removed from true reason.
Surely, when the sun touches with its warmth the watery body of the spring,
It does not manage to give back heat to the upper part,
Though the light above enjoys such blazing heat —
How then could it, under so dense a body of earth,
Cook through the moisture and join it to warm vapor?
Especially when it can scarcely send its burning heat
Through the walls of houses.
What then is the reason? Surely the earth around the spring
Is more porous and open than the rest of the ground.

LIB. IV.

Many seeds of fire are present near the body of water.
Hence when night covers the earth with dew-bearing shadows,
The earth beneath quickly grows cold, and so forth.
For this reason it happens that, as if compressed by a hand,
It squeezes out into a spring whatever seeds of fire it holds,
Which make the touch of the liquid warm with their vapor.
Then when the sun at its rising has stirred the earth with its rays,
And rarefies it with warming vapor mingling,
The first-beginnings return again to their ancient seats,
And all the heat of water retreats back into the earth,
And for this reason a spring is cold in the light of day.
Besides, the moisture of water is tossed by the sun's rays,
And in the light it thins away under the trembling heat,
And so it happens that whatever seeds of fire the water holds,
It releases, when it often changes the cold that it contains within itself,
And dissolves the ice and relaxes its veins.
There is also a cold spring, above which tow placed
Often catches flame immediately from the fire conceived there.
And torches lit in the same way glow through the waves
Wherever they are driven, floating on the winds,
Because, of course, there are very many seeds of vapor in the water,
And it is necessary that the very bodies of fire rise up
From the earth throughout the whole of the spring,
And at the same time breathe out and pass away into the air,
Yet not so abundantly that the spring could become hot.
Moreover, a force drives them scattered outward to burst forth
Suddenly through the water, and to gather them upward,
Just as from the sea there breathes a spring of fresh water,
Which bubbles up and pushes the salt waves aside from itself.
And to many other regions the sea provides

...a timely benefit for thirsty sailors,
because it vomits fresh water among the salt waves.
Thus through it the springs can burst forth,
and scatter those seeds outward into tow, which when
they meet, or when they cling to the body of a torch,
they catch fire easily at once, because the tow and torch
hold within themselves many seeds of fire.
Do you not also see that linen, recently
extinguished near a nocturnal lamp, catches fire
before it touches the flame? And similarly a torch
ignites at a distance, having first been touched by vapor alone,
before the fire can reach it closely.
So too must we think this happens with that spring.
Next I shall begin to treat the question: by what law
does this stone of nature draw iron to itself —
the stone which the Greeks call magnet by its native name,
because it has its origin in the native land of the Magnetes.
Men marvel at this stone, for it often makes a chain
of rings hanging from it one after another;
sometimes you may see five or more in a row
swaying gently, suspended in the air,
one hanging from another beneath it,
each feeling the binding force of the stone above it —
so persistently does its power prevail throughout.
In such matters much must be established first
before we can give an account of the thing itself;
we must approach by a very long and winding road,
and so I call back your attentive ears and mind.
First, from all things that we see around us
it is necessary that a flow streams off and is emitted and scattered continuously...

BOOK IV.

Bodies that strike the eyes and assail our sight
Flow perpetually from things as odors.
As cold flows from rivers, heat from the sun, spray from the waves
Of the sea that gnaws the shores along the coasts,
And varied sounds do not cease to flow through the air,
And often a salty moisture comes to the mouth with flavor,
When we walk near the sea, and when we watch
Wormwood being mixed and diluted, bitterness touches us.
So thoroughly do all things flow from everything,
Carried and dispersed in all directions everywhere,
With no pause, no rest ever granted to the flowing,
Since we perpetually sense, and can always
See, smell, and hear sound.
Now I will repeat that all things are of rare-bodied substance,
A point that is made clear in the first book of my poem.
For indeed, though this pertains to many things to understand,
It pertains above all to the very subject
Which I now set out to discuss and establish:
That nothing exists in our experience but body mixed with void.
First, it happens that rocks in caves overhead
Sweat with moisture, and drip with trickling drops.
Likewise sweat flows from our entire body,
The beard grows, and hair spreads through all our limbs and joints,
Food is distributed into all our veins, it nourishes and feeds
Even the outermost parts of the body, and the fingernails.
We feel cold pass through bronze, and warm vapor
Pass through gold, we likewise feel it pass through silver
When we hold full cups in our hands.
Finally, through the stone partitions of houses voices
Fly through, odor seeps, cold, and vapor too.

Fire, which has also been accustomed to penetrate the strength of iron.
And then, whatever armor surrounds the body,
When you have shaken off the diseased vapors along with it, they seep in.
And the storm of earth and the whirlwind of sky
Fears the heavens, the earth, and cracks all around,
Since nothing exists but what is bound together by a rare body.
Add to this that not all bodies thrown
From things are endowed with the same sense,
Nor are they suited in the same way to all things.
First, the sun bakes the earth and makes it dry,
But it dissolves ice and on the high mountains
Forces the heaped-up snows to melt away under its rays.
Then wax melts when placed under its heat.
Fire likewise makes bronze liquid and melts gold,
But it shrinks hides and flesh and draws them together.
Water, on the other hand, hardens iron when taken from fire,
But softens hides and flesh made hard by heat.
The wild olive tree gives such pleasure to the bearded she-goats,
As though it flowed with ambrosia and was touched with nectar,
Than which nothing more bitter could sprout for man.
Again, the pig avoids marjoram and fears every
Ointment, for to bristled swine it is a sharp poison,
Which to us at times seems to refresh and revive.
But though mud is for us the foulest filth,
This same filth appears pleasant to swine,
So that they roll in it insatiably with their whole bodies.
There remains also this, which I proceed
To address, which seems it must first be said:
Since many pores are assigned to various things,
They must be endowed with a nature unlike one another.

LIB. VI.

That each thing has its own nature and its own pathways.
For indeed various senses are present in living creatures,
And each one perceives its own proper object within itself.
For we observe that sound penetrates one way, and flavor
From liquids another way, and the smells of smoke another,
Since the nature of the channels compels this to happen,
Varying in many ways, as we showed a little earlier,
On account of the unlike nature and texture of things.
Furthermore, one thing is seen to seep through stones,
Another through wood, another to pass through gold,
Another to make its way out through silver, another through glass.
For in one direction a flow of images is seen, in another heat travels,
And the same channels transmit one thing more quickly to some, another to others.
Since the nature of the channels compels this to happen,
Varying in many ways, as we showed a little earlier.
Therefore, when these things have been well established and set in place,
And all has been laid out and prepared for us,
What remains will easily be explained from this, and every
Cause that draws out the force of iron will be made clear.
First, it is necessary that very many seeds flow from that stone,
Or a current, which strikes the air between
The stone and the iron, wherever it is placed.
When this space is emptied out, and a great void opens
In the middle, straightway the first elements of iron
Fall forward together into the vacuum, so that the ring itself
Follows and moves with its whole body,
And nothing is more tightly bound and closely connected
By its primal elements than the cold stiffness of strong iron.
So it is less surprising, as they say, that from the elements
Bodies...

If the many bodies streaming from the iron cannot be carried into the void without the ring itself following along,
which it does, and follows until it reaches the stone itself and clings to it with hidden bonds —
this happens likewise in every direction from which there is empty space,
whether sideways or from above:
the neighboring bodies are continuously borne into the void.
For they are stirred by blows from elsewhere, and cannot of their own accord rise upward into the air.
To this is added another reason why this effect is greater:
this phenomenon is also aided by the motion of the air.
For as soon as the air in front of the ring becomes rarer
and the space more emptied and void,
it immediately follows that all the air situated behind it
pushes and drives it forward from the rear.
For the air surrounding things always strikes them.
But in such a circumstance the iron is propelled
because on one side there is empty space that receives it,
and the air, slipping subtly through the many pores of the iron toward that side,
pushes and drives it as wind drives a ship with its sails.
Furthermore, all things must contain air within their body,
since all things are of loose texture, and air surrounds and is present about all things.
This air, then, hidden deep within the iron,
is always tossed about in restless motion, and thereby
strikes the ring from within without doubt, and agitates it —
and is carried in the same direction into which it has already once rushed,
striving toward the empty space.
It also happens that the nature of iron retreats from this stone,

Sometimes you see them fleeing and pursuing each other in turn,
And I have even seen Samothracian iron rings leap up,
And iron filings rage within bronze bowls
When a lodestone was placed beneath them —
So eagerly do they seem to flee from the stone:
Such great discord is created by the interposed bronze.
The reason is that when the warm current of air
Has first entered and taken possession of the open passages of the iron,
The lodestone's warm current comes afterwards and finds everything full
In the iron, and has no passage through as before.
It is therefore forced to beat and buffet with its flow
Against the iron texture, and so repels it from itself,
And drives through the bronze that which it often resorbs without it.
Do not wonder at this in these matters: that the warm current
From this stone cannot likewise drive other things.
For some things stand firm by their weight — gold, for example —
And others, being of loose texture, are such that the current
Flies through them untouched and cannot drive them at all;
Wood appears to be of this latter kind.
The nature of iron, situated between the two,
When it receives certain particles of bronze, is then
Pushed along by the Magnesian stone with its stream.
Nor are these phenomena so foreign to other things
That I cannot supply many more of the same kind,
Which I can recall one by one in relation to each other.
You see that stones are first bound together by the mortar of lime;
If a wooden framework is joined with sand,
It will crack along flaws in its grain more readily
Than the joints can be loosened by bull-hide straps.
The juices of the vine dare to mingle in the springs of water

Heavy pitch cannot mix with light oil,
nor can the purple color of the murex shell, once joined
with the body of wool, be separated from it,
not if Neptune's waves were set to work on it,
not if the whole sea wished to wash it out with all its waters.
Furthermore, one substance joins gold to silver,
and bronze is not joined to lead as if from white.
Many other such examples can be found — but why go on?
You have no need of such lengthy explanations,
nor is it right that I spend so much labor here.
It is better briefly to comprehend much in a few words:
those things whose textures have so mutually fallen together
that the hollow parts of one fit the full parts of another —
these make the best joint between them.
Some things, moreover, can be held together as if linked
by rings and hooks interlaced with each other;
this seems to happen more with stone and iron.
Now I will explain what causes diseases, and from where
a deadly destructive force can suddenly arise,
a sickening power against the race of men and herds of cattle.
First, I have shown above that there are seeds of many things
that are life-giving to us,
and on the other hand, those that bring disease and death. It must be
that many of these fly about; and when by chance they have gathered
and disturbed the sky, the air becomes diseased.
All this force of disease and pestilence
either comes from outside, like clouds and mists from above,
through the sky, or often rising of itself
from the earth, when, made damp, it has acquired rot,
struck by unseasonable rains and by the sun's heat.

Do you not see that even the novelty of sky and waters
Tries those who travel far from homeland and home
As they arrive? Because things differ so greatly there.
What do we think the sky over Britain differs
From that which is in Egypt, where the world's axis tilts?
And what of that which differs in the Black Sea, and at Gades,
Right up to the dark-skinned generations burned by the sun?
Since we see four skies differing among themselves,
Corresponding to the four winds and four quarters of the heavens,
So too the color and appearance of men are seen to differ greatly,
And diseases hold the generations each in their own way.
There is the elephant disease, which near the rivers of the Nile
Is born in the midst of Egypt, and nowhere else beyond.
In Attica men's steps are afflicted, and in the regions of Achaea
Their eyes; and so in different parts and limbs
A different place is hostile — varied air brings this about.
Therefore when a sky that happens to be foreign to us
Stirs itself, and a hostile air begins to creep,
Gliding little by little like mist and cloud,
Disturbs everything in its path, and works to transform it —
It comes to pass that when it finally reaches our sky,
It corrupts it and makes it like its own, though equally alien.
So this sudden new plague and pestilence
Either falls upon the waters, or settles upon the crops themselves,
Or upon other foods of men and the fodder of cattle,
Or else its force remains suspended in the air itself.
And when we draw in the mingled breezes from it as we breathe,
We must likewise absorb those things into our bodies.
By a similar reasoning, pestilence often comes to cattle too,
And sickness even to the bleating of ailing flocks.

It matters not whether we come to places
Different from our own, and change the sky's cover,
Or whether the sky brings in a corrupted nature
Or something we are not accustomed to use,
Which might assail us with its unfamiliar onset.
This principle once brought deadly pestilence and burning heat
To the fatal fields of Cecrops' land,
Laid waste the roads, and drained the city of its citizens.
For rising deep from within the borders of Egypt,
Traversing vast stretches of air and swimming plains,
It settled at last upon the people of Pandion, and all
Were given over in crowds to death and disease.
First they bore heads burning with fever,
And both eyes suffused with reddened light.
The throat, too, sweated inwardly with dark
Blood, and the passage of the voice was blocked with ulcers,
And the tongue, interpreter of the mind, oozed with gore,
Weakened by sickness, heavy in movement, rough to the touch.
Then, when through the throat the force had filled the chest,
And the diseased power had flowed into the stricken heart,
All the barriers of life began to give way.
The breath rolled out through the mouth a foul stench,
Like the rank smell that rotting corpses give off.
And then all the strength of mind and every part
Of the body languished already on the very threshold of death.
Intolerable anguish was the constant companion
Of unbearable afflictions, mixed with groaning and lament.
Frequent hiccupping, again and again, through night and day,
Kept seizing the sinews, racking and constricting the limbs,
And wore them out, exhausting them before their strength gave out.

BOOK IV.

Nor could you bear to look upon another with too great a burning gaze,
As the uppermost surface of the body burned at its peak,
But rather to offer a lukewarm touch with the hands,
And at the same time all the flesh reddened as if seared by ulcers,
As the body is, when sacred fire spreads through all its limbs.
The innermost parts of men burned truly to the bones.
A flame burned in the stomach, as if in furnaces within.
Nothing placed upon the limbs felt light or gentle.
They turned whatever was useful toward the wind and cold always.
Many headlong into the deep water of wells,
And partly into cold rivers they cast their limbs burning with disease,
Throwing their naked bodies into the waves.
They fell in with open mouths as they came,
An unquenchable thirst submerging their parched bodies,
Making a little moisture equal to a great rain.
There was no relief at all from the suffering; the exhausted bodies lay prostrate,
And medicine muttered in silent fear,
Since those eyes wide open with such frequent burning disease
Rolled about without any sleep.
And many other signs of death were given at that time.
The mind disturbed, grief in sorrow, and fear,
A gloomy brow, a fierce and furious expression,
The ears troubled and full of ringing sounds,
Breathing quick and heavy, or rarely drawn,
A shining moisture dripping with sweat upon the neck,
Thin spittle, scanty, tinged with the color of saffron,
And salty, barely expelled through the throat with a hoarse cough.
In the hands the sinews contracted, and the limbs trembled,
And cold crept up gradually from the feet.
Nor did it fail to come at last to the final hour,

.VI. CXXIIII.

The nostrils were pinched, the tip of the nose sharp,
The eyes sunken, the temples hollow, the skin cold,
And the tight forehead lay hard and stiff about the mouth,
Not long after, rigid, they lay prostrate in death,
By about the eighth day in the bright light of the sun,
Or on the ninth they gave back their life to the lamp.
If any among them (as it happened) had escaped the funeral rites of death
Through the foul entrails and black discharge of the bowels,
Yet afterward wasting and death still awaited him,
Or else with frequent severe pain in the head
The corrupted blood flowed from the filled nostrils,
Thither flowed all the strength of the man and his body.
If the bitter flux of foul blood had gone out,
Yet the disease still passed into the sinews and limbs,
And into the very parts of the body's genitals,
And some, gravely fearing the threshold of death,
Lived on deprived by the blade of their manhood,
And some remained in life without their hands and feet,
And some lost part of their sight—
So fiercely had the sharp dread of death struck them.
And indeed forgetfulness of all things began to seize some,
So that they could not even know themselves.
And while many unburied bodies lay upon the ground,
The race of birds and wild beasts nonetheless
Would spring back from them, so as not to breathe the sharp stench,
Or if they tasted, they would languish near to death.
Nor indeed did any bird appear rashly in those places,
Nor did the bold generations of wild beasts come forth from the forests;
Most were languishing with the plague,
And were dying—above all, the faithful race of dogs.

Book IV (continuing)

Laid prostrate in the streets, the plague left every soul sick.
For a violent disease wrenched the life from the limbs.
Vast, unaccompanied funeral processions hastened away.
No reliable common remedy was available.
For what had given some the breath of life's air,
To breathe freely and behold the vaults of heaven,
Was to others cause of death and brought their end.
And in these circumstances one thing above all was pitiful
And wretched: whoever saw himself
Caught in the disease and condemned to die,
Lay despairing, with a sorrowful heart,
Looking upon his own funeral, and there gave up his soul.
For indeed they never ceased at any time to contract
From one another the contagion of the greedy plague,
And this above all heaped death upon death.
For those who fled their sick (as tends to happen),
Too eager for life and too afraid of death,
Were punished soon after with shameful and wretched death,
Abandoned, without help, slain by neglect,
Like wool-bearing flocks and herds of cattle.
Those who had stayed to tend the sick were infected by contagion,
And the labor which shame then compelled them to perform,
And the soft voices of the weary mingled with cries of lament —
The best would thus undergo this kind of death.
And returning exhausted with tears and grief,
They competed to bury one after another of their people.
From there many took to their beds, overcome by sorrow,
And no one could be found whom neither disease,
Nor death, nor grief would assail in such a time.
Moreover by then every shepherd and herdsman,

And the sturdy plowman, guide of the curved plow,
lay languishing; bodies thrust deep within their hovels
lay given over to poverty and sickness and death.
You could see the lifeless bodies of children lying
upon the lifeless bodies of their parents,
and mothers and fathers breathing their last over their children.
And no small part of this grief flowed from the fields into the city,
as the sick throng that the farmers brought
came together from every stricken region.
They filled every place and building; the summer heat
made death pile them up all the more densely together.
Many bodies, felled by thirst, sprawled along the road and rolled about;
they lay strewn beside the streams and rivers,
their breath cut off by the excessive sweetness of the water.
Throughout the public spaces and roads you could see
limbs with half-dead bodies languishing,
filthy with squalor and covered in rags,
wasting away in bodily corruption, nothing but skin over bones,
already nearly buried in foul decay of the viscera.
Death had filled all the sacred shrines of the gods with lifeless bodies,
and all the temples of the heavenly ones remained
burdened everywhere with corpses,
packed with guests that the temple-keepers had taken in.
No longer did reverence for the gods or their divine power
carry any weight — the present pain overwhelmed everything.
Nor did the old custom of burial remain in the city,
by which this pious people had always been accustomed to inter their dead.
For the whole population was thrown into confusion, and each person,
grief-stricken, buried his own loved one as best he could.
And sudden calamity and dreadful poverty drove many to do things

For they would place their own blood-relations on the pyres of strangers,
Dragged out amid great lamentation,
And would set torches beneath them, often with much bloodshed,
Fighting rather than let the bodies be abandoned.

PETRUS CANDIDUS TO STUDENTS
Greetings.

Lest we be seen as having pledged ourselves too strongly to any one master's word, we have decided to include here at the end, drawn from the varied reading of this poem, certain passages which, just as we do not particularly approve of them, so neither do we reject them outright. You who are listeners of noble writers — to use the words of Flaccus — and avengers of them, weigh each one carefully with the sharp judgment of good sense. Indeed, from the vast forest of material laid before us, we have selected what seemed most important, following, as we stated in the preface, the great authors, taking care to restore passages to their proper places, with no prohibition whatsoever on deletion, and with the freedom to substitute other readings at one's discretion — as those authors well know.

In the very letter of ours to Sotherine, it was printed by those who so decided with an aspiration — those who derive [the name] from θαρα τὸ σῴ χὺ θέρω, whence θεξῖνος — by which words "safe and sound" and "to save" are signified, wishing thereby to attribute to it the name of a most illustrious family. Yet it can also be derived without aspiration from θαρα τὸ σῴξειν, whence σωτηρ. And so it may also be written without aspiration: others think it should be written with a D, from the same rationale,

namely the relationship that exists between the letters T and D, or they argue on the basis of a variant etymology. But we, content with the kernel of the matter and not much caring about such husks, do not attach great importance to this. Nevertheless, let each person (I place no obstacle in anyone's way) satisfy his own taste in this as in other matters, and advance his own literary endeavor to the best of his ability.
